topic.title: Classicism
topic.framework: The fixed base is Bacon and Dorr’s Classicism (C) in their relational type system. Types are generated from e and t by forming sigma→tau when tau is not e; every non-base type therefore ends in t. C is the smallest H-theory containing Logical Equivalence (Classicism, §1.3): lambda abstractions of H-equivalent formulas are identical. Preserve the theoremhood side condition; equivalence under optional assumptions does not satisfy it.

principles.name: Actual Profile
principles.statement: Every finite tuple has a true relational profile entailing every relation it instantiates; the tuple may be empty.
principles.formal: $\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,Y[\bar x]\land\forall Z^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,Z[\bar x]\to Y\le Z$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, n. 31, p. 25.

principles.name: Actuality
principles.statement: There is a true proposition that entails every true proposition.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 25.

principles.name: Atomicity
principles.statement: Every non-bottom entity of each relational type has an atom below it.
principles.formal: $\forall x^\tau\, .\,x\le_\tau\neg_\tau x\lor\exists y^\tau\, .\,\operatorname{Atom}_\tau(y)\land y\le_\tau x\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
principles.definitions:
where $\operatorname{Atom}_	au(y):= orall z^	au\, .\,(z\le_	au y\land z
e y)\leftrightarrow z\le_	au
eg_	au z$:
the entities strictly below $y$ are exactly the bottom elements of $	au$. In particular an atom is
not itself bottom. Here $x\le_	au
eg_	au x$ says that $x$ is bottom.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 24.

references.note: Bacon states the same principle as the Weak Leibniz Biconditionals, with weak worlds in place of atoms, and notes that Classicism calls its substantive direction Atomicity.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Added the alias Weak Leibniz Biconditionals and a reference to Bacon’s 2024 book; the statement is unchanged.

principles.about:
At type $t$, entailment orders the propositions, and an atom is a maximally specific possibility: a
proposition that is possible and settles every proposition one way or the other. Atomicity says that
every possible proposition is entailed by such a possibility. So the propositions behave as if they
were sets of possible worlds, with the atoms as the worlds. At a type $\sigma\to t$ the same holds for
properties, ordered by necessary inclusion.

Atomicity says nothing about how many atoms there are or which of them obtains. That some atom is true
is Actuality. That every property of propositions has a meet is Boolean Completeness. Together the two
make the propositions isomorphic to the powerset of the atoms.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is entailed by every atom of its type is the top element of that type.
variants.formal: $\forall x^\tau\, .\,(\forall y^\tau\, .\,\operatorname{Atom}_\tau(y)\to y\le_\tau x)\to\neg_\tau x\le_\tau x\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence:
In C each relational type is a Boolean algebra under $\le_\tau$, with $\neg_\tau$ an order-reversing
involution; $x\le_\tau\neg_\tau x$ says that $x$ is the bottom element, and $\neg_\tau x\le_\tau x$
that it is the top. An atom $y$ is not bottom (take $z:=y$ in the definition). It also lies below
$z$ or below $\neg_\tau z$ for every $z$: the meet $y\land z$ lies below $y$, so it is either $y$
itself or bottom.

Official form to dual form. Suppose every atom lies below $x$. Apply Atomicity to $\neg_\tau x$. If
$\neg_\tau x$ is bottom, $x$ is top. Otherwise some atom lies below $\neg_\tau x$ and below $x$, hence
below bottom, which is impossible.

Dual form to official form. Suppose $x$ is not bottom but no atom lies below it. Then every atom lies
below $\neg_\tau x$, so by the dual form $\neg_\tau x$ is top and $x$ is bottom, a contradiction.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is entailed by every atom is necessary.
variants.formal: $\forall p\, .\,(\forall q\, .\,\operatorname{Atom}_t(q)\to q\le p)\to\Box p$
variants.equivalence: The argument for the dual form of Atomicity, at type $t$, where $\neg p\le p$ says that $p$ is necessary.

principles.name: Atomlessness
principles.statement: Atomlessness in the displayed closed propositional formulation.
principles.formal: $\forall p\, .\,\Diamond p\to\exists q\, .\,\Diamond q\land q\le p\land q\ne p$

principles.name: Axiom of Infinity (type e)
principles.statement: There are not finitely many individuals. No finite cardinality holds of the universal property, so the domain of the type cannot be exhausted by finitely many steps from the empty property.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 19 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 47, p. 32.

references.note: The draft's informal infinity claim, which the map had recorded only in its schematic form.

principles.notes: See Background for $\mathbf{0}$, $\operatorname{Suc}$ and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$. The quantified form is what is normally meant by an axiom of infinity. It implies the schema of the same name, and the converse fails by a compactness argument, so the two are kept as separate principles. Possible Infinity (type e), this axiom under a diamond, is recorded as a separate principle.

principles.name: Axiom of Infinity (type t)
principles.statement: There are not finitely many propositions. No finite cardinality holds of the universal property, so the domain of the type cannot be exhausted by finitely many steps from the empty property.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 19 September 2026.

principles.name: BF
principles.statement: The Barcan Formula at every type. The predicate formulation closes the formula schema using lambda abstraction.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Proposition 2.1, pp. 20–21.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: BF for relations with any finite number of arguments.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Box X[\bar x])\to\Box(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar x])$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Conversely, apply BF one variable at a time from the innermost. From $\forall x_1\ldots x_n\, .\,\Box X[\bar x]$, BF at $\sigma_n$, applied to $\lambda x_n\, .\,X[x_1\ldots x_n]$, gives $\forall x_1\ldots x_{n-1}\, .\,\Box\forall x_n\, .\,X[\bar x]$; repeat $n$ times. For the empty tuple both sides are $\Box X$.

Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=

variants.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Diamond(\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar x])\to\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Diamond X[\bar x]$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=

eg r\le

principles.name: BF (relational types)
principles.statement: The Barcan Formula at every relational type, that is, at every type other than e.
principles.formal: $\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\Box Xx)\to\Box(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,Xx)\qquad(\sigma\ne e)$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 11 October 2026.

references.note: Bacon's theorem concludes □BF at every relational type.

principles.notes: BF with its type variable restricted to the relational types, between BF and BF (type t). Bacon's Theorem 8.2 derives its necessitation from □Strong Leibniz and Rigid Comprehension. It does not imply BF: in full-two-object-chain-new-individual it holds, necessarily, while BF fails at type e. Whether BF (type t) implies it is open; every model on the map that satisfies BF (type t) satisfies BF.

principles.name: BF (type t)
principles.statement: BF (type t) in the displayed closed propositional formulation.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, p. 59.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If possibly some proposition has a property, then some proposition possibly has it.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{tt}\, .\,\Diamond(\exists p\, .\,Xp)\to\exists p\, .\,\Diamond Xp$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$ and $q\le r\leftrightarrow
eg r\le
eg q$. This yields the other form, and the same steps lead back.

principles.name: Boolean Completeness
principles.statement: Every property of entities of a relational type has a greatest lower bound in that type.
principles.definitions:
where $\operatorname{GLB}_\tau(y,X):=\forall z^\tau\, .\,(\forall w^\tau\, .\,Xw\to z\le_\tau w)\leftrightarrow
z\le_\tau y$: the lower bounds of $X$ are exactly the entities below $y$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, pp. 23–24.
principles.about:
Classicism already makes each relational type a Boolean algebra under entailment, with finite meets
and joins: conjunction, disjunction and negation, pointwise at types $\sigma\to t$. Boolean
Completeness adds infinitary meets. However many entities a property collects, there is a strongest
entity entailed by all of them, the conjunction of the property's instances at type $t$. It is
needed whenever a construction conjoins an arbitrary collection of propositions, for instance in
building a world as the conjunction of all truths.

It fails in most of the finite-support action models, where the would-be meet of an infinite property need
not be pinned down by any finite set. Dorr's symmetric models show that it does not bring Rigid
Comprehension with it.

variants.name: Least-upper-bound form
variants.statement: Every property of entities of a relational type has a least upper bound in that type.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{\tau t}\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,\operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X)\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.definitions:
where $\operatorname{LUB}_\tau(y,X):=\forall z^\tau\, .\,(\forall w^\tau\, .\,Xw\to w\le_\tau z)\leftrightarrow
y\le_\tau z$: the upper bounds of $X$ are exactly the entities above $y$.
variants.equivalence:
Negation reverses the order and is an involution in C, so it exchanges least upper bounds and
greatest lower bounds. Given $X^{\tau t}$, let $X^\neg:=\lambda z\, .\,X(\neg_\tau z)$. For any $z$,
$z$ is an upper bound of $X$ iff $\neg_\tau z$ is a lower bound of $X^\neg$. So if $y$ is a greatest
lower bound of $X^\neg$, then for every $z$: $z$ is an upper bound of $X$ iff
$\neg_\tau z\le_\tau y$ iff $\neg_\tau y\le_\tau z$. That is, $\neg_\tau y$ is a least upper bound
of $X$. The converse direction is symmetric. Each instance at $\tau$ uses the other form only at
the same $\tau$.

Background records the same equivalence where it defines $\operatorname{LUB}$.

principles.name: Boolean Completeness (type t)
principles.statement: Boolean Completeness (type t) in the displayed closed propositional formulation.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, pp. 23–26; Appendix D, n. 92, p. 74.

variants.name: Least-upper-bound form
variants.statement: Every property of propositions has a least upper bound.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{tt}\, .\,\exists p\, .\,\operatorname{LUB}_t(p,X)$
variants.equivalence: The argument for the least-upper-bound form of Boolean Completeness, at type $t$.

principles.name: Broad Necessitism
principles.statement: Every entity of an type is necessarily identical to something.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.5, p. 19.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every tuple of entities is necessarily identical to some tuple.
variants.formal: $\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Box(\exists\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar y=\bar x)$
variants.equivalence: Both forms are theorems of C, so they are equivalent there. Take $\bar y:=\bar x$ coordinatewise.

principles.name: CBF
principles.statement: The Converse Barcan Formula at every type.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.5, p. 19.

variants.name: Polyadic form

variants.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar x])\to(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Box X[\bar x])$
variants.equivalence: Both forms are theorems of C, so they are equivalent there. The polyadic form also follows from the original by instantiating one variable at a time.

variants.formal: $\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\exists x^\sigma\, .\,\Diamond Xx)\to\Diamond(\exists x^\sigma\, .\,Xx)$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=

Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=

principles.name: Converse Witnessed Possibility
principles.statement: The converse of Witnessed Possibility, with precisely the same formula, type and constant side conditions.
principles.formal: $\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\to(\exists\bar x\, .\,P)\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, n. 57, p. 38.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If a pure formula holds of everything, it is necessary of any distinct constants.
variants.formal: $(\forall\bar x\, .\,P)\to\Box P[\bar c/\bar x]\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: Countable Boolean Completeness
principles.statement: Every countable property of entities of a relational type has a least upper bound in that type, where a property is countable relative to a type $\sigma$ when it injects into the finite cardinalities of properties of type $\sigma$; one instance for each $\sigma$.
sources: Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, §3.1, eq. (10), p. 8; Definition 6, p. 13.

references.note: The source states the principle for property types $\sigma t$ with least upper bounds; the map ranges over every relational type, as its Boolean Completeness does. The source leaves the number type $\nu$, $0$ and successor as parameters; the map takes them to be $(\sigma t)t$, $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ for every type $\sigma$, a schema in $\sigma$.

principles.notes: See Background for $\operatorname{Ctbl}$ and $\operatorname{LUB}$. The restriction of Boolean Completeness to countable properties; the least-upper-bound form is used to match the source, and is equivalent in C to a greatest-lower-bound form, since the pointwise negation of a countable property is countable. The source's hypothesis that the properties form a countably complete Boolean algebra modulo necessary equivalence. Countability is measured at every type $\sigma$: where $\sigma$ has only finitely many members the instances are trivial, so the principle has content whenever some type is infinite, not only when there are infinitely many individuals. It suffices for the Necessity of Arithmetic at each $\sigma$ and is therefore incompatible with Maximalist Classicism.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
changes.summary: Made the type at which countability is measured schematic. The principle had fixed the source's number type at $(et)t$, so countable meant injectable into the finite cardinalities of individuals, and with finitely many individuals the principle held trivially. The old principle is the instance $\sigma=e$ of the new one, which is therefore stronger; verdicts that the old principle holds because there are few individuals are withdrawn.

variants.name: Greatest-lower-bound form
variants.statement: Every countable property of entities of a relational type has a greatest lower bound in that type.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Ctbl}_{\sigma,\tau}(X)\to\exists y^\tau\, .\,\operatorname{GLB}_\tau(y,X)\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence:
As for the least-upper-bound form of Boolean Completeness: negation exchanges least upper bounds of $X$ and greatest lower bounds of $X^
eg:=\lambda z\, .\,X(
eg_	au z)$. Negation is a bijection between the instances of $X$ and of $X^
eg$, so composing it with an injection into the natural numbers counted at $\sigma$ shows that $X^
eg$ is countable relative to $\sigma$ iff $X$ is.

principles.name: ND
principles.statement: Distinct things of any type are necessarily distinct.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–22.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Distinct tuples of entities are necessarily distinct.
variants.formal: $\forall\bar x\,\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar x\ne\bar y\to\Box(\bar x\ne\bar y)$
variants.equivalence:
The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Conversely, if $ ar x
e ar y$ then $x_i
e y_i$ for some $i$, and ND at $\sigma_i$ gives $\Box(x_i
e y_i)$, hence $\Box( ar x
e ar y)$. For the empty tuple, $ ar x
e ar y$ is false.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Things of any type that could be identical are identical.
variants.formal: $\forall x y^\sigma\, .\,\Diamond(x=y)\to x=y$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of one form is the contrapositive of the corresponding instance of the other.

variants.name: Dual polyadic form
variants.statement: Tuples that could be identical are identical.
variants.formal: $\forall\bar x\,\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\Diamond(\bar x=\bar y)\to\bar x=\bar y$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of one form is the contrapositive of the corresponding instance of the other. Combined with the polyadic form, this gives the equivalence with the official form.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Propositions that could be identical are identical.
variants.formal: $\forall p q\, .\,\Diamond(p=q)\to p=q$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of one form is the contrapositive of the corresponding instance of the other.

principles.name: Truth implies ND-necessity
principles.statement: Every truth is ND-necessary, that is, necessary under the distinctness-preserving modality.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix E, p. 83.
principles.notes: Formerly named Distinctness-preserving collapse; renamed on 14 October 2026 when the Varieties of necessity category was added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun. The id is unchanged.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is possible under the distinctness-preserving modality is true.
variants.formal: $\forall p\, .\,\Diamond_{\ne}p\to p$

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
changes.summary: Renamed from Distinctness-preserving collapse to Truth implies ND-necessity and moved to the new category Varieties of necessity; statement reworded, formal statement unchanged.

principles.name: Maximalism (pure)
principles.statement: Every closed pure identity not provable in C is false. The non-theorem condition is metalinguistic.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.4, pp. 35–36.
principles.notes: The reference theory in the side condition is the fixed background C. Until 8 October 2026 this was Distinctness Maximalism (pure), with Possibility Maximalism (pure) a separate principle, provably equivalent; they were unified at Cian Dorr's direction, the distinctness form official since it remains the interesting one over logics weaker than Classicism.

variants.name: Possibility form
variants.statement: Every closed pure sentence consistent with C is possible.
variants.formal: $\Diamond P\quad(P\text{ closed and pure; }C+P\text{ consistent})$
variants.equivalence:
Possibility to Distinctness: if a closed identity $A=B$ is not a theorem of C, its negation is consistent with C, so the possibility form gives $\Diamond(A
e B)$; by NI, $A=B$ would make this impossible, so $A
e B$. Distinctness to Possibility: if $P$ is consistent with C, the closed identity $
eg P=	op$ is not a theorem of C, so the distinctness form gives $
eg P
e	op$, equivalently $\Diamond P$.

principles.name: Maximalism (signature Σ)
principles.statement: The Maximalism schema for the fixed nonlogical signature Σ: every closed identity of its language not provable in C(Σ) is false.
principles.formal: $A\ne B\quad(A=B\text{ closed in }\mathcal L(\Sigma);\ C(\Sigma)\nvdash A=B)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 37–39.
principles.notes: Until 8 October 2026 this was Distinctness Maximalism (signature Σ), with Possibility Maximalism (signature Σ) a separate principle, provably equivalent; they were unified at Cian Dorr's direction.

variants.name: Possibility form
variants.statement: Every closed sentence of the language of Σ consistent with C(Σ) is possible.
variants.formal: $\Diamond P\quad(P\text{ closed in }\mathcal L(\Sigma);\ C(\Sigma)+P\text{ consistent})$
variants.equivalence:
Possibility to Distinctness: if a closed identity $A=B$ is not a theorem of C(Σ), its negation is consistent with C(Σ), so the possibility form gives $\Diamond(A
e B)$; by NI, $A=B$ would make this impossible, so $A
e B$. Distinctness to Possibility: if $P$ is consistent with C(Σ), the closed identity $
eg P=	op$ is not a theorem of C(Σ), so the distinctness form gives $
eg P
e	op$, equivalently $\Diamond P$.

principles.name: Existence
principles.statement: Every type is inhabited.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.1, p. 7.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every finite tuple of types is jointly inhabited.
variants.formal: $\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar x=\bar x$
variants.equivalence: Both forms are theorems of C, so they are equivalent there. The polyadic form is the conjunction of the original at each $\sigma_i$; for the empty tuple it is $\top$.

principles.name: Extensionality
principles.statement: At each relational type, coextensive relations are identical; include the nullary propositional case.
principles.formal: $\forall X Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])\to X=Y$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.4, pp. 15–16.

principles.name: 5-necessity implies ND-necessity
principles.statement: Whatever is 5-necessary is ND-necessary.
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. The converse implication is a theorem of C (Background, Hats, two-hat necessity and 5-necessity), so this principle says that the two operators are coextensive.
sources: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne, and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, pp. 400–409 (definitions of the hat operation and of the 5-necessity operator; the principles themselves are not stated there).

principles.name: 5-necessity implies two-hat necessity
principles.statement: Whatever is 5-necessary is two-hat necessary.
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. The converse implication is a theorem of C (Background, Hats, two-hat necessity and 5-necessity), so this principle says that the two operators are coextensive.
sources: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne, and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, pp. 400–409 (definitions of the hat operation and of the 5-necessity operator; the principles themselves are not stated there).

principles.name: Fregean Axiom
principles.statement: Materially equivalent propositions are identical.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.4, pp. 15–16.

principles.name: Functional Choice
principles.statement: Every serial binary relation admits a selecting operation. Its output type is relational, as required by the type system.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every serial relation from tuples admits a selecting operation of several arguments.
variants.formal: $\forall U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Serial}(U)\to\exists X^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,\forall\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(U[\bar y])(X[\bar y])\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Given a serial $U$, put $U':=\lambda A\,y\, .\,(\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land(U[\bar x])y)\lor\neg\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}$, of type $(\bar\sigma t)\tau t$, which is serial. The original form gives $X'$ selecting from $U'$, and $X:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,X'(H_{\bar y})$ selects from $U$.

principles.name: Functionality
principles.statement: Operations with the same value on every argument are identical. The output type is relational.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.4, pp. 15–16, especially n. 18.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Operations of several arguments with the same value on every tuple of arguments are identical.
variants.formal: $\forall X Y^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]=Y[\bar z])\to X=Y\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Conversely, by induction on the length of the tuple, one argument at a time. If $X[z_1\bar z']=Y[z_1\bar z']$ for all $z_1,\bar z'$, then for each $z_1$ the operations $Xz_1$ and $Yz_1$, of type $\sigma_2\cdots\sigma_n\tau$, agree on every tuple, so they are identical by the induction hypothesis. Functionality at $\sigma_1$ then gives $X=Y$. For the empty tuple the condition is $X=Y$ itself.

principles.name: Gallin Extensional Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation is coextensive with one that is persistent and has a persistent pointwise negation. This is the source’s comparison with Gallin’s different rigidity convention.
principles.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)\land\operatorname{Persistent}(\neg Y)\land(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 37, p. 28.

references.locator: p. 77, as described in Classicism n. 37

principles.name: NI
principles.statement: Identity is necessary at every type.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, p. 22.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Identical tuples of entities are necessarily identical.
variants.formal: $\forall\bar x\,\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\bar x=\bar y\to\Box(\bar x=\bar y)$
variants.equivalence: Both forms are theorems of C, so they are equivalent there. Directly: $\bar x=\bar y$ is a conjunction of identities, each necessary, and a conjunction of necessities is necessary.

principles.name: Independence (signature Σ)
principles.statement: No constant of Sigma is a pure operation applied to other constants: for a closed pure term A and distinct constants c, d_1,…,d_n with n ≥ 0, c differs from A applied to the d’s. With n = 0, no constant denotes a pure entity.
principles.formal: $c\ne A\,d_1\cdots d_n\quad(A\text{ closed and pure};\ c,d_1,\ldots,d_n\text{ distinct constants};\ n\ge0)$
sources: Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §4, p. 568 and n. 53.
principles.notes: Bacon’s independence of the fundamental, read for the constants of a fundamental language; his n. 53 derives it from Logical Necessity. The constant c has a relational type, since the applied term does.

principles.name: Inextensible Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a inextensible one.
principles.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Inextensible}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 38, p. 29.

principles.name: Infinity Schema (type e)
principles.statement: There are arbitrarily many pairwise distinct entities of this fixed type; one sentence for each positive integer n.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 47, p. 32.
principles.notes: Schema-level reading of the source’s informal infinity claim; no choice-dependent equivalence with Dedekind infinity is assumed. One sentence for each n, so it is weaker than the quantified Axiom of Infinity (type e), which implies it. The converse fails by a compactness argument, which the map does not yet witness with a model.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Renamed from “Infinity (type e)” to mark it as the schema, now that the quantified Axiom of Infinity (type e) is recorded separately. The id, the statement and every connection are unchanged.

principles.name: Infinity Schema (type t)
principles.statement: There are arbitrarily many pairwise distinct entities of this fixed type; one sentence for each positive integer n.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 47, p. 32.
principles.notes: Schema-level reading of the source’s informal infinity claim; no choice-dependent equivalence with Dedekind infinity is assumed. One sentence for each n, so it is weaker than the quantified Axiom of Infinity (type t), which implies it. The converse fails by a compactness argument, which the map does not yet witness with a model.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Renamed from “Infinity (type t)” to mark it as the schema, now that the quantified Axiom of Infinity (type t) is recorded separately. The id, the statement and every connection are unchanged.

principles.name: Intensional Choice
principles.statement: If a property is necessarily instantiated, then some property entailing it is necessarily uniquely instantiated.
principles.formal: $\forall F^{\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\exists x^\sigma\, .\,Fx)\to\exists G^{\sigma t}\, .\,G\le F\land\Box\exists x^\sigma\, .\,(Gx\land\forall y^\sigma\, .\,Gy\to y=x)$
sources: Andrew Bacon, Could the truths of mathematics have been different?, draft of 9 October 2025, §6, p. 27.

references.note: Introduced as a modal version of choice, used with □Rigid Comprehension and Mathematical Possibilism for the contingency of CH (Theorem 6.1).

principles.notes: The source motivates it as a modalized generalization of interworld choice, which selects at each world one instance of a property instantiated at every world; the modal formulation needs no world propositions. The type $\sigma$ may be $e$. The selected property is unboxed: it exists at the evaluation point, but its unique instance may vary from world to world.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: If a relation is necessarily instantiated, then some relation entailing it is necessarily uniquely instantiated.
variants.formal: $\forall F^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,F[\bar x])\to\exists G^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,G\le F\land\Box\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(G[\bar x]\land\forall\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,G[\bar y]\to\bar y=\bar x)$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Given $F$, the property $F':=\lambda A\, .\,\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land F[\bar x]$ of type $(\bar\sigma t)t$ is necessarily instantiated. The original form at $\bar\sigma t$ gives $G'\le F'$ necessarily uniquely instantiated. Put $G:=\lambda\bar x\, .\,G'(H_{\bar x})$. Then $G\le F$. At each world the unique instance of $G'$ is a code $H_{\bar x}$, since $G'\le F'$, and by injectivity of coding $\bar x$ is then the unique instance of $G$.

principles.name: Intensionality
principles.statement: Necessarily coextensive relations are identical.
principles.formal: $\forall X Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\Box(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])\to X=Y$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.5, pp. 17–18.

principles.name: Logical Necessity
principles.statement: The Logical Necessity schema: necessity at distinct matching constants is equivalent to universal truth of the pure-formula. Preserve the side conditions of Witnessed Possibility.
principles.formal: $\Box P[\bar c/\bar x]\leftrightarrow(\forall\bar x\, .\,P)\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, n. 57, p. 38.

references.locator: Logical Necessity, cited in Classicism n. 57
references.note: Stated for a fundamental language; Bacon’s restatements with fundamentality and purity predicates (pp. 546–547) are not on the map.
Stated for a fundamental language; Bacon’s restatements with fundamentality and purity predicates (pp. 546–547) are not on the map.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Added direct locators in Logical Combinatorialism, read on this date; the statement is unchanged.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: A pure formula is possible of distinct constants iff it holds of something.
variants.formal: $\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\leftrightarrow(\exists\bar x\, .\,P)\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: B
principles.statement: Every true proposition is necessarily possible.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Proposition 2.2, p. 22.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is possibly necessary is true.
variants.formal: $\forall p\, .\,\Diamond\Box p\to p$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$ and $q\le r\leftrightarrow
eg r\le
eg q$. This yields the other form, and the same steps lead back.

principles.statement: Every possible proposition is necessarily possible.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Proposition 2.2, p. 22.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is possibly necessary is necessary.
variants.formal: $\forall p\, .\,\Diamond\Box p\to\Box p$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$ and $q\le r\leftrightarrow
eg r\le
eg q$. This yields the other form, and the same steps lead back.

principles.statement: Necessary propositions are necessarily necessary.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.5, p. 17.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is possibly possible is possible.
variants.formal: $\forall p\, .\,\Diamond\Diamond p\to\Diamond p$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$ and $q\le r\leftrightarrow
eg r\le
eg q$. This yields the other form, and the same steps lead back.

principles.name: Modal Freedom (signature Σ)
principles.statement: For pure formulas P and Q with free variables among the disjoint tuples x and y, and distinct constants c and d of matching types, if P is possible at c and Q is possible at d then P and Q are jointly possible there.
principles.formal: $\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\land\Diamond Q[\bar d/\bar y]\to\Diamond(P[\bar c/\bar x]\land Q[\bar d/\bar y])\quad(P,Q\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x\text{ resp. }\bar y;\ \bar c\bar d\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §3, pp. 556–557, principle (5) and its generalization.
principles.notes: Bacon’s formalization of Schaffer’s Modal Freedom, stated for two distinct constants R and S of a fundamental language. The instance with no constants is equivalent to No Pure Contingency.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If a disjunction of pure formulas about disjoint constants is necessary, one of the disjuncts is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box(P[\bar c/\bar x]\lor Q[\bar d/\bar y])\to\Box P[\bar c/\bar x]\lor\Box Q[\bar d/\bar y]\quad(P,Q\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x\text{ resp. }\bar y;\ \bar c\bar d\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
variants.equivalence:
The instance of either form at $
eg P,
eg Q$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P,Q$.

principles.name: K
principles.statement: Necessity distributes over implication.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.5, p. 16.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If a conditional is necessary, the possibility of its antecedent brings the possibility of its consequent.
variants.formal: $\forall p q\, .\,\Box(p\to q)\to(\Diamond p\to\Diamond q)$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at $
eg q,
eg p$ and contrapose the inner conditional, using $\Box(
eg q	o
eg p)\leftrightarrow\Box(p	o q)$ and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$. This yields the other form.

principles.name: T
principles.statement: Necessary propositions are true.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.5, p. 16.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Every truth is possible.
variants.formal: $\forall p\, .\,p\to\Diamond p$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$ and $q\le r\leftrightarrow
eg r\le
eg q$. This yields the other form, and the same steps lead back.

principles.name: Modal Well-Ordering
principles.statement: Every type, including e, has a relation that is necessarily a well-order of it.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 8 October 2026.
principles.notes: WO is defined in Background. The relation exists at the evaluation point, and at each world it well-orders what there is there; the order it induces may differ from world to world. A well-order need not be necessarily one, since distinct relata can be identical at other worlds, so this is stronger than Well-Ordering. It gives Intensional Choice at once (select the least instance), and it follows from Well-Ordering with Weak Rigid Comprehension and BF. It implies its own necessitation by 4, since $\Box\operatorname{WO}(R)$ gives $\Box\Box\operatorname{WO}(R)$, so no boxed form is recorded.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
changes.summary: □Modal Well-Ordering retired, since Modal Well-Ordering implies it by 4; its result giving □Intensional Choice now starts from Modal Well-Ordering.

principles.name: Modalized Fregean Axiom
principles.statement: Necessarily equivalent propositions are identical.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.5, p. 18.

principles.name: Modalized Functionality
principles.statement: Necessarily co-functional operations of function types are identical.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §1.5, p. 18 and n. 22.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Necessarily co-functional operations of several arguments are identical.
variants.formal: $\forall X Y^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]=Y[\bar z])\to X=Y\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence: Both forms are theorems of C, so they are equivalent there. The polyadic form also follows from the original one argument at a time, as for Functionality, with the box carried through.

principles.name: Modalized Plenitude
principles.statement: If necessarily each argument has a value that is necessarily the relation's unique value for it, then some operation necessarily represents the relation. Its output type is relational, as required by the type system.
principles.formal: $\forall U^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\bigl(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,\Box((Ux)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z)\bigr)\to\exists X^{\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\forall y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Xx\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
sources: Cian Dorr, 28 September 2026, principle and the proof for output type t.

references.note: Plenitude, of which this is the modalized form. Unlike Plenitude it is a theorem of C.

principles.notes: A theorem of C (classicism-implies-modalized-plenitude-r), recorded because it is an important fact about the logic even though it does not change the shape of the map. The inner box is what makes it provable: the unique value is then necessarily unique, and a definable operation can pick it out. Plenitude, which asks only for actual functionality and an actual representation, is not a theorem.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Modalized Plenitude for relations from tuples.
variants.formal: $\forall U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\bigl(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\exists y^\tau\, .\,\Box((U[\bar x])y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(U[\bar x])z\to y=z)\bigr)\to\exists X^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,\Box\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\forall y^\tau\, .\,(U[\bar x])y\leftrightarrow y=X[\bar x]\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence: Both forms are theorems of C, so they are equivalent there. The polyadic form also follows from the original one argument at a time, using each step's instance under the box.

principles.name: Modalized Relational Choice
principles.statement: Every necessarily serial relation is entailed by a necessarily functional relation.
principles.formal: $\forall R^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\operatorname{Serial}(R)\to\exists S^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\operatorname{Functional}(S)\land S\le R$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 11 October 2026.
principles.notes: Due to Cian Dorr. It implies Intensional Choice (its polyadic form at the empty tuple is Intensional Choice) and Relational Choice; □Relational Choice with Intensional Choice implies it, the necessarily instantiated property of being a functional subrelation of a necessarily serial relation being necessarily uniquely instantiated below. Whether unboxed Relational Choice with Intensional Choice suffices is open: the argument needs the functional subrelations to exist at every world. Boxed, □Modalized Relational Choice is equivalent to □Relational Choice with □Intensional Choice.

variants.name: Entailing form
variants.statement: Every relation is entailed by one that necessarily relates each thing bearing the first relation to something to exactly one thing.
variants.formal: $\forall R^{\sigma\tau t}\, \exists S^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,S\le R\land\Box\forall x^\sigma\, .\,(\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Rx)y)\to\exists y^\tau\, .\,(Sx)y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(Sx)z\to y=z$
variants.equivalence: From the entailing form: if $R$ is necessarily serial, an $S$ as there is necessarily functional. To the entailing form: given $R$, $R':=\lambda xy\,.\,\neg\exists z\,(Rx)z\lor(Rx)y$ is necessarily serial, every type being inhabited in C; take a necessarily functional $S'\le R'$ and put $S:=\lambda xy\,.\,(S'x)y\land(Rx)y$. Then $S\le R$, and necessarily, if $x$ bears $R$ to something, the unique $S'$-value of $x$ is an $R$-value, so the unique $S$-value.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every necessarily serial relation from tuples is entailed by a necessarily functional one.
variants.formal: $\forall R^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\operatorname{Serial}(R)\to\exists S^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\Box\operatorname{Functional}(S)\land S\le R$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Conversely, code tuples by their haecceities $H_{\bar x}$ (Background, Polyadic forms). Given a necessarily serial $R$, put $R':=\lambda A\,y\,.\,(\exists\bar x\,.\,A=H_{\bar x}\land(R[\bar x])y)\lor\neg\exists\bar x\,.\,A=H_{\bar x}$, of input type $\bar\sigma t$. It is necessarily serial: at each world a code is the haecceity of a tuple there, and $R$ is serial there. The original form gives a necessarily functional $S'\le R'$, and $S:=\lambda\bar x\,y\,.\,(S'H_{\bar x})y$ is necessarily functional and entails $R$, the coding being injective. At the empty tuple the polyadic form is Intensional Choice.

variants.name: Polyadic entailing form
variants.statement: The entailing form for relations from tuples.
variants.formal: $\forall R^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, \exists S^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,S\le R\land\Box\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(\exists y^\tau\, .\,(R[\bar x])y)\to\exists y^\tau\, .\,(S[\bar x])y\land\forall z^\tau\, .\,(S[\bar x])z\to y=z$
variants.equivalence: The two equivalences above combined: the polyadic form and the polyadic entailing form are related as the original form and the entailing form, by the same construction with tuples in place of single arguments.

principles.name: □Actuality
principles.statement: Necessarily, there is a true proposition that entails every true proposition.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Every closed instance of the dual form of Atomicity is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of the dual form of Atomicity}$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of the dual form of Atomicity is derivable in C from finitely many instances of the official form, and conversely; the derivation is on the page of Atomicity. Necessitating it and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

principles.name: □Truth implies ND-necessity
principles.statement: Necessarily, every truth is ND-necessary. In C this is the identity $\Box_{\ne}=\lambda p\, .\,p$.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix E, p. 83 (the unboxed principle, under its former name Distinctness-preserving collapse).

references.note: Formulation of the unboxed principle; the boxed form was added with the Varieties of necessity category.

principles.notes: Box the closed sentence Truth implies ND-necessity. Added 14 October 2026 to match the boxed forms of the other collapse principles, at the suggestion of Christopher Sun and Cian Dorr. Equivalent to the conjunction of □5-necessity implies ND-necessity and □Truth implies 5-necessity.

variants.equivalence: The dual form is derivable from the official form in C and conversely, as on the page of Truth implies ND-necessity; necessitating the derivation and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

principles.name: □Extensionality
principles.statement: Necessarily, at each relational type, coextensive relations are identical, including in the nullary propositional case.

principles.name: □5-necessity implies ND-necessity
principles.statement: Necessarily, whatever is 5-necessary is ND-necessary. In C this is the identity $\Box_5=\Box_{\ne}$.
sources: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne, and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, pp. 400–409 (definitions of the hat operation and of the 5-necessity operator; the principles themselves are not stated there).
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. Box the closed sentence; since identity of operators in C is necessary coextensiveness, this is the identity $\Box_5=\Box_{\ne}$.

principles.name: □5-necessity implies two-hat necessity
principles.statement: Necessarily, whatever is 5-necessary is two-hat necessary. In C this is the identity $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$.
sources: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne, and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, pp. 400–409 (definitions of the hat operation and of the 5-necessity operator; the principles themselves are not stated there).
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. Box the closed sentence; since identity of operators in C is necessary coextensiveness, this is the identity $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$.

principles.name: □Strong Actuality

principles.notes: Strong Actuality has no type parameters, so its necessitation is the single sentence $\Box\exists p\, .\,p\land\Box\forall q\, .\,p\le q\lor p\le\neg q$.

principles.name: □Strong Leibniz Biconditionals
principles.statement: Necessarily, at each relational type, every possible entity (one distinct from bottom) is entailed by a strong world: a possible entity that necessarily entails every entity of the type or its negation.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals}$
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 166, 169–170.
principles.notes: The boxed form is the one Theorem 8.2 of the book connects with □BF and □Atomicity. Since strong worlds are only required to be possible, not necessarily possible, the unboxed form does not yield 5; Exercise 8.13 shows that requiring necessarily weak worlds does.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Restated the statement as the necessitation of the base principle's statement, in place of a generic description of necessitation; the formal statement is unchanged.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Every closed instance of the dual form of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of the dual form of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals}$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of the dual form of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals is derivable in C from finitely many instances of the official form, and conversely; the derivation is on the page of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals. Necessitating it and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

principles.name: □Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t)
principles.statement: Necessarily, every possible proposition is entailed by a strong world proposition, one that is possible and necessarily entails every proposition or its negation.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t)}$
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 164–166.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Every closed instance of the dual form of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t) is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of the dual form of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t)}$

Necessitating it and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

principles.name: □Tame Rigidity
principles.statement: Every closed instance of Tame Rigidity is necessary. Box the entire object-variable closure; retain the same type range and other schema side conditions.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Tame Rigidity}$
sources: Christopher Sun, Possible Worlds Without Atomicity, draft of September 2026.
principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of Tame Rigidity. Type quantifiers remain outside the box.

principles.name: □Tractarianism
principles.statement: Necessarily, a proposition entailing every instance of a property entails its universal generalization.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.1, pp. 21–23; §§2.2–2.3, pp. 25–34.
principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of Tractarianism. Type quantifiers and formula side conditions remain outside the box.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Restated the statement as the necessitation of the base principle's statement, in place of a generic description of necessitation; the formal statement is unchanged.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every closed instance of the polyadic form of Tractarianism is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of the polyadic form of Tractarianism}$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of the polyadic form of Tractarianism is derivable in C from finitely many instances of the original form, and conversely; the derivations are on the page of the unboxed principle. Necessitating them and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Every closed instance of the dual form of Tractarianism is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of the dual form of Tractarianism}$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of the dual form of Tractarianism is derivable in C from finitely many instances of the official form, and conversely; the derivation is on the page of Tractarianism. Necessitating it and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

variants.name: Dual polyadic form
variants.statement: Every closed instance of the dual polyadic form of Tractarianism is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of the dual polyadic form of Tractarianism}$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of the dual polyadic form of Tractarianism is derivable in C from finitely many instances of the official form, and conversely; the derivation is on the page of Tractarianism. Necessitating it and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

principles.name: □Transversal Choice
principles.statement: Necessarily, every equivalence relation, at any type including e, has a transversal, that is, a property with exactly one instance in each of its cells.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Transversal Choice}$
sources: Christopher Sun, 26 September 2026, in connection with Transversal.
principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of Transversal Choice. Type quantifiers remain outside the box. Unlike Transversal Choice itself, this makes the transversal condition hold at every accessible world, for every relation that is an equivalence relation there.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every closed instance of the polyadic form of Transversal Choice is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of the polyadic form of Transversal Choice}$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of the polyadic form of Transversal Choice is derivable in C from finitely many instances of the original form, and conversely; the derivations are on the page of the unboxed principle. Necessitating them and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

principles.name: □Transversal
principles.statement: Necessarily, there is a property of properties that picks out exactly one property from each coextension class, that is, exactly one property coextensive with any given property.
sources: Christopher Sun, 26 September 2026.
principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of Transversal. Type quantifiers remain outside the box.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every closed instance of the polyadic form of Transversal is necessary.
