variants.equivalence: Each instance of the polyadic form of Transversal is derivable in C from finitely many instances of the original form, and conversely; the derivations are on the page of the unboxed principle. Necessitating them and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

principles.name: □Truth implies 5-necessity
principles.statement: Necessarily, every truth is 5-necessary: necessary under every S5 operator. In C this is the identity $\Box_5=\lambda p\, .\,p$.
sources: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne, and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, pp. 400–409 (definitions of the hat operation and of the 5-necessity operator; the principles themselves are not stated there).
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. Box the closed sentence; since identity of operators in C is necessary coextensiveness, this is the identity $\Box_5=\lambda p\, .\,p$.

principles.name: □Truth implies two-hat necessity
principles.statement: Necessarily, every truth is two-hat necessary. In C this is the identity $\hat{\hat\Box}=\lambda p\, .\,p$.
sources: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne, and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, pp. 400–409 (definitions of the hat operation and of the 5-necessity operator; the principles themselves are not stated there).
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. Box the closed sentence; since identity of operators in C is necessary coextensiveness, this is the identity $\hat{\hat\Box}=\lambda p\, .\,p$.

principles.name: □Two-hat necessity implies ND-necessity
principles.statement: Necessarily, whatever is two-hat necessary is ND-necessary: the distinctness-preserving modality agrees with its hat. In C this is the identity $\hat{\hat\Box}=\Box_{\ne}$.
sources: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne, and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, pp. 400–409 (definitions of the hat operation and of the 5-necessity operator; the principles themselves are not stated there).
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. Box the closed sentence; since identity of operators in C is necessary coextensiveness, this is the identity $\hat{\hat\Box}=\Box_{\ne}$.

principles.name: □Vicinity
principles.statement: Necessarily, there is a true proposition that entails the possibility of each true proposition.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 27 September 2026.
principles.notes: Vicinity has no type parameters, so this is the single sentence $\Box\exists p\, .\,p\land\forall q\, .\,q\to p\le\Diamond q$.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Restated the statement as the necessitation of the base principle's statement, in place of a generic description of necessitation; the formal statement is unchanged.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
changes.summary: Added the boxed ND-necessity form as a variant, mirroring Vicinity.

variants.name: ND-necessity form
variants.statement: Every closed instance of the ND-necessity form of Vicinity is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of the ND-necessity form of Vicinity}$
variants.equivalence: The two forms of Vicinity are equivalent in C (see the page of Vicinity); necessitating the derivation and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

principles.name: □Weak Rigid Comprehension
principles.statement: Every closed instance of Weak Rigid Comprehension is necessary. Box the entire object-variable closure; retain the same type range and other schema side conditions.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Weak Rigid Comprehension}$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 2 October 2026.

references.note: Formulation of the unboxed principle.

principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of Weak Rigid Comprehension. Type quantifiers remain outside the box.

variants.name: Persistent form
variants.statement: Every closed instance of the persistent form of Weak Rigid Comprehension is necessary.
variants.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of the persistent form of Weak Rigid Comprehension}$
variants.equivalence: Each instance of the persistent form of Weak Rigid Comprehension is derivable in C from the official instance at the same type, and conversely; the derivation is on the page of Weak Rigid Comprehension. Necessitating it and applying K carries the equivalence to the boxed forms.

principles.name: □Weakly Inextensible Comprehension
principles.statement: Necessarily, every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a weakly inextensible one.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Weakly Inextensible Comprehension}$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 27 September 2026.

references.note: Source of weak inextensibility.

principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of Weakly Inextensible Comprehension. Type quantifiers and formula side conditions remain outside the box. This differs from Inextensible Comprehension, which asks for a single actual witness that is weakly inextensible at every world; here the witness may vary from world to world.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Restated the statement as the necessitation of the base principle's statement, in place of a generic description of necessitation; the formal statement is unchanged.

principles.name: □Weakly Rigid Power
principles.statement: Every closed instance of Weakly Rigid Power is necessary. Box the entire object-variable closure; retain the same type range and other schema side conditions.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Weakly Rigid Power}$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 10 October 2026.
principles.notes: Box each fully closed instance of Weakly Rigid Power. Type quantifiers remain outside the box. It is equivalent to the conjunction of □Tame Rigidity and □Rigid Power.

principles.name: □Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity
principles.statement: Every closed instance of Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity is necessary. Retain the same type range.
principles.formal: $\Box\phi\quad\text{for each closed instance }\phi\text{ of Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity}$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 10 October 2026.
principles.notes: Type quantifiers remain outside the box. Equivalent to Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity.

principles.name: □Well-Ordering
principles.statement: Necessarily, every type, including e, is well-ordered by some relation.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 8 October 2026.
principles.notes: The necessitation of Well-Ordering; the instances are closed, and type quantifiers remain outside the box. The well-order may differ from world to world. Modal Well-Ordering, which asks for one relation that is necessarily a well-order, implies it.

principles.name: Necessity of Arithmetic
principles.statement: Every arithmetical sentence is either necessarily true or necessarily false, given that possibly zero is not a successor and successor is injective on numbers, where the numbers are the finite cardinalities of properties of a type $\sigma$. One sentence for each type $\sigma$ and each arithmetical sentence at $\sigma$.
principles.formal: $\Box(I_\sigma\to A)\lor\Box(I_\sigma\to\neg A)\quad(A\text{ an arithmetical sentence at }\sigma)$
sources: Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, eq. (1), p. 2; Definition 8 and Theorem 9, pp. 19–21.

references.locator: eq. (1), p. 2; Definition 8 and Theorem 9, pp. 19–21
references.note: The source's necessity schema, with its parameters $\nu$, $0$ and successor taken to be $(\sigma t)t$, $\mathbf{0}_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ for every type $\sigma$, so that its natural numbers are the finite cardinalities of properties of type $\sigma$.

principles.notes: See Background for $I_\sigma$ and for arithmetical sentences. The antecedent $I_\sigma$ is needed because the axioms of arithmetic are not theorems of C: if there is only one entity of type $\sigma$, the second numeral is the empty cardinality, so successor is not injective. In C the first conjunct of $I^*_\sigma$ is a theorem, so $I_\sigma$ amounts to the possible injectivity of $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma$ on finite cardinalities, which Possibility Maximalism (pure) grants. Where $\sigma$ necessarily has finitely many members, $I_\sigma$ is necessarily false and the instances at $\sigma$ are trivial. Each instance is a closed pure sentence, so the schema follows from No Pure Contingency; it follows in C from Countable Boolean Completeness, at each $\sigma$ from the instances counting at the same $\sigma$, and it is incompatible with Possibility Maximalism (pure) by Gödel's first incompleteness theorem.

changes.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
changes.summary: Made the type whose finite cardinalities are the numbers schematic, as for Countable Boolean Completeness; the principle had fixed it at $e$. The old principle is the instance $\sigma=e$ of the new one.

principles.name: No Contingency (signature Σ)
principles.statement: Each closed sentence of the language of the fixed signature Sigma, if true, is necessary. A sentence schema, standing to No Pure Contingency as Possibility Maximalism (signature Σ) stands to Possibility Maximalism (pure).
principles.formal: $P\to\Box P\quad(P\text{ a closed sentence of }\mathcal L(\Sigma))$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 22 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 27 (No Pure Contingency).

references.note: The pure schema of which this is the signature version.

principles.notes: Holds in every one-world model whatever the constants denote, so it is consistent; but it is incompatible with Witnessed Possibility and hence with Logical Necessity, Separated Structure and Maximalist Classicism for Σ: a constant of relational type is possibly top and possibly not top under Witnessed Possibility, while this schema makes whichever obtains necessary.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Each closed sentence of the signature, if possible, is true.
variants.formal: $\Diamond P\to P\quad(P\text{ a closed sentence of }\mathcal L(\Sigma))$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: No Pure Contingency
principles.statement: Each closed sentence of the pure language, if true, is necessary. This is a sentence schema, not a quantifier over propositions.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.2, p. 27.

references.locator: Logical Foundations of Philosophy; cited in Classicism p. 27

references.note: The empty-tuple instance of Logical Necessity.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Added a reference to Logical Combinatorialism; the statement is unchanged.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Each closed pure sentence, if possible, is true.
variants.formal: $\Diamond P\to P\quad(P\text{ a closed pure sentence})$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: Ordinary Comprehension
principles.statement: Every well-typed formula P with distinguished variables y defines a coextensive relation; X is fresh, and any other free object variables are universally closed.
principles.formal: $\exists X\, .\,\forall\bar y\, .\,X[\bar y]\leftrightarrow P\quad(P\text{ a formula in which }X\text{ is not free})$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, p. 27.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged.

principles.name: Persistent Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a persistent one.
principles.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 38, p. 29.

principles.name: Plenitude
principles.statement: Every total single-valued binary relation is represented by an operation. Its output type is relational, as required by the type system.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every total single-valued relation from tuples is represented by an operation of several arguments.
variants.formal: $\forall U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Functional}(U)\to\exists X^{\bar\sigma\tau}\, .\,\forall\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(U[\bar y])(X[\bar y])\qquad(\tau\ne e)$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Given a functional $U$, put $U':=\lambda A\,y\, .\,(\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land(U[\bar x])y)\lor(\neg\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land y=\bot_\tau)$, which is functional by injectivity of coding; $\tau$ is relational, so $\bot_\tau$ exists. The original form at $\bar\sigma t$ gives $X'$ representing $U'$, and $X:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,X'(H_{\bar y})$ represents $U$.

principles.name: Possibility+ (pure)
principles.statement: The strengthened Possibility Maximalism schema for pure C-consistent formulas whose only free variables are the displayed individual variables; include the empty tuple.
principles.formal: $\forall x_1^e\cdots x_n^e\, .\,(\bigwedge_{i<j}x_i\ne x_j)\to\Diamond P\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }x_1\ldots x_n;\ C+P\text{ consistent};\ n\ge0)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.6, p. 41 and n. 60; Appendix E, p. 83.

references.locator: §2.6, p. 41 and n. 60; Appendix E, p. 83

principles.notes: The consistency and purity restrictions are inherited from Possibility Maximalism, which the surrounding text says this strengthens; the shortened display on p. 41 must not be read as admitting contradictory P.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged. Renamed from “Possibility+” to mark it as the pure-language version, now that Possibility+ (signature Σ) is recorded; id and connections unchanged.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If a pure formula is necessary of some individuals and its negation is consistent with C, two of those individuals are identical.
variants.formal: $\forall x_1^e\cdots x_n^e\, .\,\Box P\to\bigvee_{i<j}x_i=x_j\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }x_1\ldots x_n;\ C+\neg P\text{ consistent};\ n\ge0)$
variants.equivalence:
The instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$; $
eg P$ is pure with the same free variables. For $n=0$ the disjunction is $ ot$.

principles.name: Possibility+ (signature Σ)
principles.statement: The Possibility+ schema for the fixed nonlogical signature Sigma: for a formula P of L(Sigma) consistent with C(Sigma) whose free variables are the displayed individual variables, if those individuals are pairwise distinct and distinct from every individual denoted by a constant occurring in P, then P is possible. Include the empty tuple.
principles.formal: $\forall x_1^e\cdots x_n^e\, .\,\bigl(\bigwedge_{i<j}x_i\ne x_j\land\bigwedge_{i,\,c}x_i\ne c\bigr)\to\Diamond P\quad(P\in\mathcal L(\Sigma),\text{ free variables among }x_1\ldots x_n;\ c\text{ over the individual constants in }P;\ C(\Sigma)+P\text{ consistent};\ n\ge0)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.6, p. 41 and n. 60, read with the signature convention of §2.5, pp. 37–39.

references.note: The draft states Possibility+ in the pure language; this is its analogue for L(Σ), added at Cian Dorr’s request to parallel Possibility (signature Σ).

principles.notes: The clause requiring the individuals to differ from the constants named in P is forced: without it the C(Σ)-consistent formula x ≠ c would yield ◇(c ≠ c).

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If a formula of the signature is necessary of some individuals and its negation is consistent with C(Σ), two of those individuals are identical or one of them is denoted by a constant of the formula.
variants.formal: $\forall x_1^e\cdots x_n^e\, .\,\Box P\to\bigl(\bigvee_{i<j}x_i=x_j\lor\bigvee_{i,\,c}x_i=c\bigr)\quad(P\in\mathcal L(\Sigma),\text{ free variables among }x_1\ldots x_n;\ c\text{ over the individual constants in }P;\ C(\Sigma)+\neg P\text{ consistent};\ n\ge0)$
variants.equivalence:
The instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$; $
eg P$ has the same free variables and constants as $P$.

principles.name: Possible Infinity (type e)
principles.statement: Possibly there are not finitely many individuals: the Axiom of Infinity at this type, under a diamond.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 20 September 2026.
principles.notes: Weaker than the Axiom of Infinity at this type by T. Since the Axiom of Infinity at type $e$ is consistent with C, Possibility Maximalism (pure) implies this principle. With No Pure Contingency, or with BF, it gives the Axiom back; whether it does so in C alone is recorded as an open question. See Background for $\mathbf{0}$, $\operatorname{Suc}$ and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$.

principles.name: Possible Infinity (type t)
principles.statement: Possibly there are not finitely many propositions: the Axiom of Infinity at this type, under a diamond.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 20 September 2026.
principles.notes: Weaker than the Axiom of Infinity at this type by T. Since the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ is consistent with C, Possibility Maximalism (pure) implies this principle, and indeed the Axiom itself by a longer route. With No Pure Contingency, or with BF (type $t$), this principle gives the Axiom back; whether it does so in C alone is recorded as an open question. See Background for $\mathbf{0}$, $\operatorname{Suc}$ and $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$.

principles.name: Possibly Witnessed Possibility
principles.statement: For pure formulas P with free variables among a finite tuple x and distinct matching constants c, a possible witness to P entails that P at those constants is possible. Equivalently, P necessary at the constants is necessary universally.
principles.formal: $\Diamond(\exists\bar x\, .\,P)\to\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 22 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 38–39 and n. 57.

references.note: Separated Structure and Witnessed Possibility, between which this principle sits.
Separated Structure, to which this principle is equivalent in C.

principles.notes: Strengthens Witnessed Possibility by weakening its antecedent from an actual to a possible witness; its contrapositive is □P[c̄/x̄] → □∀x̄ P, the left-to-right direction of Logical Necessity with a box on the right. Equivalent in C to Separated Structure by the recorded results, so Logical Necessity is Separated Structure together with No Pure Contingency.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: If a pure formula is necessary of distinct constants, it is necessary that it holds of everything.
variants.formal: $\Box P[\bar c/\bar x]\to\Box(\forall\bar x\, .\,P)\quad(P\text{ pure, free variables among }\bar x;\ \bar c\text{ distinct constants of }\Sigma)$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: B for pure sentences
principles.statement: The B instance for every closed sentence in the pure language.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, n. 81, p. 59.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Each closed pure sentence that is possibly necessary is true.
variants.formal: $\Diamond\Box P\to P\quad(P\text{ a closed pure sentence})$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: Relational Choice
principles.statement: Every serial binary relation has a functional subrelation.
principles.formal: $\forall U^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Serial}(U)\to\exists S^{\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Functional}(S)\land(\forall x y\, .\,(Sx)y\to(Ux)y)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 31–33.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every serial relation from tuples has a functional subrelation.
variants.formal: $\forall U^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Serial}(U)\to\exists S^{\bar\sigma\tau t}\, .\,\operatorname{Functional}(S)\land(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\,y^\tau\, .\,(S[\bar x])y\to(U[\bar x])y)$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Given a serial $U$, put $U':=\lambda A\,y\, .\,(\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land(U[\bar x])y)\lor\neg\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}$, which is serial. The original form at $\bar\sigma t$ and $\tau$ gives a functional $S'\subseteq U'$, and $S:=\lambda\bar x\,y\, .\,(S'H_{\bar x})y$ is a functional subrelation of $U$. The output type $\tau$ could be made a tuple as well, giving an equivalent doubly polyadic form; it is not listed.

principles.name: Rigid Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a rigid one.
principles.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, pp. 28–30.

principles.name: Rigid Power
principles.statement: If a relation is rigid, so is the property of being a rigid relation that entails it.
principles.formal: $\forall F^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(F)\to\operatorname{Rigid}(\lambda X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F)$
sources: Zachary Goodsell, 2019, as credited by Cian Dorr on 3 October 2026; full citation to be supplied.
principles.notes: Due to Zachary Goodsell. Gloss: sets cannot acquire new subsets, where rigid relations play the role of sets. It matters for the contingency of claims of analysis such as CH. Here $X$ ranges over relations of the same type as $F$, so the power property has type $(\bar\sigma\to t)\to t$. That property is persistent in C alone, since rigidity and entailment are both necessitated conditions and 4 holds; so the principle's content is the boxed weak inextensibility of the power property.

principles.name: Rigid Rigidity
principles.statement: Being rigid is a rigid property of relations, including propositions.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 10 October 2026.
principles.notes: Due to Cian Dorr. The property has type $(\bar\sigma t)t$. Its persistence is a theorem of C, so the content is that rigidity is inextensible. It is the instance of Rigid Power at $\lambda\bar x\, .\,\top$, whose power property is rigidity itself; so it follows from Rigid Power wherever $\lambda\bar x\, .\,\top$ is rigid, that is, given □BF (and at type $t$ outright). It implies □BF, and its own necessitation by 4. Whether it implies Rigid Power is open: the argument would need rigidity to be closed under conjunction, which fails in C when identity is contingent (the conjunction of the haecceities of distinct but possibly identical $x,y$ is persistent but not weakly inextensible).

principles.name: Separated Structure
principles.statement: For each typed nonlogical constant c and closed same-typed terms F,G not containing c, equality after application to c implies equality of F and G.
principles.formal: $Fc=Gc\to F=G\quad(c\text{ a constant of }\Sigma;\ F,G\text{ closed, not containing }c)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 38–39.

references.note: Derived from Quantified Separated Structure and the assumptions Purity and Fundamentality; General Separated Structure on p. 565.

principles.notes: Until 8 October 2026 the general form below was a separate principle, General Separated Structure, equivalent in C by two recorded results; it became a form of this principle at Cian Dorr's direction. Bacon's instances of it: Rab = Sba implies R and S are converses; Rab = Fb implies R forgets its first argument; Raa = Fa implies F is the reflexivization of R.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Added direct locators in Logical Combinatorialism; the statement is unchanged.

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
changes.summary: Displayed the schema’s side conditions inside the math block, at Cian Dorr’s request; the statement is unchanged.

variants.name: General form
variants.statement: Let a_1…a_n and b_1…b_m be constants of Sigma, possibly with repetitions, none occurring in the closed terms F and G, and let pi be a bijection from variables x_1…x_k to the distinct constants among them. If F applied to the a’s equals G applied to the b’s, then abstracting the constants yields identical pure-position operations.
variants.formal: $F a_1\cdots a_n=G b_1\cdots b_m\to\lambda\bar x\, .\,F(\pi a_1)\cdots(\pi a_n)=\lambda\bar x\, .\,G(\pi b_1)\cdots(\pi b_m)\quad(a_i,b_j\text{ constants of }\Sigma,\text{ none in the closed }F,G;\ \pi\text{ a bijection from }\bar x\text{ to the distinct ones})$
variants.equivalence: General to official: take $n=m=1$ with $a_1=b_1=c$, so $k=1$; the instance reads $Fc=Gc\to\lambda x\, .\,Fx=\lambda x\, .\,Gx$, and $\eta$ turns the consequent into $F=G$. Official to general: let $c_1,\ldots,c_k$ be the distinct constants among $a_1\ldots a_n,b_1\ldots b_m$, with $\pi x_j=c_j$, and put $F^{\prime}:=\lambda x_1\ldots x_k\, .\,F(\pi a_1)\cdots(\pi a_n)$ and $G^{\prime}:=\lambda x_1\ldots x_k\, .\,G(\pi b_1)\cdots(\pi b_m)$. Neither contains any $c_j$, and by $\beta$, $F^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_k=Fa_1\cdots a_n$ and $G^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_k=Gb_1\cdots b_m$. Given the antecedent, $(F^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_{k-1})c_k=(G^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_{k-1})c_k$ with $c_k$ in neither applied term, so the official form gives $F^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_{k-1}=G^{\prime}c_1\cdots c_{k-1}$; after $k$ such steps $F^{\prime}=G^{\prime}$. Bacon derives the general form from Logical Necessity; the official form alone suffices (Claude Fable 5.1, 22 September 2026). If $k=0$ the schema is trivial.

principles.name: B for sentences of Σ
principles.statement: The B instance for every closed sentence of the language of the fixed signature Sigma.
principles.formal: $P\to\Box\Diamond P\quad(P\text{ a closed sentence of }\mathcal L(\Sigma))$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 22 September 2026.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, n. 81, p. 59 (B for pure sentences).
Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §3, n. 32, p. 556.

references.note: Bacon’s observation that B for sentences with a nonlogical predicate is undermined by Witnessed Possibility independently of contingent distinctness.

principles.notes: Sits between B and B for pure sentences. Incompatible with Witnessed Possibility, unlike its pure counterpart, which Witnessed Possibility tolerates.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Each closed sentence of the signature that is possibly necessary is true.
variants.formal: $\Diamond\Box P\to P\quad(P\text{ a closed sentence of }\mathcal L(\Sigma))$
variants.equivalence:
Pure sentences (resp. sentences of $\mathcal L(\Sigma)$) are closed under negation, so the instance of either form at $
eg P$ is, after contraposition and $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$, the instance of the other at $P$.

principles.name: Strong Actuality
principles.statement: There is a true strong world proposition: a true proposition that necessarily entails every proposition or its negation.
sources: Cian Dorr, formulation and name, 6 October 2026.

references.note: Strong worlds; the principle says that some strong world at type $t$ is true, as Actuality says that some weak world (atom) is.
Source of Actuality, which this strengthens.

principles.notes: Equivalently $\exists w\, .\,w\land\operatorname{SWorld}_t(w)$, since a true proposition is possible. It stands to Actuality as the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type $t$) stand to Atomicity (type $t$): Actuality asks for a true proposition that settles every proposition, Strong Actuality for one that necessarily settles every proposition, including propositions that do not actually exist. In a full action model it holds at an object $W$ iff every arrow out of $W$ has at most one retraction.

principles.name: Strong Leibniz Biconditionals
principles.statement: At each relational type, every possible entity (one distinct from bottom) is entailed by a strong world: a possible entity that necessarily entails every entity of the type or its negation. The right-to-left direction is a theorem of C; the principle records the substantive direction.
principles.formal: $\forall X^\sigma\, .\,\Diamond_\sigma X\to\exists W^\sigma\, .\,\operatorname{SWorld}_\sigma(W)\land W\le_\sigma X\qquad(\sigma\ne e)$
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 164–166.
principles.notes: Bacon’s higher-order rendering of the possible-worlds thesis that a proposition is possible iff true at some world, with worlds required to settle merely possible propositions too. Definitions in Background. The book presents the connection between the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals and BF at relational types as new to it (§8.4, p. 177).

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is entailed by every strong world of its type is the top element of that type.
variants.formal: $\forall X^\sigma\, .\,(\forall W^\sigma\, .\,\operatorname{SWorld}_\sigma(W)\to W\le_\sigma X)\to\neg_\sigma X\le_\sigma X\qquad(\sigma\ne e)$
variants.equivalence:
As for the dual form of Atomicity. A strong world $W$ is non-bottom and, by T applied to its boxed clause, lies below $Y$ or below $
eg_\sigma Y$ for every $Y$. Official to dual: if every strong world lies below $X$ but $
eg_\sigma X$ is non-bottom, a strong world lies below $
eg_\sigma X$ and $X$, hence below bottom, which is impossible. Dual to official: if $X$ is non-bottom and no strong world lies below it, every strong world lies below $
eg_\sigma X$, so $X$ is bottom by the dual form.

principles.name: Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t)
principles.statement: The type-t instance of the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals: every possible proposition is entailed by a strong world proposition, one that is possible and necessarily entails every proposition or its negation.
sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, pp. 164–165.

references.locator: Definition 3.19 and satisfaction clauses, pp. 55–57; idempotent model, p. 59
references.note: Semantics used to correct the supplementary singleton claim on 25 September 2026; the defining SL formula is unchanged.

principles.notes:
Broken out as its own principle, like Atomicity (type t), at Cian Dorr’s request, because the type-t case can be settled in many models where the higher types have not been checked. A singleton need not be a strong world in a one-object action model.
At an arrow h its shift is the precomposition fibre, but a proposition newly quantified
inside the box ranges over the entire target domain, not just shifted root propositions.
For the full monoid {1,k} with k²=k≠1, the singleton {k} shifts under k to {1,k},
which the target proposition {k} splits. Group actions do send singletons to singletons.
Correction found by the DeepSeek deepseek-flash trawl and informally checked against
Classicism pp. 55–57 by OpenAI Codex (GPT-6), 25 September 2026; see the handwritten
strong-worlds-one-object-action-models proof and the full-idempotent-monoid change history.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: Whatever is entailed by every strong world is necessary.
variants.formal: $\forall p\, .\,(\forall w\, .\,\operatorname{SWorld}_t(w)\to w\le p)\to\Box p$
variants.equivalence: The argument for the dual form of the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals, at type $t$.

principles.name: Strong Possibility (pure)
principles.statement: Each closed pure sentence consistent with Maximalist Classicism is possible under the distinctness-preserving modality.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.6, p. 42.
principles.notes: The paper leaves consistency open. The definition of Box_ne and its dual is given in Background. Whatever is consistent with Max(C) is already possible by Possibility Maximalism (pure), which this principle implies; what it adds is possibility under the distinctness-preserving modality. So incompatibilities of the form Strong Possibility + □Y are recorded at Possibility Maximalism (pure) and inherited, and the collapse is the one recorded principle refuted by the stronger modality alone.

principles.name: Strong Possibility (signature Σ)
principles.statement: Every closed sentence of the fixed signature consistent with its Maximalist Classicism is possible under the distinctness-preserving modality.
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.5, pp. 37–39; §2.6, p. 42.
principles.notes: This keeps the signature-expanded reference theory throughout the consistency side condition. The separate pure-language variant uses Max(C). No conservativity between these two maximalizations is assumed. Consistency of Strong Possibility is left open in the source. Whatever is consistent with Max(C(Σ)) is already possible by Possibility Maximalism (signature Σ), which this principle implies; what it adds is possibility under the distinctness-preserving modality. Incompatibilities of the form Strong Possibility (signature Σ) + □Y are inherited through Possibility Maximalism (signature Σ) and Possibility Maximalism (pure); the collapse is refuted directly.

principles.name: Tame Rigidity
principles.statement: Every weakly rigid relation, including a proposition, is rigid.
sources: Christopher Sun, Possible Worlds Without Atomicity, draft of September 2026.

references.note: Source of the weak rigidity conditions.

principles.notes: Due to Christopher Sun. Persistence is a conjunct of both conditions, so the principle says that a persistent, weakly inextensible relation is also inextensible, that is, necessarily weakly inextensible. See Background for the definitions. Together with Weak Rigid Comprehension it is equivalent to Rigid Comprehension.

principles.name: Tractarianism
principles.statement: A proposition entailing every instance of a property entails its universal generalization.
principles.formal: $\forall p^t X^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,p\le Xx)\to p\le(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,Xx)$
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Proposition 2.1 and n. 27, pp. 20–21.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: A proposition entailing every instance of a relation entails its universal generalization.
variants.formal: $\forall p^t X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,p\le X[\bar x])\to p\le(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar x])$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Conversely, apply the original one variable at a time from the innermost, as for BF. For the empty tuple both sides are $p\le X$.

variants.name: Dual form
variants.statement: A proposition entailed by every instance of a property is entailed by its existential generalization.
variants.formal: $\forall p^t X^{\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall x^\sigma\, .\,Xx\le p)\to(\exists x^\sigma\, .\,Xx)\le p$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$ and $q\le r\leftrightarrow
eg r\le
eg q$. This yields the other form, and the same steps lead back.

variants.name: Dual polyadic form
variants.statement: A proposition entailed by every instance of a relation is entailed by its existential generalization.
variants.formal: $\forall p^t X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,(\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar x]\le p)\to(\exists\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar x])\le p$
variants.equivalence:
Instantiate either form at the negations of its propositional or relational variables, contrapose, and rewrite with $\Diamond=
eg\Box
eg$ and $q\le r\leftrightarrow
eg r\le
eg q$. This yields the other form, and the same steps lead back. Combined with the polyadic form, this gives the equivalence with the official form.

principles.name: Transversal Choice
principles.statement: Every equivalence relation, at any type including e, has a transversal, that is, a property with exactly one instance in each of its cells.
principles.formal: $\forall R^{\sigma\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Equiv}(R)\to\exists F^{\sigma t}\, .\,\forall x^\sigma\, .\,\exists y^\sigma\, .\,(Rx)y\land Fy\land\forall z^\sigma\, .\,((Rx)z\land Fz)\to y=z$
sources: Christopher Sun, observation communicated by Zachary Goodsell on 25 September 2026, that this formulation of choice for equivalence relations is used in the literature without a proof from Relational Choice; stated here in the map's relational type system.

references.note: The source's choice principles are Relational and Functional Choice. Transversal Choice is the selector form. It implies Relational Choice, and follows from it under Extensionality or Weak Rigid Comprehension, by the recorded results.

principles.notes: Equiv is defined in Background. The relation is required to be an equivalence relation only actually, and the transversal condition is unboxed, so both concern the evaluation point. The cell of $x$ is $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$. Two members of one cell have coextensive cells, but in C properties are identical only when necessarily coextensive; this is what separates the principle from Relational Choice, which chooses from each property separately.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: Every equivalence relation on tuples has a transversal.
variants.formal: $\forall R^{\bar\sigma\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Equiv}(R)\to\exists F^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\forall\bar x^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,\exists\bar y^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,(R[\bar x])[\bar y]\land F[\bar y]\land\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,((R[\bar x])[\bar z]\land F[\bar z])\to\bar y=\bar z$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Given an equivalence $R$ on tuples, put $R':=\lambda A\,B\, .\,A=B\lor\exists\bar x\,\bar y\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land B=H_{\bar y}\land(R[\bar x])[\bar y]$, an equivalence on $\bar\sigma t$ whose cells are either the codes of one $R$-cell or singletons of non-codes. The original form gives a transversal $F'$ of $R'$, and $F:=\lambda\bar y\, .\,F'(H_{\bar y})$ is a transversal of $R$.

principles.name: Transversal
principles.statement: There is a property of properties that picks out exactly one property from each coextension class, that is, exactly one property coextensive with any given property.
principles.formal: $\exists F^{(\sigma t)t}\, .\,\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\sigma t}\, .\,FY\land(\forall z^\sigma\, .\,Xz\leftrightarrow Yz)\land\forall Y'^{\sigma t}\, .\,(FY'\land\forall z^\sigma\, .\,Xz\leftrightarrow Y'z)\to Y'=Y$
sources: Christopher Sun, 26 September 2026, principle and its connections to Transversal Choice, Relational Choice and Actuality.

references.note: The source's choice principles are Relational and Functional Choice; Transversal Choice is recorded separately.

principles.notes: Due to Christopher Sun. It is the instance of Transversal Choice at type $\sigma\to t$ for the equivalence relation of coextensiveness, and Transversal Choice is equivalent to it together with Relational Choice. It isolates what Relational Choice lacks for the quotient argument: a canonical representative of each coextension class of properties, shared by coextensive properties even when they are distinct. The coextension and the choice are unboxed, so both concern the evaluation point. The type $\sigma$ may be $e$; the type $(\sigma\to t)\to t$ of $F$ is admitted since its output is $t$.

variants.name: Polyadic form
variants.statement: There is a property of relations that picks out exactly one relation from each coextension class.
variants.formal: $\exists F^{(\bar\sigma t)t}\, .\,\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,FY\land(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])\land\forall Y'^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,(FY'\land\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y'[\bar z])\to Y'=Y$
variants.equivalence: The original form is the case of a one-element tuple. Code tuples by their haecceities (Background, Polyadic forms). Let $F''$ witness the original form at $\bar\sigma t$, and let $\operatorname{Code}:=\lambda A\, .\,\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}$. Put $F:=\lambda Y\, .\,\exists Z\, .\,F''Z\land(\forall A\, .\,ZA\to\operatorname{Code}(A))\land Y=\lambda\bar x\, .\,Z(H_{\bar x})$. For each $X$, let $X'':=\lambda A\, .\,\exists\bar x\, .\,A=H_{\bar x}\land X[\bar x]$. A relation $Y$ with $FY$, built from $Z$, is coextensive with $X$ iff $Z$ is coextensive with $X''$, since both $Z$ and $X''$ hold only of codes. So exactly one such $Y$ is coextensive with $X$, namely the one built from the $Z$ that $F''$ picks in the coextension class of $X''$.

principles.name: Truth implies 5-necessity
principles.statement: Every truth is 5-necessary: necessary under every S5 operator.
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. The converse implication is a theorem of C (Background, Hats, two-hat necessity and 5-necessity), so this principle says that the two operators are coextensive.
sources: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne, and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, pp. 400–409 (definitions of the hat operation and of the 5-necessity operator; the principles themselves are not stated there).

principles.name: Truth implies two-hat necessity
principles.statement: Every truth is two-hat necessary.
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. The converse implication is a theorem of C (Background, Hats, two-hat necessity and 5-necessity), so this principle says that the two operators are coextensive.
sources: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne, and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, pp. 400–409 (definitions of the hat operation and of the 5-necessity operator; the principles themselves are not stated there).

principles.name: Two-hat necessity implies ND-necessity
principles.statement: Whatever is two-hat necessary is ND-necessary: the distinctness-preserving modality agrees with its hat.
principles.notes: Added at the suggestion of Christopher Sun, 14 October 2026. The converse implication is a theorem of C (Background, Hats, two-hat necessity and 5-necessity), so this principle says that the two operators are coextensive.
sources: Cian Dorr, John Hawthorne, and Juhani Yli-Vakkuri, The Bounds of Possibility, Appendix D, pp. 400–409 (definitions of the hat operation and of the 5-necessity operator; the principles themselves are not stated there).

principles.name: Vicinity
principles.statement: There is a true proposition that entails the possibility of each true proposition.
sources: Christopher Sun, 27 September 2026, who recognised the principle's interest by showing that together with Weakly Inextensible Comprehension it implies Actuality.
Cian Dorr, formulation and name, 27 September 2026.

references.note: Source of Actuality, of which this is the weakening that asks the witness to entail only the possibility of each truth.

principles.notes: Weakens Actuality by replacing $p\le q$ with $p\le\Diamond q$. Its interest was recognised by Christopher Sun, who showed that it recovers Actuality from Weakly Inextensible Comprehension, so that Actuality is equivalent to Vicinity together with Weakly Inextensible Comprehension. ND at type $t$ gives it trivially, with $\top$ as witness.

variants.name: ND-necessity form
variants.statement: There is a truth that entails every ND-necessary truth.
variants.formal: $\exists p\, .\,p\land\forall q\, .\,\Box_{\ne}q\to p\le q$

changes.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
changes.summary: Added the ND-necessity form as a variant: there is a truth that entails every ND-necessary truth.

principles.name: Weak Rigid Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a weakly rigid one, that is, with one that is weakly persistent and weakly inextensible.
principles.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Cian Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026, Proposition 1, p. 2; p. 12.
Cian Dorr, suggestion of 19 September 2026.

references.note: The draft's unqualified "weakly rigid" is this map's, the whole matrix of Rigid shorn of its leading boxes.
Source of Rigid Comprehension, of which this is the un-necessitated weakening.

principles.notes: Weak rigidity drops the leading boxes from both conjuncts of Rigid. A weakly rigid relation is nevertheless persistent, so the principle is equivalent to its persistent form. See Background for the definitions. The draft that introduces the principle is a work in progress. Until 8 October 2026 the map's "weakly rigid" meant persistent and weakly inextensible, the persistent form below was this principle's official statement, and the present statement was a separate principle, Very Weak Rigid Comprehension, retired then at Cian Dorr's direction.

variants.name: Persistent form
variants.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with one that is persistent and weakly inextensible.
variants.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)\land \operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
variants.equivalence: Persistence implies weak persistence by T, so the persistent form implies the official one. The interesting direction: a weakly rigid $Y$ is persistent. Apply its weak inextensibility to $X:=\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]$. The hypothesis $\forall\bar x\, .\,Y[\bar x]\to\Box X[\bar x]$, that is $Y[\bar x]\to\Box\Box Y[\bar x]$, holds by weak persistence and 4; so $Y\le\lambda\bar x\, .\,\Box Y[\bar x]$, which is $\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)$. The same $Y$ therefore witnesses both forms.

principles.name: Weakly Inextensible Comprehension
principles.statement: Every relation, including a proposition, is coextensive with a weakly inextensible one.
principles.formal: $\forall X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\exists Y^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y)\land(\forall\bar z^{\bar\sigma}\, .\,X[\bar z]\leftrightarrow Y[\bar z])$
sources: Cian Dorr, Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension, draft of 30 July 2026, Proposition 1, p. 2; p. 12.
Cian Dorr, suggestion of 25 September 2026.

references.note: Source of weak inextensibility, the inextensibility conjunct of Rigid shorn of its leading box.
Source of Inextensible Comprehension, of which this is the un-necessitated weakening.

principles.notes: Weak inextensibility drops the leading box from Inextensible; see Background for the definitions. A relation $Y$ is weakly inextensible exactly when $Y\le Z$ for every $Z$ that necessarily holds of each actual $Y$-instance, that is, when $Y$ lies below every upper bound of the haecceities $\lambda\bar z\, .\,\bigwedge_i z_i=y_i$ of its instances: $Y$ may lose instances at other worlds, but it cannot gain any beyond those its actual instances necessitate. Adding weak persistence, which says that $Y$ is itself such an upper bound, turns this into $Y$ being the least upper bound of those haecceities, which is weak rigidity. The type-$t$ instances are trivial, since $\top$ and $\bot$ witness them; haecceities and their finite joins are rigid; and the instance at $X=\top$ is a relativised Barcan Formula, $\top$ itself being weakly inextensible exactly when BF holds at the argument types. The principle follows from Actuality and separately from Boolean Completeness, which the recorded models show to be independent of one another, so it is strictly weaker than each. Whether it implies the boxed principle, Inextensible Comprehension, is open.

principles.name: Weakly Rigid Power
principles.statement: If a relation is weakly rigid, so is the property of being a weakly rigid relation that entails it.
principles.formal: $\forall F^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(F)\to\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(\lambda X^{\bar\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)\land X\le F)$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 10 October 2026.
principles.notes: Due to Cian Dorr. The variant of Rigid Power with "weakly rigid" in all three places (the $(W,W,W)$ variant in the candidate list). Here $X$ ranges over relations of the same type as $F$, so the power property has type $(\bar\sigma t)t$. principles.name: Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity
principles.statement: Being weakly rigid is a weakly rigid property of relations, including propositions.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 10 October 2026.
principles.notes: Due to Cian Dorr. The property has type $(\bar\sigma t)t$. Since a weakly rigid relation is persistent (Background), it implies □Tame Rigidity, so weak rigidity and rigidity are then identical; it is equivalent to the conjunction of Rigid Rigidity and □Tame Rigidity, and hence to its own necessitation. It follows from BF with Weakly Rigid Power.

principles.name: Well-Ordering
principles.statement: Every type, including e, is well-ordered by some relation.
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 8 October 2026.
principles.notes: WO is defined in Background: $R$ is transitive, antisymmetric and total, and every instantiated property has an $R$-minimal instance. The condition is unboxed, so it concerns the evaluation point only, and the well-order need not remain one at other worlds, since its field may contract there by contingent identities. Modal Well-Ordering asks for a relation that is necessarily a well-order. Well-Ordering is equivalent to Transversal Choice and to Zorn's Lemma, by the recorded results, as the well-ordering theorem is to the axiom of choice in set theory (Cian Dorr's conjecture of 7 October 2026). Relational Choice is enough only if it implies Transversal Choice, which is open.

principles.name: Zorn's Lemma
principles.statement: If a preorder is such that every chain, that is, every property it totally orders, has an upper bound, then something is maximal: everything above it is also below it.
principles.formal: $\forall R^{\sigma\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{Preorder}(R)\land(\forall X^{\sigma t}\, .\,\operatorname{TotalOrder}(R,X)\to\exists u^\sigma\, .\,\forall x^\sigma\, .\,Xx\to(Rx)u)\to\exists m^\sigma\, .\,\forall y^\sigma\, .\,(Rm)y\to(Ry)m$
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 8 October 2026, to add Zorn's Lemma in preorder form with a proof from Transversal Choice of the shape of Lewin's.
Jonathan Lewin, A Simple Proof of Zorn's Lemma, American Mathematical Monthly 98 (1991), pp. 353–354.

references.note: Zorn's Lemma for partial orders on sets, with a proof from the axiom of choice by conforming subsets.

principles.notes: Preorder and TotalOrder are as in Background; everything is unboxed. The preorder form is used because the orders to which Zorn's Lemma is applied at higher types, such as extension of relations, are antisymmetric only up to coextension. Chains are required to be totally ordered, and so antisymmetric, so the hypothesis concerns fewer properties than comparability alone would; this makes the principle stronger. For a partial order the conclusion says that $m$ is maximal in the usual sense. Zorn's Lemma is equivalent to Transversal Choice and to Well-Ordering, by the recorded results; the proof from Transversal Choice follows Lewin and uses Transversal Choice only to make the choice relation give coextensive chains the same value.

results.proof: Let $a$ witness Actuality and write $L(a)$ for $a\land\forall q\, .\,q\to a\le q$. Applying Distinctness-preserving collapse to the truth $L(a)$ gives a true $q^*$ with $\Box(\Diamond q^*\to L(a))$; since $a\le q^*$, 4 and K give $\Box(\Diamond a\to\Diamond q^*)$, hence $\Box(\Diamond a\to L(a))$. Now fix $X$ and put $Y:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,a\land X[\bar z]$, coextensive with $X$. Two theorems of C: (i) $L(a)$ implies that $Y$ is weakly inextensible, by the recorded argument from Actuality; (ii) $\Box\neg a$ implies that $Y$ is weakly inextensible, since then $Y\le\bot\le Z$. So $(\Diamond a\to L(a))\to\operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y)$ is a theorem; necessitating it and using $\Box(\Diamond a\to L(a))$ gives $\Box\operatorname{WeaklyInextensible}(Y)$, which is $\operatorname{Inextensible}(Y)$.

references.note: The witness is the one note 38 uses for Actuality; the distinctness-preserving modality is that of §2.6, and the collapse principle is from Appendix E.

results.notes: The collapse principle is used only to obtain that the Actuality witness is, necessarily, the least truth wherever it is so much as possible. That is exactly what the recorded action models with Actuality have: their witness is a set of arrows, typically a symmetry group or the identity alone, that no arrow outside it composes back into. So Inextensible Comprehension holds in every recorded model with Actuality and Distinctness-preserving collapse, including the symmetric models and the finite-support models in which Rigid Comprehension, Boolean Completeness or Weak Rigid Comprehension fail. A countermodel to Actuality alone implying Inextensible Comprehension would have to make the witness possible at some world where it is false, which the collapse principle forbids and C5 renders harmless; none is recorded, and the question is open.

results.proof: Let $w$ witness Actuality: $w$ is true and $w\le q$ for every true $q$. Fix $\sigma$ and put $FY:=\Box\forall z^\sigma\, .\,Yz\to w$, the property of being a property that can be instantiated only if $w$ obtains. Existence: given $X$, let $Y:=\lambda z\, .\,Xz\land w$. Since $w$ is true, $Y$ is coextensive with $X$, and $FY$ holds because $\forall z\, .\,(Xz\land w)\to w$ is a theorem, hence necessary. Uniqueness: let $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ satisfy $F$ and be coextensive with $X$. Then $\forall z\, .\,Y_1z\leftrightarrow Y_2z$ is true, so Actuality gives $\Box(w\to\forall z\, .\,Y_1z\leftrightarrow Y_2z)$. Together with $\Box\forall z\, .\,Y_1z\to w$ and $\Box\forall z\, .\,Y_2z\to w$, K gives $\Box\forall z\, .\,Y_1z\leftrightarrow Y_2z$: at any $z$, if either side holds then $w$ does, and then the two sides agree. Necessarily coextensive properties are identical in C (Intensionality), so $Y_1=Y_2$.

references.note: Intensionality, the identity of necessarily coextensive relations.

results.notes: Two coextensive $F$-properties are necessarily coextensive. The dual witness $FY:=\Box\forall z\, .\,w\lor Yz$, with representative $\lambda z\, .\,Xz\lor\neg w$, works equally well. With Transversal and Relational Choice implying Transversal Choice, Actuality and Relational Choice together imply Transversal Choice.

results.proof: Let $w$ witness Actuality and put $Y:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,w\land X[\bar z]$. Since $w$ is true, $Y$ is coextensive with $X$. For weak inextensibility, suppose $\forall\bar z\, .\,Y[\bar z]\to\Box Z[\bar z]$. By T, $\forall\bar z\, .\,w\land X[\bar z]\to Z[\bar z]$ is true, so $w$ entails it: $\Box(w\to\forall\bar z\, .\,w\land X[\bar z]\to Z[\bar z])$. The formula in the box is H-equivalent to $\forall\bar z\, .\,w\land X[\bar z]\to Z[\bar z]$, so by Logical Equivalence they are the same proposition, and $\Box\forall\bar z\, .\,Y[\bar z]\to Z[\bar z]$, which is $Y\le Z$. The box in the antecedent is not used: every relation that actually includes $Y$ is entailed by $Y$.
results.notes: The argument establishes weak inextensibility at the world of evaluation only. It does not give Inextensible Comprehension, whose witness must be weakly inextensible at every world: at a world where $w$ is false but still possible, $\lambda\bar z\, .\,w\land X[\bar z]$ has no instances, so inextensibility there would need it to entail $\bot$, which fails whenever $w\land\exists\bar z\, .\,X[\bar z]$ is possible there. Under C5 the gap closes by Proposition 2.10, and it also closes under Distinctness-preserving collapse; see the recorded results. Whether Actuality alone implies Inextensible Comprehension is open.

results.proof:
Let $a$ be a strongest truth, as Actuality supplies. Since $a$ is true, $a
e ot$, so $\Diamond a$. Atomlessness then gives $q$ with $\Diamond q$, $q\le a$ and $q
e a$. If $q$ were true, Actuality would give $a\le q$, and with $q\le a$ antisymmetry gives $q=a$, contrary to $q
e a$. So $q$ is false, and $a\land
eg q$ is true, whence $a\le a\land
eg q\le
eg q$. Combined with $q\le a$ this gives $q\le
eg q$, so $q=q\land
eg q= ot$, contradicting $\Diamond q$. In short, a strongest truth is an atom.

references.note: The draft does not state the incompatibility, but its discussion of the Part 4 model observes that only the restriction of Atomlessness to false propositions can hold once the strongest truth is available.

results.notes: This explains why Atomlessness holds only in Parts 1–3 of Proposition D.5, since Parts 4, 5, 7 and 8 satisfy Actuality and Parts 6–8 satisfy Atomicity. The restriction of Atomlessness to false propositions, which the draft notes holds in Part 4, is not a principle of the map.

Tractarianism, equivalent to BF, combines these into the universal claim that w entails every truth. Hence w entails Actuality. Atomicity says every possible proposition has an atom below it, so no possible proposition can entail the negation of Actuality. Thus that negation is $\bot$ and Actuality is necessary.

results.proof:
Call $q$ a floor of $X^{tt}$ when $Xq$, $\Diamond q$, and no possible instance of $X$ lies strictly below $q$. Let $W$ be the property of cardinalities holding of $Z$ when every instance of $Z$ that has a possible instance has a floor.

$W$ holds of $\mathbf{0}_t$, since its only instance has no instances at all, so the condition is vacuous.

$W$ is closed under $\operatorname{Suc}_t$. Let $WY$ and $(\operatorname{Suc}_t Y)X$, and take the witness $y$ with $Xy$ and $Y(\lambda u\, .\,Xu\land u\ne y)$; write $X^-$ for that abstract, whose instances are exactly the instances of $X$ other than $y$. Suppose $X$ has a possible instance. If $X^-$ has none then $y$ is the only one, and is a floor. Otherwise the hypothesis on $Y$, applied to $X^-$ as $\operatorname{Suc}_t$ presents it, gives a floor $q$ of $X^-$. If $y$ is not possible, or is not strictly below $q$, then $q$ is a floor of $X$, since a possible instance of $X$ strictly below $q$ is either an instance of $X^-$, against the choice of $q$, or is $y$, which this case excludes. If instead $y$ is possible and strictly below $q$, then $y$ is a floor of $X$. For a possible instance $r$ of $X$ strictly below $y$ is not $y$, hence is an instance of $X^-$, and $r\le y\le q$. If $r=q$ then $q\le y\le q$ makes $y=q$, against $y\ne q$; so $r$ is an instance of $X^-$ strictly below $q$, again against the choice of $q$.

So every finite cardinality has the property. Now suppose some finite $Z$ held of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$. That property has the possible instance $\top$, since $\top\ne\bot$ in C, so it would have a floor $q$. Atomlessness applied to $q$ supplies a possible $q'$ with $q'\le q$ and $q'\ne q$, and $q'$ is an instance of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$, contradicting the floor. Hence no finite cardinality holds of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$.

references.note: Formulation of Atomlessness. The draft does not draw the connection.

results.notes: The induction stays inside the presentation that $\operatorname{Suc}_t$ supplies, applying the hypothesis to the abstract $\lambda u\, .\,Xu\land u\ne y$ itself rather than to a coextensive property. That is what makes it go through without Extensionality. The recorded implication to the Infinity schema is a consequence of this one and is left in place as the shorter argument.

results.proof: In C the top and bottom propositions differ, so $\Diamond\top$. Atomlessness applied to $\top$ gives a possible $q_1$ with $q_1\le\top$ and $q_1\ne\top$; applied to $q_1$ it gives a possible $q_2$ strictly below $q_1$, and so on. After $n$ steps the chain $\top,q_1,\ldots,q_n$ descends strictly in the algebraic order, and a strictly descending chain in a partial order has pairwise distinct members. For if $q_i=q_j$ with $i<j$ then $q_i\le q_{i+1}$, since $q_j\le q_{i+1}$, while $q_{i+1}\le q_i$, so antisymmetry gives $q_{i+1}=q_i$, against the choice of $q_{i+1}$. Each instance of the Infinity schema therefore needs only finitely many applications of the single Atomlessness sentence.

results.proof: Fix two distinct atoms $w,w^{\prime}$ of type $t$ and let $F:=\lambda p\, .\,(\neg(w\lor w^{\prime})\land p)\lor(w\land(w^{\prime}\le p))\lor(w^{\prime}\land(w\le p))$, which exchanges the two atoms: $w\le Fp$ iff $w^{\prime}\le p$. Under $\Box$ND identity propositions are rigid, so $F$ is an involution commuting with the connectives, with $\forall$ (by BF) and with identity, as identities, not just materially: the hypothesis that $w,w^{\prime}$ are distinct atoms is rigid, so material equivalences proved under it lift to identities by the Modalized Fregean Axiom and pass under $\lambda$ by Modalized Functionality. Extend $F$ by conjugation to every type, $F^*_{\sigma\tau}X:=\lambda y\, .\,F^*_\tau(X(F^*_\sigma y))$; $F^*$ is an involution fixing every logical constant, so by induction on terms $F^*A=A[F^*\bar x/\bar x]$ for pure $A$, and $FP=P$ for closed pure $P$. Hence $w\le P$ iff $w^{\prime}\le P$. If $P$ is true and not $\top$, Atomicity at type $t$ gives atoms $w\le P$ and $w^{\prime}\le\neg P$, necessarily distinct, and the agreement puts $w^{\prime}$ below $\bot$. Full proof in the write-up.

results.proof:
Let $X$ be given and let $Y$ be a persistent coextension, which Persistent Comprehension supplies. Only persistence of $Y$ is used. What has to be added is that $
eg Y$ is persistent, which is the necessitation of a pointwise implication, so the argument must run at every world; that is what the boxed premise supplies. At any world, take $ ar x$ with $
eg Y[ ar x]$ and suppose $\Diamond Y[ ar x]$. Persistence of $Y$ is itself necessary, so $\Diamond Y[ ar x]$ yields $\Diamond\Box Y[ ar x]$. Boxed ND gives B at every world, and B in the form $\Diamond\Box p	o p$ then yields $Y[ ar x]$, against the assumption. So $\Box
eg Y[ ar x]$, which is persistence of $
eg Y$. Hence $Y$ is Gallin-extensional and coextensive with $X$.

results.notes: Rigid Comprehension implies Persistent Comprehension, so this covers the reading on which rigidity yields Gallin-extensionality. The boxed form of ND is needed rather than the plain form, because persistence of the negation is itself a boxed claim and the argument has to be available at every world. In the other direction the draft's note uses BF, which is doing separate work: it stops a world from having instances that the base world does not supply, and no amount of ND replaces it.

results.proof: Let $\tau=\bar\rho\to t$, which covers $\tau=t$ with the empty tuple, and fix $U^{\sigma\tau t}$. Write $\varphi(x,y):=(Ux)y\land\forall z\, .\,(Ux)z\to y=z$ and define the operation $F:=\lambda x^\sigma\, .\,\lambda\bar u\, .\,\forall y^\tau\, .\,(Ux)y\to y[\bar u]$; for $\tau=t$ this is $\lambda x\, .\,\forall p\, .\,(Ux)p\to p$. (1) Lemma, a theorem of C: $\varphi(x,y_0)\to\forall\bar u\, .\,y_0[\bar u]\leftrightarrow(Fx)[\bar u]$. Assume $\varphi(x,y_0)$. If $y_0[\bar u]$ and $(Ux)y$, then $y=y_0$ by uniqueness, so $y[\bar u]$; hence $(Fx)[\bar u]$. Conversely, if $(Fx)[\bar u]$, instantiate $y:=y_0$ and use $(Ux)y_0$. (2) Necessitate the lemma and apply K: $\Box\varphi(x,y_0)$ gives $\Box\forall\bar u\, .\,y_0[\bar u]\leftrightarrow(Fx)[\bar u]$, and Intensionality gives $y_0=Fx$. (3) Let $H:=\forall x\, .\,\exists y\, .\,\Box\varphi(x,y)$ and $G:=\forall x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Fx$. Then $H\to G$ is a theorem of C. Given $x$ and $y$, take $y_0$ with $\Box\varphi(x,y_0)$; by (2) $y_0=Fx$, and by T $\varphi(x,y_0)$. If $(Ux)y$ then $y=y_0=Fx$ by uniqueness. If $y=Fx$ then $y=y_0$, and $(Ux)y_0$ gives $(Ux)y$. (4) Necessitate $H\to G$ and apply K: $\Box H\to\Box G$. Existential generalization on the closed term $F$ (with parameter $U$) gives $\Box H\to\exists X\, .\,\Box\forall x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Xx$. Only necessitation of theorems of C is used, so the theoremhood side condition is respected.

references.note: Necessitation, T and Intensionality (necessarily coextensive relations are identical).

results.notes: The operation is definable from $U$, so no choice is involved. The outer box of the hypothesis is used only to get the boxed conclusion: the same proof shows, as a theorem of C, the unboxed variant $H\to\exists X\, .\,\forall x\, .\,\forall y\, .\,(Ux)y\leftrightarrow y=Xx$. The inner box is essential; it is what licenses the identity $y_0=Fx$ in step (2). A natural target for a Lean proof, at every relational output type.

results.proof:
Fix a relational type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ and $X^\tau$. Write $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar u}:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,\bigwedge_i z_i=u_i$ and put $H:=\lambda Z^\tau\, .\,\exists\bar y\, .\,X[\bar y]\land Z=\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar y}$, the property of being the haecceity of some $X$ things. By Boolean Completeness in its least-upper-bound form, let $Y$ be a least upper bound of $H$. Two observations do the work. (i) If $X[\bar u]$ then $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar u}\le_\tau Y$, and instantiating at $\bar u$ with $\bar u=\bar u$ gives $\Box Y[\bar u]$. (ii) If $\Box Z[\bar u]$ whenever $X[\bar u]$, then $\operatorname{Haec}_{\bar u}\le_\tau Z$ for each such $\bar u$, so $Z$ is an upper bound of $H$ and $Y\le_\tau Z$.

Coextensiveness. $X[\bar u]\to Y[\bar u]$ by (i). Conversely, let $w$ witness Actuality and put $P:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,(w\le X[\bar z])$. If $X[\bar u]$ then $X[\bar u]$ is true, so $w\le X[\bar u]$; a true entailment is necessary, so $\Box P[\bar u]$. By (ii), $Y\le_\tau P$, so $Y[\bar u]\to w\le X[\bar u]$; and $w$ is true, so $Y[\bar u]\to X[\bar u]$.

Persistence. Take $Z:=\lambda\bar z\, .\,\Box Y[\bar z]$ in (ii). If $X[\bar u]$ then $\Box Y[\bar u]$ by (i), hence $\Box Z[\bar u]$ by 4. So $Y\le_\tau\lambda\bar z\, .\,\Box Y[\bar z]$, which is $\operatorname{Persistent}(Y)$.

Weak inextensibility. Suppose $\forall\bar z\, .\,Y[\bar z]\to\Box Z[\bar z]$. If $X[\bar u]$ then $Y[\bar u]$ by coextensiveness, so $\Box Z[\bar u]$; hence $Y\le_\tau Z$ by (ii).

references.note: Boolean Completeness and Actuality; the least-upper-bound form of Boolean Completeness is equivalent to the stated greatest-lower-bound form in C.

results.notes: The argument stops short of Rigid Comprehension exactly at the leading box of Inextensible. It delivers a $Y$ that is inextensible at the actual world, while Rigid demands the biconditional at every world. The models recorded from the same draft show that the gap is real.

sources: Zachary Goodsell, Arithmetic is Necessary, draft of 5 June 2024, §5, Lemmas 2–8 and Theorem 9, pp. 14–21.
results.proof: Theorem 9 of the source, proved in HKC, which C extends. Natural numberhood is necessary (Lemma 3, an induction using the converse Barcan formula), distinct numbers are necessarily distinct given $I^*$ (Lemma 4, a double induction), $I$ implies $I^*$ (Lemma 5), so distinctness and, by tedious inductions, Sum and Prod are necessary or necessarily false given $I$ (Lemmas 6–7). Countable Boolean Completeness is used once, in Lemma 8: the property of being a singleton of a number is countable, so it has a least upper bound $B$; $B$ necessarily holds of every number, so the property of being the successor of a $B$ is also an upper bound, hence $B$ necessitates it, and induction gives that necessarily every number is a $B$; thus any property necessarily had by each number is necessarily had by every number. Theorem 9 then proceeds by induction on arithmetical formulas, Lemma 8 handling the restricted universal quantifier. See the write-up.
results.notes: Lemma 3 of the source is the persistence of being a finite cardinality, Lemma 1 of the write-up for pure-possibility-implies-axiom-of-infinity-t. Lemma 8 says that natural numberhood is a rigid property in the source's sense, the Barcan direction; the converse Barcan direction is Lemma 3. The source's logic lacks T, 4 and Logical Equivalence, so the proof transfers to C unchanged.

results.proof:
Under ND the two necessities coincide. If $\Box_{
e}p$, there is a true $q$ with $\Box(\Diamond q	o p)$; $q$ true gives $q
e ot$, and ND at type $t$ gives $\Box(q
e ot)$, that is $\Box\Diamond q$; K then gives $\Box p$. So the collapse yields $ orall p\, .\,p	o\Box p$: every truth is $	op$. Then materially equivalent propositions are identical: if both are true both are $	op$; if both are false their negations are $	op$, so both are $ ot$. That is the Fregean Axiom.
results.notes: The converse of the first step holds without ND: $\Box p$ gives $\Box_{\ne}p$ with $q:=\top$. So ND makes $\Diamond$ and $\Diamond_{\ne}$ coextensive, and with it the collapse is Extensionalism. This settles the collapse as false in every model with ND and more than two propositions.

results.proof:
Strong worlds are necessarily strong: if $\operatorname{SWorld}(w)$, then 5 gives $\Box\Diamond w$ and 4 gives $\Box\Box orall Y\,(w\le Y\lor w\le
eg Y)$, so $\Box\operatorname{SWorld}(w)$. Let $q:=\exists w\, .\,\Box\operatorname{SWorld}(w)\land w$. Then $\Box q$: if $\Diamond
eg q$, the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals give a strong world $w\le
eg q$, and $\Box\Box\operatorname{SWorld}(w)$ by the above and 4, so at a world where $w$ holds, as one does since $\Diamond w$, $q$ holds too, contradicting $w\le
eg q$. Next, $q	o orall p\, .\,p	o\Box\Diamond p$ is a theorem of C: given $\Box\operatorname{SWorld}(w_0)\land w_0$ and a true $p$, T twice gives $w_0\le p$ or $w_0\le
eg p$, and the second contradicts $w_0\land p$; and $\Box\operatorname{SWorld}(w_0)$ gives $\Box\Diamond w_0$, so $w_0\le p$ gives $\Box\Diamond p$. Necessitating this theorem and applying K to $\Box q$ gives $\Box orall p\, .\,p	o\Box\Diamond p$, which yields each closed instance of $\Box$B.

references.note: Strong worlds and the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals.

results.notes: 5 is equivalent to ND in C, by the recorded results, so this gives □ND from ND and the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t). 5 is used only to make the strong worlds necessarily possible. Weak worlds do not suffice: ND with □Atomicity (type t) does not give □ND, by the recorded models.

results.proof: Under the Fregean Axiom a true $p$ is materially equivalent to $\top$, hence identical to it, so $\Box p$. And $\Box p$ gives $\Box_{\ne}p$: take $q:=\top$, which is true, and $\Box(\Diamond\top\to p)$ is $\Box p$.
results.notes: With the converse record, the collapse is equivalent to the Fregean Axiom in the presence of ND, while without ND it is weaker: the coalesced-sum roots satisfy it with infinitely many propositions.

results.proof: Choose an operation X selecting from the serial relation U. Its graph, $\lambda x y\, .\,Xx=y$, is a functional subrelation of U. If the output type is e, first replace each output individual by its haecceity of type et. Functional Choice selects such a haecceity; equality with that selected haecceity defines a functional subrelation of the original relation. Haecceities are injective by identity elimination, so this covers the individual-output case without assuming a selecting operation into e.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.3, n. 37, p. 28.
results.proof: The source states that, under BF, persistence of a relation and of its negation implies its inextensibility. Given pointwise necessary consequences on its instances, the persistent complement makes all non-instance cases necessary too; BF assembles the resulting pointwise necessary conditional into entailment. Use the Gallin-rigid coextension, which is then rigid in the source’s sense. Inextensibility is a boxed condition, so the assembly has to be available at every world. The plain premise supplies that, because Gallin Extensional Comprehension gives ND, ND with BF gives □ND, and □ND gives □BF, each a recorded result; both persistence conditions of the witness are boxed already.
results.notes: The source’s note states the predicate implication. This record applies it to the same comprehension witness; no converse is inferred. The part of the argument that uses BF only at the world of evaluation yields weak rigidity and is recorded separately as gallin-comprehension-and-bf-imply-weak-rigid-comprehension.

Let $X$ be given and let $Y$ be the coextension that Gallin Extensional Comprehension supplies, with $Y$ and $
eg Y$ persistent. Persistence of $Y$ gives, by T, its weak persistence, the first conjunct of weak rigidity. For weak inextensibility, let $Z$ satisfy $ orall ar x\, .\,Y[ ar x]	o\Box Z[ ar x]$. For any $ ar x$, either $Y[ ar x]$, and then $\Box Z[ ar x]$, or $
eg Y[ ar x]$, and then $\Box
eg Y[ ar x]$ by persistence of $
eg Y$ (with T); in both cases $\Box(Y[ ar x]	o Z[ ar x])$ by K. So $ orall ar x\, .\,\Box(Y[ ar x]	o Z[ ar x])$, and BF, applied to the abstract $\lambda ar x\, .\,Y[ ar x]	o Z[ ar x]$ one argument at a time, gives $\Box orall ar x\, .\,Y[ ar x]	o Z[ ar x]$, which is $Y\le Z$. Hence $Y$ is weakly rigid and coextensive with $X$.

sources: Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), §4, pp. 561–562.
results.proof: Let $c$ be a constant of type $\sigma$ and $F,G$ closed terms of type $\sigma\tau$ not containing $c$, with $Fc=Gc$. Enumerate the constants occurring in $F$ or $G$ as $\bar d$, all distinct from $c$, and abstract them: $F=F^\circ\bar d$, $G=G^\circ\bar d$ with $F^\circ,G^\circ$ closed and pure, by $\beta$. Let $P:=F^\circ\bar y\,x=G^\circ\bar y\,x$, pure with free variables $\bar y,x$. NI gives $\Box P[\bar d,c/\bar y,x]$, so Logical Necessity, left to right, gives $\forall\bar y x\, .\,P$. This closed pure truth is necessary by the empty-tuple instance of Logical Necessity, so $\Box\forall\bar y x\, .\,F^\circ\bar y x=G^\circ\bar y x$. CBF gives $\forall\bar y\, .\,\Box\forall x\, .\,F^\circ\bar yx=G^\circ\bar yx$ and Modalized Functionality, a theorem of C, gives $\forall\bar y\, .\,F^\circ\bar y=G^\circ\bar y$. Instantiating $\bar y:=\bar d$ yields $F=G$.
results.notes: Bacon derives the quantified form from Quantified Logical Necessity and Modalized Functionality and says the schematic form follows in the same way. Both directions of Logical Necessity are used: the witnessed direction to pass from the necessary identity at the constants to the universal claim, and No Pure Contingency to necessitate that claim before applying Modalized Functionality.

Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.6, p. 41.
results.proof: Distinctness Maximalism (pure) is equivalent to Possibility Maximalism (pure). Rigid Comprehension implies Boolean Completeness, which restricts to Countable Boolean Completeness, which gives the Necessity of Arithmetic (the source's Theorem 9). Possibility Maximalism (pure) is incompatible with the Necessity of Arithmetic (the source's Theorem 11): Gödel's first incompleteness theorem supplies an arithmetical sentence $A$ with $I\land A$ and $I\land\neg A$ both consistent with C, both are then possible, and the necessity schema forbids that. The source draws exactly this consequence for Rigid Comprehension in the remark after Theorem 11.

references.locator: §6, Theorem 11 and the following remark, p. 25

results.notes:
Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 28 September 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. The source's proof (Proposition 2.11, note 42) has two gaps, found that day by an agent working in the Lean-Classicism formalization project; the write-up sets out the paper's argument with the gaps marked. (a) Part (iv) of note 42 boxes a claim that holds pointwise in the object variables by BF, where □BF would be needed. Cian Dorr agreed. (b) The same part's "without loss of generality" step replaces the atom $w'$ by $w''$, the greatest lower bound of the propositions $p$ with $w\le(p=w')$. The proof then needs $w\le(w''=w')$, so that $w''$ is still possible and below $X^*z\land\neg Yz$ where $w$ holds; nothing in the premises gives this, and □BF does not help. A propositional structure in which that step fails is sketched in the project's VERIFICATION.md; it has not been extended to a model of C with all the premises, so it shows that the step needs an argument, not that the proposition is false. What is proved there: Actuality, Boolean Completeness and BF (at the relevant types), together with a restriction principle, give Rigid Comprehension with the paper's witness $X^*$. The restriction principle says that for all $p,q$ there is an $r$ with $p\le(r=q)$ such that $r\le s$ whenever $p\le(q\le s)$. It holds in C5, with $r:=q\land\Diamond p$. Restructured this way, gap (a) disappears, and gap (b) becomes the question whether the premises here give the restriction principle. What would settle the conjecture: a derivation of the restriction principle, or another argument, from boxed Atomicity, Boolean Completeness and BF; or a model of C with those three principles that fails Rigid Comprehension. The source's first cross-reference to Proposition 2.6 was replaced in the earlier transcription by Proposition 2.7; the statement and premises are unchanged.

Refuted, 1 October 2026: the model ultralimit-fork, from Branden Fitelson (with Claude and GPT-6 Astra), satisfies Classicism, □Atomicity, □Boolean Completeness, □BF and □Actuality, and fails Rigid Comprehension at type $t\to t$. It extends the propositional structure mentioned above to a model of C with all the premises, so gap (b) is a genuine gap. The record stays conjectured, as the map's convention requires; the model is the refuting evidence. Gap-free in the end is part (ii), which gets Actuality: Atomicity (type $t$) and Weak Inextensible Comprehension imply Actuality (atomicity-t-and-weakly-inextensible-comprehension-imply-actuality), and Boolean Completeness implies Weak Inextensible Comprehension.
