results.proof:
Let $w$ witness Actuality and fix $F$ of type $ ar\sigma t$. Put $C:=\lambda ar z\, .\,\Diamond(w\land F[ ar z])$. $C$ is coextensive with $F$: if $F[ ar z]$ then $w\land F[ ar z]$ is true, hence possible; if $
eg F[ ar z]$ then $w\le
eg F[ ar z]$ by Actuality, so $
eg\Diamond(w\land F[ ar z])$. For inextensibility, two theorems of C: (i) $
eg C[ ar z]$ is $\Box(w	o
eg F[ ar z])$, so by 4 $
eg C[ ar z]	o\Box
eg C[ ar z]$, and hence $(C[ ar z]	o\Box X[ ar z])	o\Box(C[ ar z]	o X[ ar z])$; (ii) therefore $( orall ar z\, .\,C[ ar z]	o\Box X[ ar z])	o orall ar z\, .\,\Box(C[ ar z]	o X[ ar z])$. The closed instance of BF for the property $\lambda ar z\, .\,C[ ar z]	o X[ ar z]$, universally closed in $X$, turns the consequent of (ii) into $\Box orall ar z\, .\,C[ ar z]	o X[ ar z]$, which is $C\le X$. So BF (this instance) implies $ orall X\, .\,( orall ar z\, .\,C[ ar z]	o\Box X[ ar z])	o C\le X$ in C; necessitating and using the necessity of that instance gives $\Box orall X\, .\,( orall ar z\, .\,C[ ar z]	o\Box X[ ar z])	o C\le X$, which is $\operatorname{Inextensible}(C)$. The box on BF is used exactly once, to discharge the instance under the leading box of inextensibility.

references.note: Definitions of inextensibility and the BF principle. The witness is not one the paper uses.

results.proof: Let $R^{\sigma\tau t}$ be necessarily serial and $F:=\lambda Z\,.\,\operatorname{Functional}(Z)\land\forall xy\,.\,(Zx)y\to(Rx)y$. By □Relational Choice, necessarily some $Z$ has $FZ$. Intensional Choice at $\sigma\tau t$ gives $G\le F$ that is necessarily uniquely instantiated. Then $S:=\lambda xy\,.\,\exists Z\,.\,GZ\land(Zx)y$ is necessarily functional, since at each world it is coextensive with the unique instance of $G$, a functional relation; and $S\le R$, since $G\le F$.
results.notes: With unboxed Relational Choice the argument fails: $F$ is then instantiated only at the evaluation point, while Intensional Choice needs it necessarily instantiated. Whether Relational Choice with Intensional Choice implies Modalized Relational Choice is open.

sources: Andrew Bacon, A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, Routledge, 2024, §8.2, Theorem 8.2, pp. 169–171.
results.notes: Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 11 October 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. The proof of Theorem 8.2 in the book has a gap, found while formalizing it in Lean and confirmed by Cian Dorr; the write-up sets out the book's argument with the gap marked. The argument proves $\forall p\,.\,Wp\to p=r$ at the evaluation point and then boxes it as following "from necessary assumptions". But step (i), that a $W$-proposition $p$ falls under some member of $H$ at every world, uses the claim that the world property $U=\lambda q\,.\,v\land q=p$ is $H$ because it is a world property accessible to $W$; that holds at the evaluation point, where $H$ is coextensive with the accessible world properties, but at another world $H$ is known only to be rigid, and need not contain the world properties built there from that world's $v$ and $p$. The step is needed exactly at such worlds, since $W$ may have no actual instance. Boxing Rigid Comprehension does not obviously help, since $r$ must be defined from a single actual $H$. What would settle the conjecture: a repair of step (i), or a model of C with □Strong Leibniz and Rigid Comprehension in which BF fails at some relational type. No recorded model refutes it, and without this record the map does not derive it. With □Rigid Comprehension and Rigid Power in place of Rigid Comprehension the conclusion holds (strong-leibniz-necessary-rigid-comprehension-and-rigid-power-imply-bf-relational, Cian Dorr), so a countermodel must fail one of those. The converse half of Theorem 8.2, atomicity-and-bf-relational-imply-strong-leibniz and its boxed form, is unaffected.

results.proof:
Fix an arbitrary admitted relational type $\tau$, and let $\varphi_\tau$
be the fully closed instance of the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals at that type.
The premise supplies $\Box\varphi_\tau$. The axiom T of C gives
$\Box\varphi_\tau\to\varphi_\tau$, so modus ponens yields
$\varphi_\tau$. Applying this argument separately at every relational type
gives the conclusion schema. No metalinguistic type quantifier moves inside
the box, and no necessitation of an optional premise is used.

results.proof:
First the unboxed statement, for a relational type $	au= ar\sigma t$. Let $X^	au
e ot$. Intensionality’s contrapositive gives $\Diamond\exists ar y\, .\,X ar y$, and BF at the argument types gives $ ar x$ with $\Diamond X ar x$. The type-t Strong Leibniz Biconditionals give a strong world $w\le X ar x$: $w
e ot$ and $\Box orall q\, .\,(w\le q\lor w\le
eg q)$. Put $W:=\lambda ar y\, .\,w\land ar y= ar x$. Then $W
e ot$, since $W ar x=w$, and $W\le X$, since $\Box(w	o X ar x)$ and Leibniz’s law give $\Box orall ar y\, .\,W ar y	o X ar y$ by K. $W$ is a strong world at $	au$: under the box, for any $Y^	au$, instantiate the strong-world clause of $w$ at $q:=Y ar x$; if $w\le Y ar x$ then $\Box orall ar y\, .\,W ar y	o Y ar y$, that is $W\le Y$, by the same K step, and if $w\le
eg Y ar x$ then $W\le
eg Y$ likewise; so $\Box orall Y\, .\,(W\le Y\lor W\le
eg Y)$, the passage under the outer box being by necessitation and K since each step is a theorem of C. For each $	au$ this derives the closed instance $\mathrm{SL}_	au$ from $\mathrm{SL}_t$ and finitely many BF instances in C; necessitating that conditional and applying K gives $\Box\mathrm{SL}_	au$ from $\Box\mathrm{SL}_t$ and $\Box$BF.

references.note: Strong worlds and the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals.

results.notes: The unboxed form, Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t) + BF ⇒ Strong Leibniz Biconditionals, is already derivable on the map through Atomicity: SL (t) gives Atomicity (t), Atomicity (t) + BF gives Atomicity, and Atomicity + BF gives SL. The direct construction above proves it in one step and is what is necessitated here; the boxed form was not derivable, since no record boxes the type-t instance of Atomicity. Only BF at the argument types of the target type is used, as in atomicity-t-and-bf-imply-atomicity.

results.proof: Fix the type tuple, with $P_F$ and $R_F$ as in weakly-rigid-power-implies-rigid-power. □Tame Rigidity at this type gives, necessarily, that every weakly rigid relation is rigid; with T the converse holds at every world. So $\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}$ and $\operatorname{Rigid}$ are necessarily coextensive at this type, $P_F$ and $R_F$ are necessarily coextensive, and they are identical in C. Now suppose $\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(F)$. Tame Rigidity (by T) makes $F$ rigid; Rigid Power makes $R_F$ rigid, so by T weakly rigid; so $P_F=R_F$ is weakly rigid. Without the box the argument fails at weak inextensibility: $Z:=R_F$ satisfies $\forall X\, .\,P_FX\to\Box ZX$ at the evaluation point, so the weak inextensibility of $P_F$ requires $P_F\le R_F$, which is Tame Rigidity below $F$ at every accessible world.

references.note: T for the fixed background modality.

results.proof: Apply Intensional Choice at the type $\sigma\sigma t$ to $F:=\lambda R\, .\,\operatorname{WO}(R)$, which is necessarily instantiated by $\Box$Well-Ordering. This gives $G\le F$ that is necessarily uniquely instantiated. Put $R':=\lambda x\,y\, .\,\exists R\, .\,GR\land(Rx)y$. At any world the unique instance $R_0$ of $G$ there is a well-order, since $G\le F$, and $R'$ is coextensive with $R_0$ there. WO depends only on the extension of its argument at the evaluation point (Background), so $\operatorname{WO}(R')$ holds there. Hence $\Box\operatorname{WO}(R')$.
results.notes: Intensional Choice is used at the type $\sigma\sigma t$ to obtain Modal Well-Ordering at $\sigma$.

results.proof:
Let $c$ be a constant of $\Sigma$ of some relational type $	au$. The pure formulas $x=	op_	au$ and $x
e	op_	au$ have witnesses, so Witnessed Possibility gives $\Diamond(c=	op_	au)$ and $\Diamond(c
e	op_	au)$. By excluded middle one of the closed $\Sigma$-sentences $c=	op_	au$, $c
e	op_	au$ is true, and No Contingency (signature Σ) makes it necessary, contradicting the possibility of the other.
results.notes: Hence No Contingency (signature Σ) excludes Logical Necessity, Separated Structure, Possibly Witnessed Possibility and Maximalist Classicism for Σ, while it is consistent with No Pure Contingency and holds in every one-world model.

results.proof: Applying the schema to the closed sentences $\neg P[\bar c/\bar x]$ and $\neg Q[\bar d/\bar y]$ and contraposing gives $\Diamond P[\bar c/\bar x]\to P[\bar c/\bar x]$ and likewise for $Q$. So the antecedent of Modal Freedom (signature Σ) yields $P[\bar c/\bar x]\land Q[\bar d/\bar y]$, and T gives its possibility.
results.notes: The signature analogue of the equivalence between the empty-constant instance of Modal Freedom and No Pure Contingency.

results.proof: Every closed instance of Actuality is a closed sentence of the pure language, since the principle is stated with object-language quantifiers and contains no nonlogical constant. Given Actuality, each of those instances is true, and No Pure Contingency makes a true closed pure sentence necessary. So every closed instance is necessary, which is what the boxed principle asserts. Any type range and side conditions stay outside the box, as the Modal scope convention requires.

references.note: Formulation of No Pure Contingency. The draft does not draw this consequence.

results.notes: One of a uniform family. No Pure Contingency carries any pure principle of the map to its boxed form, because a boxed principle here says exactly that each closed instance of the base is necessary. The argument turns on the base being stated with quantifiers rather than as a schema over arbitrary formulas, since an instance carrying a nonlogical constant would fall outside No Pure Contingency.

results.proof:
The type-$e$ instance of Intensional Choice fails in symmetric-all-surjections, a model of C. Let $a$ be an individual and $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x
e a$, which is necessarily instantiated since every world has infinitely many individuals. Suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated, pinned down by a finite $N
i a$. Let $h$ be a surjection sending all of $N$ to one individual $p$; at $h$, $G$ has a single instance $y
eq p$, since $G\le F$ and $h(a)=p$. A permutation $\sigma$ fixing $p$ and moving $y$ gives an arrow $\sigma\circ h$ agreeing with $h$ on $N$, so by pinning $G$ has the same extension at both arrows, while by symmetry its extension at $\sigma\circ h$ is $\{\sigma(y)\}$. Contradiction. So the negation of that closed pure instance is consistent with C, Possibility Maximalism (pure) makes it possible, and □Intensional Choice says the instance is necessary.

references.note: The symmetric ideally full action models.

results.proof:
Theorem 11 of the source, applied to C. The theorems of C are recursively enumerable, and C is consistent with $I$, since $I^*$ and hence $I$ hold in the full Henkin model with a countably infinite individual domain. So the arithmetical sentences $A$ with $C\vdash I	o A$ form a consistent, recursively enumerable extension of Peano arithmetic (the source's Lemma 1 supplies the axioms). By Gödel's first incompleteness theorem there is an arithmetical sentence $A$ for which neither $I	o A$ nor $I	o
eg A$ is a theorem of C, so $I\land A$ and $I\land
eg A$ are both consistent with C. Both are closed pure sentences, so Possibility Maximalism (pure) gives $\Diamond(I\land A)$ and $\Diamond(I\land
eg A)$. But the instance of the Necessity of Arithmetic at $A$ says $\Box(I	o A)$ or $\Box(I	o
eg A)$, and by K each disjunct contradicts one of the two possibilities.
results.notes: The source's theorem is general: the maximalization of any recursively enumerable extension of HK consistent with $I$ refutes some instance of the necessity schema. The record uses Possibility Maximalism (pure) directly; the equivalent Distinctness Maximalism form gives the same through the recorded equivalence. The argument is metatheoretic in two places, the recursive enumerability of C and Gödel's theorem, like the consistency side condition of Possibility Maximalism itself.

sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §2.4, pp. 35–37 (Distinctness); §3.2, Definition 3.6 and Proposition 3.7, pp. 47–48 (full Henkin models); §2.3, n. 47, p. 32 (Infinity).
results.proof:
For $k\ge1$ let $E_k$ be the closed pure sentence saying that there are exactly $k$ individuals, $\exists x_1^e\cdots x_k^e\, .\,( igwedge_{i<j}x_i
e x_j)\land orall y^e\, .\, igvee_i y=x_i$. Fix $n$ and take $E_1,\ldots,E_n$. For $i
e j$ the identity $E_i=E_j$ is closed and pure, and C does not prove it. A full Henkin model whose individual domain has exactly $i$ members is a model of C in which $E_i$ is true and $E_j$ is false, and at type $t$ that model's propositions are its two truth values, so the two sentences denote different things there. Distinctness Maximalism therefore gives $E_i
e E_j$. So $E_1,\ldots,E_n$ are $n$ pairwise distinct propositions, which is the $n$-th instance of Infinity at type $t$.

references.note: Formulations of Distinctness and Infinity, and the full Henkin models that supply the non-theoremhood side condition. The draft does not draw the connection between them.

results.notes:
Recorded from Distinctness Maximalism because the proof uses its non-theoremhood side condition directly. The equivalent Possibility Maximalism form gives the same result through the recorded equivalence. The witnesses need not be possible propositions, and at most one of them is true. What Distinctness Maximalism supplies is that C proves no identity among them. Only the type-$t$ instance follows, since the witnesses are propositions about how many individuals there are, not individuals.

The argument does not lift to the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$, and it is worth recording how far it does reach. For each fixed $k$ it refutes the claim that there are exactly $k$ propositions. If there were, then among the $k+1$ sentences $E_1,\ldots,E_{k+1}$ two would have to coincide, so C proves the finite disjunction of those identities, and Distinctness Maximalism refutes every disjunct. That is the schema over again, one sentence at a time. The axiom asks for the same of every cardinality falling under $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$, including ones that no closed term names, and Distinctness Maximalism bears only on identities between closed pure terms, so it says nothing about the domain over which $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$ quantifies. Any one derivation uses finitely many of its instances, and those are satisfiable while the universal property still carries a cardinality that the induction clause admits. The route through Atomlessness is closed too, since the map carries a model of the signature Distinctness Maximalism schema that satisfies Actuality, and Actuality excludes Atomlessness.

Added 20 September 2026: a different argument does reach the axiom. Applying the consistency side condition once, to the single sentence that every finite cardinality has a possibly instantiated successor, gives that sentence outright by persistence, and from it the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ follows in C; see pure-possibility-implies-axiom-of-infinity-t. The limits described above concern the numeral-by-numeral argument recorded here.

results.proof: Write $g(Z)$ for $(\operatorname{Suc}_e Z)(\lambda x^e\, .\,\top)$ and let $\Pi$ be the closed pure sentence $\forall Z^{(et)t}\, .\,\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_e(Z)\to\Diamond g(Z)$: there could be any positive number of individuals. Zero must be left out, since Existence makes $\mathbf{0}_e(\lambda x\, .\,\top)$ identical to $\bot$. $\Pi$ is true at the root of the model coalesced-all-finite-individual-domains, so it is consistent with C and Possibility Maximalism gives $\Diamond\Pi$. Being a finite cardinality is persistent, and the defined necessity satisfies 4, so $\Diamond\Pi$ yields $\Pi$ itself. Under $\Pi$ the map $g$ is injective on finite cardinalities: two finite cardinalities are either identical or necessarily share no instance, by an induction that stays inside the presentation $\operatorname{Suc}_e$ supplies, and the second disjunct is excluded when the two values of $g$ coincide and are possible. Hence the propositions $g(Z)$, $Z$ finite, carry a copy of the successor structure: the relation taking $g(Z)$ to $g(\operatorname{Suc}_e Z)$, and every other proposition to itself, is total and injective on $\lambda p\, .\,\top$ and misses $g(\mathbf{0}_e)$. A property with such a relation has no finite cardinality, by induction on the cardinality. So no finite cardinality of type $(tt)t$ holds of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$. The full proof, with the six lemmas, is in the write-up.

references.note: Formulations of Possibility and Infinity, the S4 laws of the defined necessity, the full Henkin models, and the coalesced-sum construction that the consistency model follows. The draft does not draw the connection between Possibility and the Axiom of Infinity.

results.notes: Recorded from Possibility Maximalism because the proof applies its consistency side condition to one sentence, $\Pi$, which quantifies over every finite cardinality at once. That is what reaches the domain over which $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}$ quantifies, where the numeral-by-numeral argument recorded for the Infinity schema could not. The equivalent Distinctness Maximalism form gives the same result through the recorded equivalence, so Pure Maximalist Classicism implies the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$. ND is never used. The sentence $\Pi$ is not implied by the Axiom of Infinity at type $e$, by the model full-henkin-infinite-base. The argument can also be run entirely at type $t$, using the powers of two as the possible numbers of propositions; the write-up sketches this variant without carrying it out.

results.proof: Let $R^{\sigma\sigma t}$ be an equivalence relation and write $[x]$ for the cell $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$. The relation $U^{(\sigma t)\sigma t}$ with $(UC)y:=Cy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Cz$ is serial, so Relational Choice gives a functional $S$ with $(SC)y\to(UC)y$. Put $Fy:=\exists x\, .\,(S[x])y$. Existence: given $x$, functionality gives $y$ with $(S[x])y$; the cell $[x]$ has the instance $x$, so $(U[x])y$ gives $(Rx)y$, and $Fy$ holds. Uniqueness: suppose $(Rx)y$, $Fy$, $(Rx)y'$ and $Fy'$, with witnesses $x_1$ and $x_2$, so that $(S[x_1])y$ and $(S[x_2])y'$. As before $(Rx_1)y$ and $(Rx_2)y'$, so $x_1$, $y$, $x$, $y'$ and $x_2$ lie in one cell and $\forall z\, .\,(Rx_1)z\leftrightarrow(Rx_2)z$. Extensionality at type $\sigma t$ gives $[x_1]=[x_2]$, and functionality of $S$ gives $y=y'$.
results.notes: The only use of Extensionality is to identify the coextensive cells $[x_1]$ and $[x_2]$. In C alone properties are identical only when necessarily coextensive, which the hypothesis does not supply; see the recorded question relational-choice-r-implies-transversal-choice-r. The arrow is also derivable through Extensionality implies Rigid Comprehension and the arrow from Relational Choice with Weak Rigid Comprehension; it is recorded directly because it is the argument usually given.

results.proof: First, two weakly rigid properties $C$ and $C'$ of type $\sigma t$ that are coextensive are identical. If $Cz$ then $C'z$, and weak persistence of $C'$ gives $\Box C'z$; so $\forall z\, .\,Cz\to\Box C'z$, and weak inextensibility of $C$ with $X:=C'$ gives $C\le C'$, that is $\Box\forall z\, .\,Cz\to C'z$. By symmetry $C'\le C$, so $\Box\forall z\, .\,Cz\leftrightarrow C'z$, and Intensionality (necessarily coextensive relations are identical, a theorem of C, Classicism §1.5) gives $C=C'$. Now let $R^{\sigma\sigma t}$ be an equivalence relation. Relational Choice at types $(\sigma t,\sigma)$ gives a functional subrelation $S$ of the serial $(UC)y:=Cy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Cz$. Put $Fy:=\exists C\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(C)\land(\forall z\, .\,Cz\leftrightarrow(Ry)z)\land(SC)y$. Existence: given $x$, Weak Rigid Comprehension gives a weakly rigid $C$ coextensive with $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$; $C$ has the instance $x$, so the $y$ with $(SC)y$ satisfies $Cy$, hence $(Rx)y$; then $\lambda z\, .\,(Ry)z$ is coextensive with $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$ and so with $C$, which gives $Fy$. Uniqueness: if $(Rx)y$, $(Rx)y'$, $Fy$ through $C$ and $Fy'$ through $C'$, then $C$ and $C'$ are both coextensive with the cell of $x$, hence with each other, so $C=C'$ by the first paragraph, and $(SC)y\land(SC)y'$ gives $y=y'$ by functionality.
results.notes: Weak rigidity is the weakest rigidity condition on the map, so the same proof runs from full Rigid Comprehension, and through the recorded arrows from Extensionality, Gallin comprehension with BF, C5 with Actuality, and boxed Functional Choice, which gives boxed Plenitude and so C5 and Actuality. Only the type-$\sigma t$ instance of the comprehension principle is used.

sources: Christopher Sun, observation communicated by Zachary Goodsell on 25 September 2026, that the transversal formulation of choice is claimed in the literature without a proof from Relational Choice.
results.notes:
Does Relational Choice alone give a transversal for every equivalence relation? Christopher Sun observed that the literature claims this without proof. The converse is recorded. The quotient argument chooses from each cell $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$ and needs the cells of two members of one class to be the same property; in C that is necessary coextension, and the hypothesis gives actual coextension only. No definable substitute for the cell helps, since an operation definable from $R$ identifies $x$ with $x'$ only when they are necessarily indiscernible with respect to $R$. A Zermelo-style well-ordering argument breaks at the same point: coextensive but distinct stages receive different chosen elements. The expectation is that the implication fails. What would settle it: a proof that uses the chosen relation to break the symmetry between coextensive cells, or a model of C with Relational Choice that is not extensionally full at its evaluation point. Every recorded model of Relational Choice is extensionally full there, in that every set of tuples from the domains is the extension of a rigid element, and that fullness verifies Transversal Choice by the same metatheoretic choice, so none separates the two. Symmetric Henkin models in the Fraenkel–Mostowski style cannot separate them either; see the write-up.
Update of 28 September 2026: Christopher Sun showed on 26 September that Transversal Choice is equivalent to Relational Choice together with Transversal (transversal-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice), so this question is equivalent to whether Relational Choice implies Transversal. Anything that implies Transversal, such as Actuality, closes the gap.

results.proof: Choose a rigid property F coextensive with self-identity. Persistence gives $\forall x\, .\,\Box Fx$ and BF gives $\Box\forall x\, .\,Fx$. The inextensibility of F supplies boxed BF with its quantifiers restricted to F. Inside the box everything is F, so the restrictions can be removed. This is the boxed, universally closed BF instance at the chosen type.

sources: Christopher Sun, Possible Worlds Without Atomicity, draft of September 2026.
results.proof: Lemma: coextensive weakly rigid relations are identical. Let $F$ and $G$ be weakly rigid with $\forall\bar x\, .\,F[\bar x]\leftrightarrow G[\bar x]$. If $F[\bar x]$ then $G[\bar x]$, and the weak persistence of $G$ gives $\Box G[\bar x]$. So $\forall\bar x\, .\,F[\bar x]\to\Box G[\bar x]$, and the weak inextensibility of $F$, instantiated at $G$, gives $F\le G$. Symmetrically $G\le F$. Together these say $\Box\forall\bar x\, .\,F[\bar x]\leftrightarrow G[\bar x]$, and necessarily coextensive relations are identical in C (Intensionality), so $F=G$. Now let $F$ be weakly rigid. Rigid Comprehension at the same type supplies a rigid $G$ coextensive with $F$. A rigid relation is weakly rigid, since T strips the leading boxes from both its conjuncts. By the lemma $F=G$, so $F$ is rigid.

references.note: Intensionality and T.

results.notes: The lemma uses only the unboxed persistence of $F$ and $G$, so Rigid Comprehension makes every very weakly rigid relation rigid as well. With Rigid Comprehension ⇒ Weak Rigid Comprehension, this gives Sun's equivalence of Rigid Comprehension with Tame Rigidity plus Weak Rigid Comprehension.

results.proof: Let $R^{\sigma\sigma t}$ be an equivalence relation, and write $[x]$ for its cell $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$. Transversal at $\sigma$ gives $F^{(\sigma t)t}$ such that each property is coextensive with exactly one $F$-property. Relational Choice at types $(\sigma t,\sigma)$, applied to the serial relation $(UC)y:=Cy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Cz$, gives a functional $S$ with $(SC)y\to(UC)y$. Put $Gy:=\exists Y\, .\,FY\land(\forall z\, .\,Yz\leftrightarrow(Ry)z)\land(SY)y$. Existence: given $x$, let $Y_x$ be the $F$-property coextensive with $[x]$. It has the instance $x$, so the $y$ with $(SY_x)y$ satisfies $Y_xy$, hence $(Rx)y$. Then $[y]$ is coextensive with $[x]$ and so with $Y_x$, and $Gy$ holds through $Y_x$. Uniqueness: suppose $(Rx)y$ and $(Rx)y'$, with $Gy$ through $Y$ and $Gy'$ through $Y'$. Then $Y$ is coextensive with $[y]$, $[y]$ with $[x]$, $[x]$ with $[y']$, and $[y']$ with $Y'$; so $Y$ and $Y'$ are $F$-properties coextensive with $[x]$, and $Y=Y'$ by the uniqueness clause of Transversal. Now $(SY)y$ and $(SY)y'$, so $y=y'$ by functionality of $S$. Thus $G$ is a transversal of $R$.
results.notes: With the converse arrows from Transversal Choice to Transversal and to Relational Choice, Transversal Choice is equivalent to Transversal together with Relational Choice. The argument is the quotient argument of relational-choice-and-extensionality-imply-transversal-choice, with the $F$-representative of each cell in place of the cell itself; this is the step Relational Choice alone does not supply. Consequently Relational Choice implies Transversal Choice if and only if it implies Transversal.

results.proof: Let $U^{\sigma\tau t}$ be serial. For $x^\sigma$ and $y^\tau$ write $\langle x,y\rangle$ for the rigid pair $\lambda u^\sigma v^\tau\, .\,u=x\land v=y$, of the admitted type $\sigma\tau t$; the case $\tau=e$ is included. Pairing is injective: if $\langle x,y\rangle=\langle x',y'\rangle$, apply both sides to $x$ and $y$. The left side is $x=x\land y=y$, a theorem of H, so by Logical Equivalence it is $\top$; hence $x=x'\land y=y'$ is $\top$ and so true. Call $P$ a $U$-pair if $\exists x y\, .\,(Ux)y\land P=\langle x,y\rangle$. Let $E$ relate two $U$-pairs when some $x$ is the first coordinate of both, and relate any two non-$U$-pairs. By injectivity $E$ is an equivalence relation on type $\sigma\tau t$, and the cell of a $U$-pair $\langle x,y_0\rangle$ consists exactly of the pairs $\langle x,y\rangle$ with $(Ux)y$. Transversal Choice gives $F^{(\sigma\tau t)t}$ with exactly one instance in each cell. Put $(Sx)y:=(Ux)y\land F\langle x,y\rangle$; this is a subrelation of $U$. Given $x$, seriality gives $y_0$ with $(Ux)y_0$, so the cell of $\langle x,y_0\rangle$ has a unique $F$-instance $\langle x,y_x\rangle$, and $(Sx)y$ holds iff $\langle x,y\rangle$ is that instance iff $y=y_x$. So $S$ is functional.
results.notes: Transversal Choice is therefore at least as strong as Relational Choice over C. Whether it is strictly stronger is the recorded question relational-choice-r-implies-transversal-choice-r.

results.proof: See the write-up. Suppose a preorder $R$ has upper bounds for all its chains and no maximal element. Relational Choice, which follows from Transversal Choice, gives a functional relation choosing, for each chain $C$, something strictly above all of $C$. Composing it with a transversal of coextensiveness at $\sigma t$, which Transversal Choice also gives, makes it extensional: coextensive chains receive the same value. Lewin's argument then translates step by step, with properties for sets and existential quantification for unions: the union of the conforming properties is conforming, and extending it by its chosen value gives a conforming property not included in it, a contradiction.

references.note: Lewin proves Zorn's Lemma for partial orders on sets from a choice function. The translation replaces sets by properties and the choice function by a functional relation, adapts the argument to preorders, and uses Transversal Choice to make the relation extensional, which Lewin uses at four steps without comment.

results.notes: Only extensionality of the choice relation goes beyond Relational Choice: at four steps two properties are shown to be coextensive and must receive the same value. Since Zorn's Lemma implies Well-Ordering and so Transversal Choice, proving it from Relational Choice alone would settle whether Relational Choice implies Transversal Choice, which is open.

results.proof: Take the propositional case first. Given $F^{tt}$, let $C^{tt}$ be weakly rigid and coextensive with $F$, and put $q:=\exists p\, .\,Cp\land p$. Every $F$ proposition $p$ is $C$, hence necessarily $C$ by persistence, so $p$ entails $Cp\land p$ and thereby $q$; so $q$ is an upper bound of the $F$ propositions. Now suppose every $F$ proposition entails $r$. The $C$ propositions are the $F$ propositions, so every $C$ proposition entails $r$; entailments are necessary if true, so $\forall p\, .\,Cp\to\Box(p\le r)$. Weak inextensibility with $X:=\lambda p\, .\,(p\le r)$ gives $C\le X$, so at every world $Cp$ implies $p\le r$; hence $Cp\land p$ entails $r$ whatever $p$ may be, and $q\le r$. So $q$ is a least upper bound of the $F$ propositions. The same reasoning with extra parameters gives the least-upper-bound form at every relational type, and that form is equivalent in C to the greatest-lower-bound form in which the principle is stated.

results.proof: See the write-up. Given a well-order $R$, take weakly rigid properties coextensive with the initial segments of $R$, and a weakly rigid property $R^*$ coextensive with being one of them. Weak inextensibility of $R^*$ carries facts that hold necessarily of each actual segment to every instance of $R^*$ at every world. In this way $R^*$ is necessarily a chain under $\le$ that is well-ordered by $\le$; BF at $\sigma$ makes its instances necessarily cover $\sigma$; and an induction using weak inextensibility of the strict segments shows that its instances necessarily separate any two distinct individuals. Then $\lambda x\,y\, .\,\forall M\, .\,R^*M\land My\to Mx$ is necessarily a well-order.
results.notes: Well-Ordering is used only at the evaluation point, Weak Rigid Comprehension only at the types $\sigma t$ and $(\sigma t)t$, and BF only at $\sigma$, once. Modal Well-Ordering implies its own necessitation and Intensional Choice, so the premises give boxed Intensional Choice; this improves on bf-weak-rigid-comprehension-atomicity-and-relational-choice-imply-intensional-choice by trading Atomicity and Relational Choice for Well-Ordering. e	op_	au)$. If $c=	op_	au$, then by Leibniz's law $(c
e	op_	au)=(	op_	au

e	op_	au)$, i.e. $(c

results.proof: Fix $\sigma$ and apply Zorn's Lemma at $\sigma\sigma t$. For $S^{\sigma\sigma t}$ let $\operatorname{Fld}(S):=\lambda x\, .\,(Sx)x$, and call $S$ good if $\forall x\,y\, .\,(Sx)y\to(Sx)x\land(Sy)y$ and $\operatorname{WO}(S,\operatorname{Fld}(S))$. Say $S\sqsubseteq S'$ ($S'$ end-extends $S$) if $\forall x\,y\, .\,(Sx)y\to(S'x)y$ and $\forall x\,y\, .\,(Sx)x\land(S'y)x\to(Sy)x$; this is reflexive and transitive, and if $S\sqsubseteq S'$ then $S'$ agrees with $S$ on $\operatorname{Fld}(S)$. Put $(\mathsf RS)S':=\neg\operatorname{Good}(S)\lor(\operatorname{Good}(S')\land S\sqsubseteq S')$, a preorder on $\sigma\sigma t$ in which everything not good lies below everything. Chains have upper bounds: if $\mathsf R$ totally orders $\mathcal X$, its good members are $\sqsubseteq$-comparable, and $T:=\lambda x\,y\, .\,\exists S\, .\,\mathcal XS\land\operatorname{Good}(S)\land(Sx)y$ end-extends each of them. $T$ is good: any finitely many points of $\operatorname{Fld}(T)$ lie in the field of one good member $S$, on which $T$ agrees with $S$; and if $Y\subseteq\operatorname{Fld}(T)$ has an instance in $\operatorname{Fld}(S)$, the $S$-minimal instance of $\lambda w\, .\,Yw\land(Sw)w$ is $T$-minimal in $Y$, since $(Tw)m$ with $(Sm)m$ gives $(Sw)m$. So $T$ is an $\mathsf R$-upper bound of $\mathcal X$. Zorn's Lemma gives a maximal $m$. It is good, since otherwise $(\mathsf Rm)(\lambda x\,y\, .\,\bot)$ holds and the converse fails, the empty relation being good. If some $z$ had $\neg(mz)z$, then $m':=\lambda x\,y\, .\,(mx)y\lor((mx)x\land y=z)\lor(x=z\land y=z)$, which puts $z$ on top, would be good with $m\sqsubseteq m'$; maximality gives $m'\sqsubseteq m$, so $(mz)z$, a contradiction. So $\operatorname{Fld}(m)$ is coextensive with $\lambda x\, .\,\top$, and $\operatorname{WO}(m)$, since WO depends only on extensions.
results.notes: The standard argument. End-extension of relations is only a preorder, since coextensive but distinct relations end-extend each other, which is why Zorn's Lemma is recorded for preorders. The non-good relations are placed at the bottom so that the preorder is defined on the whole type.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: At a type $\sigma\to t$ a root entity is a pair $(G_0,(G_n)_n)$ with $G_0$ any function on the root domain and $G_n$ in the full domain of $M_n$; entailment is componentwise. Atomicity: below a nonzero $G$ lies the atom that is true at the root of one argument $a$ with $G_0(a)=1$ and bottom in every component, or, if $G_0=0$, the atom that is bottom at the root and in all but one component $M_n$, where it is an atom of that full model below $G_n$. Both kinds of atom are strong worlds: at the root they entail every entity or its negation, being singletons in one coordinate and bottom elsewhere, and their shifts to the components are bottom or atoms of a one-world full model. So the Strong Leibniz Biconditionals hold at every type. Boolean Completeness: the componentwise meet of any set of root entities is a root entity and is the greatest lower bound. Rigid Comprehension: given $X$ with root extension $E$, let $Y$ have root component $X_0$ and, in $M_n$, the projection of $E$ to the $n$-th coordinates; $Y$ is persistent, since a root instance has its projection in every component, and inextensible, since a relation necessary of every root instance contains those projections, while in the one-world components persistence and inextensibility are automatic. Each component is a full Henkin model, in which all of these hold, so the boxed forms hold at the root; Countable Boolean Completeness, the weak rigid comprehension principles and Necessity of Arithmetic follow by the recorded results.

So Intensional Choice holds at every world.

At the root every truth is ND-necessary (recorded), so every truth is 5-necessary there. Every other world is a one-world Henkin model $M_n$, in which $\Box$ is the identity operator, hence so is every operator in the tower from $\Box$ to $\Box_5$, and every truth is 5-necessary. So the principle holds at every world.

settings.construction: For a signature Σ with countably infinitely many individual constants and at least one relational constant, take a set of action models for L(Σ) complete for C(Σ), and coalesce them at a new root whose individual domain is the set of individual constants, each constant denoting itself there and being carried by the distinguished arrow to each component onto its interpretation in that component; relational constants are glued as in Definition E.2, with free root extensions. Evaluation point: the root.

arguments.text: The root satisfies Maximalist Classicism for Σ, since every C(Σ)-consistent sentence holds at some component root. It satisfies Possibility+ (signature Σ): for P with free individual variables x̄, instantiate x̄ by pairwise distinct root individuals, that is, distinct constants c̄′ not occurring in P; P[c̄′/x̄] is C(Σ)-consistent because the c̄′ are fresh, so it is possible at the root. The instances of the pure form follow.

Distinct constants denote distinct root individuals, so there are infinitely many individuals at the root, giving the Infinity Schema at type e and, the root domains being as full as possible so that the numeral intensions exist, the Axiom of Infinity at type e.

arguments.text: Tame Rigidity fails at a relational argument type in models of C (ultralimit-fork, symmetric-qualitative-links), so some component $M$ refutes it at its root $M_0$: some $F_M$ of type $\sigma\to t$, $\sigma$ relational, is weakly rigid there but not rigid. A root entity $F$ of that type is a root extension $F_o$ together with a component $F_N$ in each component $N$, and a formula about $F$ at a world of $N$ is the same formula about $F_N$ in $N$. Since the components of root entities are arbitrary, $F$ is weakly inextensible at the root exactly when, for every $N$, every $X_N$ that necessarily holds of the $N$-components of the members of $F_o$ has $F_N\le X_N$. For each other component $N$ fix $z_N$, and for each $y$ in the extension of $F_M$ at $M_0$ let $x_y$ be the root entity with $M$-component $y$ and $N$-components $z_N$, free at the root by the condition. Put $F_o:=\{x_y\}$, $F_N:=\lambda y\, .\,y=z_N$, a haecceity, rigid in every model of C, and keep $F_M$. Then $F$ is persistent and weakly inextensible at the root, each component's condition being the weak inextensibility of its own component, but not inextensible, since $F_M$ is not inextensible in $M$ and every arrow from the root into $M$ factors through the distinguished one. So Tame Rigidity fails at the root.

arguments.text:
The transfer of tame-rigidity-component, applied to a rigid relation whose power property is not rigid. The pure sentence $\exists A^{tt}\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(A)\land\neg\operatorname{Rigid} (\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le A)$ is consistent with C (it holds in the one-individual variants of finite-support-pair-injections-or-collapses and symmetric-collapse-pair, with $A:=\top$), so some component $m$ satisfies it at its root, with witness $A$. Its extension $D$ there is nonempty: otherwise weak inextensibility tested on $\bot$ makes $A=\bot$, whose power property is the haecceity of $\bot$, which is rigid.
For $p\in D$ let $\widehat p$ be the root proposition false at the root, with $m$-component $p$ and $\bot$ in every other component; let $F$ have root extension $\{\widehat p:p\in D\}$, $m$-component $A$, and in each other component $i$ the haecceity of $\bot$. Both are in the domain, the root domains being fullest. $F$ is weakly persistent at the root, $A$ and the haecceities being persistent. It is weakly inextensible there: if $H$ necessarily holds of every $\widehat p$, its root extension contains them, $A\le H_m$ by the weak inextensibility of $A$, and the haecceity of $\bot$ entails $H_i$; entailment in the sum is componentwise. Every other accessible world lies in a component, where $F$'s components are rigid; so $F$ is rigid. The $m$-component of its power property is that of $A$, transport respecting abstraction, rigidity and entailment, and every arrow into $m$ factors through the distinguished one; so it is not rigid. Rigid Power fails at the root, at type $t\to t$.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 7 (p. 78): the arrows are the maps $f_n$, for $n$ a power of $2$, sending $m$ to the greatest multiple of $n$ not exceeding $m$; $f_1$ is the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. The individuals are the natural numbers, acted on by the arrows themselves. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals are the natural numbers.
met.arrows-finitely-determined: Each $\{f_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set: $f_n$ is the only arrow sending $n$ to $n$ and $n-1$ to $0$.
met.actual-world-pinned: $\{f_1\}$, $f_1$ being the identity, is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$.
met.pinned-atoms: Each $\{f_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set ($\{n-2,n-1,n\}$ for $n>1$, $\{0,1\}$ for the identity).
met.unbounded-haecceities: With $A:=\mathbb N$: the strongest persistent property with extension $\mathbb N$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ has, at $f_m$, the multiples of $\min\{m,n\}$ as extension.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: An arrow $f_n$ is determined by its value at any $m\ge n$ and all $f_n$ with $n>N$ agree on $\{0,\ldots,N\}$, so the finitely pinned propositions are exactly the finite and cofinite sets of arrows. Let $F$ be the family of singletons $\{f_n\}$ for $n$ an even power of $2$: a finitely pinned superset of $\bigcup F$ is a cofinite set, and removing from it an odd-power member gives a strictly smaller one.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is in the domain, being pinned down by a finite set; at every arrow some composite is not the identity, since every other arrow is non-injective, so it is necessary at no arrow, and a non-identity arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: A non-identity arrow is non-injective, so no arrow composes it back to the identity.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 7 (p. 78): the arrows are the maps $f_n$, for $n$ a power of $2$, sending $m$ to the greatest multiple of $n$ not exceeding $m$; $f_1$ is the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. There is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on $\mathbb N$, which supplies the pinning sets. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.

met.arrows-finitely-determined: Each $\{f_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set: $f_n$ is the only arrow sending $n$ to $n$ and $n-1$ to $0$.
met.actual-world-pinned: $\{f_1\}$, $f_1$ being the identity, is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$.
met.pinned-atoms: Each $\{f_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set ($\{n-2,n-1,n\}$ for $n>1$, $\{0,1\}$ for the identity).
met.unbounded-haecceities: With $A:=\mathbb N$: the strongest persistent property with extension $\mathbb N$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ has, at $f_m$, the multiples of $\min\{m,n\}$ as extension.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: An arrow $f_n$ is determined by its value at any $m\ge n$ and all $f_n$ with $n>N$ agree on $\{0,\ldots,N\}$, so the finitely pinned propositions are exactly the finite and cofinite sets of arrows. met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.

references.locator: Appendix D, Proposition D.5(5), pp. 74–75; construction p. 78, Part 5; p. 79 (No Pure Contingency)

settings.monoid: Proposition D.5, part 5 (p. 78): the arrows are the monotone surjections $h$ of $\mathbb N$ with $h0=h1$, together with the identity.

meets.factorizable-arrows: If $h$ is the identity, take $N^{\prime\prime}:=N\cup S$, $k^{\prime\prime}:=1$ and $j:=k^{\prime}$. Otherwise $h$ collapses $0$ and $1$; take $N^{\prime\prime}$ as for the monotone surjections, with $0,1\in N$. If $k$ is the identity, $k^{\prime}$ agrees with $h$ on $\{0,1\}$, so it is a collapse; take $k^{\prime\prime}:=k^{\prime}$ and $j:=1$. If $k$ is a collapse, the construction for the monotone surjections gives $k^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ that collapse $0$ and $1$, as $h$ and $k$ do.
meets.actual-world-pinned: As in part 4: the identity is the only arrow that does not collapse $0$ and $1$, so $\{1_{\mathbb N}\}$ is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$.
meets.collapse-unpinned: The other arrows are those that collapse $0$ and $1$, pinned down by $\{0,1\}$, and a collapsing monotone surjection is not determined by its values on a finite set.
meets.d6-surjective: Restricting part 4 to surjections, every arrow is a surjection of $\mathbb N$. So each arrow acts surjectively on the pinning sets, the finite subsets of $\mathbb N$, and on the individuals, whether these are the natural numbers or a single one that every arrow fixes.
meets.unbounded-haecceities: As in parts 2–4, with $A$ the even numbers.
meets.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{2m,2m+1\}$, that the arrow sends $2m$ to $0$ and $2m+1$ to $1$, so that its first step is at the odd position $2m+1$; the identity belongs to no $A_m$. The least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ consists of the non-identity arrows whose first step is at an odd position or beyond $N$, and it strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.

settings.monoid: Proposition D.5, part 5 (p. 78): the arrows are the monotone surjections $h$ of $\mathbb N$ with $h0=h1$, together with the identity.

meets.factorizable-arrows: If $h$ is the identity, take $N^{\prime\prime}:=N\cup S$, $k^{\prime\prime}:=1$ and $j:=k^{\prime}$. Otherwise $h$ collapses $0$ and $1$; take $N^{\prime\prime}$ as for the monotone surjections, with $0,1\in N$. If $k$ is the identity, $k^{\prime}$ agrees with $h$ on $\{0,1\}$, so it is a collapse; take $k^{\prime\prime}:=k^{\prime}$ and $j:=1$. If $k$ is a collapse, the construction for the monotone surjections gives $k^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ that collapse $0$ and $1$, as $h$ and $k$ do.
meets.actual-world-pinned: As in part 4: the identity is the only arrow that does not collapse $0$ and $1$, so $\{1_{\mathbb N}\}$ is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$.
meets.collapse-unpinned: The other arrows are those that collapse $0$ and $1$, pinned down by $\{0,1\}$, and a collapsing monotone surjection is not determined by its values on a finite set.
meets.d6-surjective: Restricting part 4 to surjections, every arrow is a surjection of $\mathbb N$. So each arrow acts surjectively on the pinning sets, the finite subsets of $\mathbb N$, and on the individuals, whether these are the natural numbers or a single one that every arrow fixes.
meets.unbounded-haecceities: As in parts 2–4, with $A$ the even numbers.
meets.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{2m,2m+1\}$, that the arrow sends $2m$ to $0$ and $2m+1$ to $1$, so that its first step is at the odd position $2m+1$; the identity belongs to no $A_m$. The least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ consists of the non-identity arrows whose first step is at an odd position or beyond $N$, and it strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.

history.summary: Adopted the source’s relational type system at the user’s request. The cited construction now directly supplies the recorded model; the former type-extension obligation is removed.

Added both Axioms of Infinity at Cian Dorr's direction. The individuals are the natural numbers and identity at the evaluation arrow is literal, so no numeral counts them. The propositions that a given individual is fixed by the arrow, one for each individual, are pairwise distinct and each has that individual as finite support, so there are infinitely many propositions. The set of numerals at each type is invariant under every arrow, hence has empty support and lies in the domain, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property at either type.
Fixed an interpretation of Σ (relational constants as top, individual constants as one fixed individual) and recorded the signature schemata it refutes, at Cian Dorr’s request.
Expanded the description from Appendix D, naming Proposition D.5 and its part; added the failure of Countable Boolean Completeness at type e→t; settled the Distinctness-preserving collapse.
Re-fixed the interpretation of Σ so as to settle No Contingency (signature Σ) and B for sentences of Σ, at Cian Dorr’s request; see the notes.

Corrected the reason given for the failures of Independence (signature Σ) and Distinctness (signature Σ): the true atom is denoted by no closed pure term, since such terms denote entities fixed by every arrow; the failures come from the other relational constants, which denote top. No verdict changes.

Added Relational Choice and its necessitation at Cian Dorr’s direction: ideally full models are extensionally full at every object, and choice in the metatheory supplies the functional subrelation; see the notes.

Added Transversal Choice, by the argument recorded for Relational Choice: the model is extensionally full at every object, so for an equivalence relation at the evaluation point a transversal of its extension there, chosen in the metatheory, is the extension of an element pinned down by the empty set; the equivalence and transversal conditions are unboxed. Recorded on a question of Zachary Goodsell, after an observation of Christopher Sun.

Confirmed the trawl's BC-t conclusion with a replacement proof: alternating differences of finite agreement classes have no least upper bound. The original missing-intersection argument is invalid. Used source extensional fullness for domain membership. Also localized the source-reported Atomicity failure to t (footnote 92), with a corrected direct splitting proof.
Added the failure of Atomicity (type t) and of Boolean Completeness (type t), with the arguments in the notes.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 5 (p. 78): the arrows are the monotone surjections $h$ of $\mathbb N$ with $h0=h1$, together with the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. The individuals are the natural numbers, acted on by the arrows themselves. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity arrow; every other constant of Σ, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals are the natural numbers.
met.factorizable-arrows: If $h$ is the identity, take $N^{\prime\prime}:=N\cup S$, $k^{\prime\prime}:=1$ and $j:=k^{\prime}$. Otherwise $h$ collapses $0$ and $1$; take $N^{\prime\prime}$ as for the monotone surjections, with $0,1\in N$. If $k$ is the identity, $k^{\prime}$ agrees with $h$ on $\{0,1\}$, so it is a collapse; take $k^{\prime\prime}:=k^{\prime}$ and $j:=1$. If $k$ is a collapse, the construction for the monotone surjections gives $k^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ that collapse $0$ and $1$, as $h$ and $k$ do.
met.actual-world-pinned: As in part 4: the identity is the only arrow that does not collapse $0$ and $1$, so $\{1_{\mathbb N}\}$ is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$.
met.collapse-unpinned: The other arrows are those that collapse $0$ and $1$, pinned down by $\{0,1\}$, and a collapsing monotone surjection is not determined by its values on a finite set.
met.d6-surjective: Restricting part 4 to surjections, every arrow is a surjection of $\mathbb N$. So each arrow acts surjectively on the pinning sets, the finite subsets of $\mathbb N$, and on the individuals, whether these are the natural numbers or a single one that every arrow fixes.
met.unbounded-haecceities: As in parts 2–4, with $A$ the even numbers.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{2m,2m+1\}$, that the arrow sends $2m$ to $0$ and $2m+1$ to $1$, so that its first step is at the odd position $2m+1$; the identity belongs to no $A_m$. The least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ consists of the non-identity arrows whose first step is at an odd position or beyond $N$, and it strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is in the domain, being pinned down by a finite set; at every arrow some composite is not the identity, since every other arrow is non-injective, so it is necessary at no arrow, and a non-identity arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: A non-identity arrow is non-injective, so no arrow composes it back to the identity.

The propositions that a given individual is fixed by the arrow, one for each individual, are pairwise distinct and each has that individual as finite support, so there are infinitely many propositions. The set of numerals at each type is invariant under every arrow, hence has empty support and lies in the domain, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property at either type.
Fixed an interpretation of Σ (relational constants as top, individual constants as one fixed individual) and recorded the signature schemata it refutes, at Cian Dorr’s request.
Expanded the description from Appendix D, naming Proposition D.5 and its part; added the failure of Countable Boolean Completeness at type e→t; settled the Distinctness-preserving collapse.
Re-fixed the interpretation of Σ so as to settle No Contingency (signature Σ) and B for sentences of Σ, at Cian Dorr’s request; see the notes.

Corrected the reason given for the failures of Independence (signature Σ) and Distinctness (signature Σ): the true atom is denoted by no closed pure term, since such terms denote entities fixed by every arrow; the failures come from the other relational constants, which denote top. No verdict changes.

Added Relational Choice and its necessitation at Cian Dorr’s direction: ideally full models are extensionally full at every object, and choice in the metatheory supplies the functional subrelation; see the notes.

Added Transversal Choice, by the argument recorded for Relational Choice: the model is extensionally full at every object, so for an equivalence relation at the evaluation point a transversal of its extension there, chosen in the metatheory, is the extension of an element pinned down by the empty set; the equivalence and transversal conditions are unboxed. Recorded on a question of Zachary Goodsell, after an observation of Christopher Sun.

Added the failure of Atomicity (type t), of BF (type t) and of Boolean Completeness (type t), with the arguments in the notes.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 4 (p. 78): the arrows are the monotone maps $h$ of $\mathbb N$ with $h0=h1$, together with the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. There is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on $\mathbb N$, which supplies the pinning sets. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.one-individual: The only individual is fixed by every arrow, at the sole object.
met.uniformly-pinned-rigidity: Let $Y$ be weakly rigid, pinned down by $S=[0,s]$, with extension $E$ at the identity. Pinning and weak persistence give $Y(k)\supseteq k_2\cdot E$ for every $k_2$ agreeing with $k$ on $S$, and weak inextensibility, tested on the intension $k\mapsto\bigcup\{k_2\cdot E:k_2\text{ agrees with }k\text{ on }N\}$, pinned down by $N$, gives the reverse inclusion; so $\bigcup\{k_2\cdot E:k_2\text{ agrees with }k\text{ on }N\}=Y(k)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$. If some $p\in E$ were pinned minimally at $T$ with $t:=\max T>s$, take $s'\ge t$ and the jump map $k$, sending $0$ and $1$ to $0$, the identity on $[2,s']$ and adding $100$ beyond: an arrow agreeing with $k$ on $S$ and sending $t$ to $s'+1$ puts into the $S$-union an element pinned at $s'+1$, while every element of the $[0,s'+1]$-union is pinned inside $k([0,s'])\cup[s'+100,\infty)$. So $E\subseteq\operatorname{Pin}(S)$, and then $k_2\cdot p=k\cdot p$ whenever $k_2$ agrees with $k$ on $S$, so $Y(k)=k\cdot E$.
met.actual-world-pinned: The identity is the only arrow that does not collapse $0$ and $1$, so $\{1_{\mathbb N}\}$ is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$.
met.collapse-unpinned: The other arrows are those that collapse $0$ and $1$, pinned down by $\{0,1\}$, and a collapsing monotone map is not determined by its values on a finite set.
met.positive-preserving: Every arrow is monotone, and the arrows with $h0=h1=1$ send $0$ to a positive number.
met.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any arrow with $i0=2$ (hence $i1=2$ and range within $[2,\infty)$), and $q:=\{k : k1=1\}$, pinned down by $\{1\}$: the arrows $k$ with $k0=k1=1\le k2$ and $k^{\prime}$ with $k^{\prime}0=k^{\prime}1=0$, agreeing beyond $1$, are separated by $q$. The model is a one-object finite-support model, and the intension the argument uses is pinned down by $N$.
met.unbounded-haecceities: As in parts 2 and 3, with $A$ the even numbers.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{1,2m,2m+1\}$, that the arrow is constant on $\{1,\ldots,2m\}$ and increases at $2m+1$; the identity belongs to no $A_m$. The least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ consists of the non-identity arrows whose first increase after $1$ is at an odd position or beyond $N$, and it strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is in the domain, being pinned down by a finite set; at every arrow some composite is not the identity, since every other arrow is non-injective, so it is necessary at no arrow, and a non-identity arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: A non-identity arrow is non-injective, so no arrow composes it back to the identity.

sigma.text: Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,p_0$, where $p_0$ is the proposition that the arrow fixes $0$, pinned down by $\{0\}$; every other constant of Σ is relational and denotes the top element of its type.

meets.evens-avoidable: With $N_0\subseteq[0,M_0]$: $i$ the monotone map that is the identity on $[0,M_0]$ and adds one beyond it; an even $b>M_0+1$, whose only preimage under $i$ is the odd $b-1$; and $N^{\prime}:=[0,b]$: a monotone map agreeing with $i$ there has the same preimages of $b$ within $[0,b]$ and takes values at least $i(b)=b+1$ beyond it.
meets.positive-preserving: Every arrow is monotone, and the constant map to $1$ sends $0$ to a positive number.
meets.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any monotone map with $i0=2$, so that every $i^{\prime}$ agreeing with it on $N$ has range within $[2,\infty)$, and $q:=\{k : k1=1\}$, pinned down by $\{1\}$: two monotone maps agreeing on $[2,\infty)$ with $k2\ge1$ may take the values $1$ and $0$ at $1$. meets.unbounded-haecceities: As in part 2, with $A$ the even numbers.
meets.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{0,2m-1,2m\}$, that the arrow is constant on $\{0,\ldots,2m-1\}$ and first changes value at $2m$. The least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ consists of the arrows whose first change of value is at an even position or beyond $N$, and it strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.

If some $p\in E$ were pinned minimally at $T$ with $t:=\max T>s$, take $s'\ge t$ and the jump map $k$, the identity on $[0,s']$ and adding $100$ beyond: an arrow agreeing with $k$ on $S$ and sending $t$ to $s'+1$ puts into the $S$-union an element pinned at $s'+1$, while every element of the $[0,s'+1]$-union is pinned inside $k([0,s'])\cup[s'+100,\infty)$. met.evens-avoidable: With $N_0\subseteq[0,M_0]$: $i$ the monotone map that is the identity on $[0,M_0]$ and adds one beyond it; an even $b>M_0+1$, whose only preimage under $i$ is the odd $b-1$; and $N^{\prime}:=[0,b]$: a monotone map agreeing with $i$ there has the same preimages of $b$ within $[0,b]$ and takes values at least $i(b)=b+1$ beyond it.
met.positive-preserving: Every arrow is monotone, and the constant map to $1$ sends $0$ to a positive number.
met.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any monotone map with $i0=2$, so that every $i^{\prime}$ agreeing with it on $N$ has range within $[2,\infty)$, and $q:=\{k : k1=1\}$, pinned down by $\{1\}$: two monotone maps agreeing on $[2,\infty)$ with $k2\ge1$ may take the values $1$ and $0$ at $1$. met.unbounded-haecceities: As in part 2, with $A$ the even numbers.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{0,2m-1,2m\}$, that the arrow is constant on $\{0,\ldots,2m-1\}$ and first changes value at $2m$. The least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ consists of the arrows whose first change of value is at an even position or beyond $N$, and it strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.

In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 3 (p. 77): the one-object category whose arrows are all the monotone maps of $\mathbb N$. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. There is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on $\mathbb N$, which supplies the pinning sets. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.one-individual: The only individual is fixed by every arrow, at the sole object.
met.uniformly-pinned-rigidity: Let $Y$ be weakly rigid, pinned down by $S=[0,s]$, with extension $E$ at the identity. Pinning and weak persistence give $Y(k)\supseteq k_2\cdot E$ for every $k_2$ agreeing with $k$ on $S$, and weak inextensibility, tested on the intension $k\mapsto\bigcup\{k_2\cdot E:k_2\text{ agrees with }k\text{ on }N\}$, pinned down by $N$, gives the reverse inclusion; so $\bigcup\{k_2\cdot E:k_2\text{ agrees with }k\text{ on }N\}=Y(k)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$. If some $p\in E$ were pinned minimally at $T$ with $t:=\max T>s$, take $s'\ge t$ and the jump map $k$, the identity on $[0,s']$ and adding $100$ beyond: an arrow agreeing with $k$ on $S$ and sending $t$ to $s'+1$ puts into the $S$-union an element pinned at $s'+1$, while every element of the $[0,s'+1]$-union is pinned inside $k([0,s'])\cup[s'+100,\infty)$. So $E\subseteq\operatorname{Pin}(S)$, and then $k_2\cdot p=k\cdot p$ whenever $k_2$ agrees with $k$ on $S$, so $Y(k)=k\cdot E$.
met.evens-avoidable: With $N_0\subseteq[0,M_0]$: $i$ the monotone map that is the identity on $[0,M_0]$ and adds one beyond it; an even $b>M_0+1$, whose only preimage under $i$ is the odd $b-1$; and $N^{\prime}:=[0,b]$: a monotone map agreeing with $i$ there has the same preimages of $b$ within $[0,b]$ and takes values at least $i(b)=b+1$ beyond it.
met.positive-preserving: Every arrow is monotone, and the constant map to $1$ sends $0$ to a positive number.
met.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any monotone map with $i0=2$, so that every $i^{\prime}$ agreeing with it on $N$ has range within $[2,\infty)$, and $q:=\{k : k1=1\}$, pinned down by $\{1\}$: two monotone maps agreeing on $[2,\infty)$ with $k2\ge1$ may take the values $1$ and $0$ at $1$. The model is a one-object finite-support model, and the intension the argument uses is pinned down by $N$.
met.unbounded-haecceities: As in part 2, with $A$ the even numbers.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{0,2m-1,2m\}$, that the arrow is constant on $\{0,\ldots,2m-1\}$ and first changes value at $2m$. The least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ consists of the arrows whose first change of value is at an even position or beyond $N$, and it strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.

arguments.text: At type $e\to t$, for the property of being even, which is in the domain as the constant intension $\{\langle b,h\rangle : b\text{ even}\}$, pinned down by $\emptyset$. Unpacking $\operatorname{Inextensible}$ as in the left-to-right half of Dorr’s rigidity criterion (draft, Lemma 14, p. 7, with Lemma 13): even the unboxed matrix, evaluated at the identity, says that $Y$ is contained in every persistent (transport-closed) $B$ in the domain whose extension includes $Y$’s. For a finite $N^{\prime}$, the smallest such $B$ pinned down by $N^{\prime}$ is $B_{N^{\prime}}:=\{\langle b^{\prime\prime},i^{\prime}\rangle : i^{\prime\prime}(b)=b^{\prime\prime}\text{ for some even }b\text{ and some arrow }i^{\prime\prime}\text{ agreeing with }i^{\prime}\text{ on }N^{\prime}\}$, which is transport-closed and pinned down by $N^{\prime}$. Now let $Y$ be coextensive with evenness and pinned down by a finite $N_0$; then $\langle b,i\rangle\in Y$ for every even $b$ and every arrow $i$ fixing $N_0$ pointwise. Take the arrow $i$, the even $b$ and the finite $N^{\prime}$ that the condition provides for $N_0$: no arrow agreeing with $i$ on $N^{\prime}$ sends an even number to $b$. So $\langle b,i\rangle\in Y\setminus B_{N^{\prime}}$, and $Y$ is not even weakly inextensible.

met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.

met.factorizable-arrows: Given $h$, $N\subseteq[0,n]$ and $S\subseteq[0,s]$, take $N^{\prime\prime}:=[0,n^{\prime\prime}]$ with $n^{\prime\prime}\ge s$ and $h(n^{\prime\prime})\ge n$. met.unbounded-haecceities: With $A$ the even numbers: the strongest persistent property containing them and pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ becomes strictly stronger as $n$ grows.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of propositions $A_m$ ($m\ge1$), each pinned down by $\{2m-1,2m\}$, that the arrow sends $2m-1$ to $0$ and $2m$ to $1$, so that its first step is at the even position $2m$. settings.monoid: The arrows are the functions $f$ on $\mathbb N$ that either identify $0$ with $1$ ($f0=f1$, the collapses) or are injective and map $\{0,1\}$ onto itself (the pair-preserving injections). arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text:
At type $e\to t$, with $F:=\top$. Write $Z_k$ for the extension of a property $Z$ at the arrow $k$, so that $Z$ holds of $b$ at $k$ iff $b\in Z_k$, and $(h\cdot Z)_k=Z_{k\circ h}$. Call an arrow a collapse if it identifies $0$ with $1$.

(1) $\top$ is rigid: it is persistent, and its inextensibility is $\Box$BF at type $e$, which holds (BF holds, and with No Pure Contingency so does $\Box$BF).

(2) A rigid property that is not a disjunction of haecceities. Let $Y_k:=\mathbb N$ if $k$ is a collapse and $Y_k:=\mathbb N\setminus\{k2\}$ otherwise; $Y$ is pinned down by $\{0,1,2\}$. It is persistent: if $b\ne k2$ for a pair-preserving injection $k$, then $jb\ne jk2$ for a pair-preserving injection $j$, and every other composite is a collapse. It is inextensible at every world $w$: let $X$ be pinned down by $N\supseteq\{0,1\}$ and contain $\langle jx,j\rangle$ for every $x\in Y_w$ and arrow $j$; given $y\in Y_{j\circ w}$, there are an arrow $j'$ agreeing with $j$ on $N$ and an $x\in Y_w$ with $j'x=y$, so $\langle y,j\rangle\in X$ by pinning. For if $y=jn$ with $n\in N$ and $n\in Y_w$, take $j'=j$; if $n\notin Y_w$, then $w$ is a pair-preserving injection, $n=w2$, and $y=jw2\in Y_{j\circ w}$ makes $j\circ w$ a collapse, so $j$ identifies $w0$ with $w1$, that is $0$ with $1$, and $j$ changed at a fresh $x$ to $j'x=y$ is still a collapse; and if $y\notin jN$, change $j$ at a fresh $x\notin N\cup\{w2\}$ to $j'x=y$, after $j$ composed with the transposition of $y$ and $jx$ when $j$ is injective. So $Y$ is rigid, with the infinite, coinfinite extension $\mathbb N\setminus\{2\}$.

(3) Along a collapse, a rigid property moves to one whose extension is everything or finite. Let $Z$ be weakly rigid with extension $S$, pinned down by $N\supseteq\{0,1\}$, and let $m$ be a collapse. If $S$ is infinite, then for any $b$ change $m$ at some $x\in S\setminus N$ to $m'x=b$: $m'$ is a collapse agreeing with $m$ on $N$, and persistence gives $b\in Z_{m'}=Z_m$; so $Z_m=\mathbb N$. If $S$ is finite, the property $k\mapsto k[S]$ is pinned down by $S$ and necessarily holds of each member of $S$, so weak inextensibility gives $Z_m\subseteq m[S]$.

Now let $R:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le\top$, the value of a closed pure term, so that in a one-object model its extension at every arrow is the set of rigid properties. Let $\mathbf X$ hold of $W$ at $k$ iff $W=k'\cdot Z$ for some rigid $Z$ and some arrow $k'$ agreeing with $k$ on $\{0,1\}$. It is pinned down by $\{0,1\}$, so it is in the domain, and it necessarily holds of every instance of $R$ (take $k'=k$). But at a collapse $c$, every $k'$ agreeing with $c$ on $\{0,1\}$ is a collapse, so by (3) every property in the extension of $\mathbf X$ there has extension $\mathbb N$ or a finite one, while $Y$, in the extension of $R$ there by (2), has extension $\mathbb N\setminus\{2\}$. So $R\not\le\mathbf X$: $R$ is not even weakly inextensible, though $\top$ is rigid.

arguments.text: At type $e\to t$. In the source's terms an upper bound of the haecceities of the members of $A$ is a persistent property whose extension contains $A$. A least one, pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$, would be the strongest such property pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$, and would also lie below the strongest pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,m\}$ for each $m>n$, which by the condition is strictly stronger. models.notes: Cian Dorr proposed the functions that are injective or identify $0$ with $1$; that set is not closed under composition (the injection swapping $0$ with $2$ and $1$ with $3$, followed by the collapse of $0$ with $1$, identifies $2$ with $3$ but not $0$ with $1$), and the monoid recorded is its largest submonoid containing all the collapses, since a collapse applied after an injection $f$ must identify $f0$ with $f1$. It is the first model on the map with Vicinity without Actuality outside C5 (ND fails at type $e$ by a collapse, at type $t$ for the proposition $0\ne1$, which is impossible at a collapse, refuting 5 and B as well), and the first model refuting Rigid Power.
