models.definition:
The arrows are the functions $f$ on $\mathbb N$ that either identify $0$ with $1$ ($f0=f1$, the collapses) or are injective and map $\{0,1\}$ onto itself (the pair-preserving injections). These compose: two pair-preserving injections compose to one, and a composite with a collapse applied after a pair-preserving injection, or with a collapse applied first, identifies $0$ with $1$. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. The individuals are the natural numbers, acted on by the arrows themselves. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.one-individual: The only individual is fixed by every arrow, at the sole object.
met.factorizable-arrows: Take $N^{\prime\prime}:=S\cup\{0,1\}$ and, enlarging $N$, assume $\{0,1\}\cup h(N^{\prime\prime})\subseteq N$; then $k^{\prime}$, $k^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ below are collapses iff $kh$, $h$ and $k$ are. Let $k^{\prime\prime}$ agree with $h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$; for $m\in M\setminus N^{\prime\prime}$ let $k^{\prime\prime}m:=k^{-1}(k^{\prime}m)$ if $k$ is injective and $k^{\prime}m\in k(N)$, and otherwise a fresh point outside $N$, one for each $m$ if $h$ is injective and one for each value of $k^{\prime}$ if not. Let $j$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send each fresh point to its value. Where $h$ is injective, $k^{\prime}$ is injective or $k$ a collapse, so $k^{\prime\prime}$ is injective on $M$, its values $k^{-1}(k^{\prime}m)$ avoiding $h(N^{\prime\prime})$; where $k$ is injective, the new values of $j$ lie outside $k(N)$ and are distinct. met.no-least-pinned-cover: As for the permutations, with $2$ in place of $0$: let $F$ be the family of propositions $\{h : h2=m,\ hm=2\}$ ($m\ge3$), each pinned down by $\{2,m\}$. A pair-preserving injection $h$ belongs to the least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $S=\{0,\ldots,N\}$ iff either $h2\in S\setminus\{0,1,2\}$ and $h(h2)=2$, or $h2\notin S$ and $2\notin h(S)$; the $3$-cycle $(2\ N{+}1\ N{+}2)$, which fixes $0$ and $1$, satisfies the second clause for $S$ but neither for $\{0,\ldots,N+1\}$, so these supersets strictly shrink.

arguments.text: At type $e\to t$, for the property of being even, which is in the domain as the constant intension $\{\langle b,h\rangle : b\text{ even}\}$, pinned down by $\emptyset$. Unpacking $\operatorname{Inextensible}$ as in the left-to-right half of Dorr’s rigidity criterion (draft, Lemma 14, p. 7, with Lemma 13): even the unboxed matrix, evaluated at the identity, says that $Y$ is contained in every persistent (transport-closed) $B$ in the domain whose extension includes $Y$’s. For a finite $N^{\prime}$, the smallest such $B$ pinned down by $N^{\prime}$ is $B_{N^{\prime}}:=\{\langle b^{\prime\prime},i^{\prime}\rangle : i^{\prime\prime}(b)=b^{\prime\prime}\text{ for some even }b\text{ and some arrow }i^{\prime\prime}\text{ agreeing with }i^{\prime}\text{ on }N^{\prime}\}$, which is transport-closed and pinned down by $N^{\prime}$. Now let $Y$ be coextensive with evenness and pinned down by a finite $N_0$; then $\langle b,i\rangle\in Y$ for every even $b$ and every arrow $i$ fixing $N_0$ pointwise. Take the arrow $i$, the even $b$ and the finite $N^{\prime}$ that the condition provides for $N_0$: no arrow agreeing with $i$ on $N^{\prime}$ sends an even number to $b$. So $\langle b,i\rangle\in Y\setminus B_{N^{\prime}}$, and $Y$ is not even weakly inextensible.

models.name: Finite-support action model: N and N×2, sections and projection

certificate.produced_by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), 27 September 2026, in a session with Cian Dorr

sources: Original construction and verification by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), 27 September 2026; see the write-up.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3, pp. 73–74 (ideally full action models); p. 79 (a two-object example of the same kind).

references.note: The ideally full finitely pinned action models over a category of sets; the construction is applied here to a new two-object category.

models.definition: An ideally full finitely pinned action model over a two-object category. $W_0$ has individuals $\mathbb N$ and $W_1$ has individuals $\mathbb N\times\{0,1\}$. The arrows are the identity of $W_0$ (the only arrow $W_0\to W_0$); the sections $f_T(n)=(n,T(n))$ for every $T:\mathbb N\to\{0,1\}$, from $W_0$ to $W_1$; the projection $\pi(n,i)=n$ from $W_1$ to $W_0$; and the identity of $W_1$ with the retractions $e_T:=f_T\circ\pi$ from $W_1$ to itself. They compose by $\pi\circ f_T=1$, $e_T\circ f_U=f_T$, $e_T\circ e_U=e_T$ and $\pi\circ e_T=\pi$. The evaluation point is the identity of $W_0$; every world reachable from it can return to it through $\pi$.

meets.codomain-intensions: The model is ideally full at both objects, and an intension whose value at an arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain is pinned down by $\emptyset$ (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3).
meets.identity-singletons: $\{1_{W_0}\}$ is pinned down by $\emptyset$, the identity being the only arrow from $W_0$ to $W_0$, and $\{1_{W_1}\}$ by $\{(0,0),(0,1)\}$, which no $e_T$ fixes pointwise (see the write-up, on Actuality).
meets.unique-retractions-everywhere: Out of $W_0$, the identity has only itself as retraction and each section $f_T$ only $\pi$, the one arrow back. Out of $W_1$, the identity has only itself; $\pi$ has none, since $f_T\circ\pi=e_T\ne1$; and no $e_T$ has one, since $e_T$ is not injective.
meets.retractions: The arrows out of $W_0$ are its identity and the sections $f_T$, each retracted by $\pi$.

arguments.text: At type $e\to t$ for the universal property: an inextensible property coextensive with it would have to hold, at the world $f_T$, of exactly the range of $f_T$, and no finite set of individuals pins that down. See the write-up.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The proposition $\{f_T : T(0)=0\}$, pinned down by $\{0\}$, has no atom below it. A nonempty proposition below it pinned down by a finite $N$ contains every section agreeing on $N$ with one of its members, and the propositions pinned down by $N\cup\{m\}$, for $m\notin N$, split that set by the value $T(m)$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), on Cian Dorr's request to settle Tame Rigidity where it was open
arguments.text: Write a relation $Y$ at an object as its intension over the arrows $g$ out of it, $Y\bar a$ holding at $g$ iff $g\cdot\bar a\in Y_g$, so that $(h\cdot Y)_g=Y_{gh}$. Since the model is ideally full, for $E$ the extension at the identity the intension $B_N(E)_g:=\bigcup\{g^{\prime} \cdot E:g^{\prime}\text{ agrees with }g\text{ on }N\text{ and has its codomain}\}$ is in the domain, and weak inextensibility says exactly $Y\subseteq B_N(E)$ for every finite $N$; rigidity is weak rigidity at every world. At $W_0$, a weakly rigid $Y$ has $Y_1=E$ and $f_T\cdot E\subseteq Y_{f_T}\subseteq\bigcup\{f_{T'}\cdot E:T'\text{ agrees with }T\text{ on }N\}$ for each $N$. At the world $f_T$, with $E_T:=Y_{f_T}$: persistence holds since $\pi f_{T'}=1$ and $e_Uf_{T'}=f_U$; inextensibility along $\pi$ asks $E\subseteq\pi\cdot E_T$, true as $\pi f_T=1$, and along $e_U$ asks $Y_{f_U}\subseteq\bigcup\{e_{U'}\cdot E_T:U'\text{ agrees with }U\text{ on }N\}$, true because $Y_{f_U}$ lies in $\bigcup\{f_{U'}\cdot E\}$ over the same $U'$ and $f_{U'}\cdot E=e_{U'}\cdot(f_T\cdot E)$. So Tame Rigidity holds at $W_0$. At $W_1$, whose worlds are $\pi$, $1$ and the $e_U$: for $Y$ weakly rigid with extension $E$ there, $Y_\pi=\pi\cdot E$ (the only arrow to $W_0$ is $\pi$), and a member $x$ of $Y_{e_V}$ lies, for each $N$ containing a point off the graph of $V$, in $\bigcup\{e_{V'}\cdot E\}$ over the $V'$ agreeing with $V$ on the projection of $N$. Hence at the world $\pi$, where the intension is $1\mapsto Y_\pi$, $f_T\mapsto Y_{e_T}$, inextensibility holds, as $f_{T'}\cdot\pi\cdot E=e_{T'}\cdot E$; and at the world $e_U$, $x\in Y_{e_V}$ is $e_{V'}\cdot e=e_{V'}\cdot(e_U\cdot e)$ with $e_U\cdot e\in Y_{e_U}$, while $\pi\cdot Y_{e_U}=\pi\cdot E$ and $e_V\cdot Y_{e_U}\subseteq Y_{e_V}$ give persistence. So Tame Rigidity holds at $W_1$ as well, hence at every world.

arguments.text: At $W_0$. The proposition $q:=\{1_{W_1}\}$ is in the domain at $W_1$ (it is pinned down by $\{(0,0),(0,1)\}$, as for identity-singletons). It is the transport $f_T\cdot p=\{k:k\circ f_T\in p\}$ of no proposition $p$ at $W_0$: since $1\circ f_T=f_T$, $\pi\circ f_T=1_{W_0}$ and $e_U\circ f_T=f_U$, that would need $p$ to contain $f_T$ and no other $f_U$, and no finite set of points pins such a $p$ down, infinitely many $f_U$ agreeing with $f_T$ on any finite set. So the property $X$ that holds of every proposition at arrows into $W_0$ and of every proposition other than $q$ at arrows into $W_1$, pinned down by $\emptyset$ since it depends only on the codomain, satisfies $\forall p\, .\,\Box Xp$ at $W_0$, while after any $f_T$ it fails of $q$.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), at Cian Dorr's request; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text:
Boxed Rigid Power: every weakly rigid relation is $T(E)$ ($h\mapsto hE$) and every $T(A)$ below a rigid one is admitted, so rigid subrelations lift exactly. Criterion (1) is part (1) of tame-rigidity-factorizable, which holds with several objects.
(a) Weakly rigid relations are exact images. At $W_0$, with $E:=F_1$: by (1) a member $x$ of $F_{f_T}$ is $f_Ua$ with $a\in E$ and $U$ agreeing with $T$ on a finite $N$ containing $\pi M$, $M$ pinning $x$ down. Then $e_Ux=e_Uf_Ua=x$; $e_U$ and $e_T$ agree on $M$, so $e_Tx=x$; and $\pi x=a$; so $x=e_Tx=f_T\pi x=f_Ta$. So $F_{f_T}=f_TE$. At $W_1$, $F_\pi=\pi E$, $\pi$ being the only arrow to $W_0$; for $x\in F_{e_T}$ take $N$ containing a pin of $F$, a pin of $x$ and a whole fibre of $\pi$, which no arrow agreeing with $e_T$ on $N$ can be the identity; (1) gives $x=e_Ua$ with $a\in E$, and as before $x=e_Tx=f_T\pi a=e_Ta$.
(b) Subsets are admitted. Let $F=T(E)$ be rigid at $W_0$, pinned down by $S$. If $U,V$ agree on $S$, $f_UE=f_VE$; for $a\in E$ pick $b$ with $f_Ua=f_Vb$ and apply $\pi$: $a=b$. So $f_Ua=f_Va$ for each $a\in E$, and $T(A)$ is pinned down by $S$ for every $A\subseteq E$. At $W_1$, with a fibre of $\pi$ in $S$ (so the identity agrees with no retraction on $S$), $e_UE=e_VE$ gives $e_Ua=e_Vb$ with $\pi a=\pi b$, so $e_Ua=f_V\pi a=e_Va$.
(c) For a rigid $F=T(E)$ at either object, an arrow $h$ and a rigid $X\le h\cdot F$ with extension $D$, $A:=\{a\in E:ha\in D\}$ gives a rigid $T(A)\le F$ with $h\cdot T(A)=X$. So the power property of $F$ is the exact image of its extension, and rigid. Rigid Power holds at both objects, hence at every world.

arguments.text: At $\sigma=e$, $\tau=e\to t$. Boolean Completeness fails here by the chain Actuality + Boolean Completeness ⇒ Weak Rigid Comprehension, Tame Rigidity + Weak Rigid Comprehension ⇒ Rigid Comprehension ⇒ Inextensible Comprehension, each step taken for one property $X$, and the first uses Boolean Completeness only for the property $H$ of being the haecceity of an instance of $X$. For the witness $X=\top_e$ at $W_0$ the instances are the individuals $\mathbb N$; the numerals at $e$ are standard there and pairwise distinct, and extensional fullness at $W_0$ puts in the domain $H$ and the relation pairing the haecceity of $n$ with the $n$-th numeral. So $H$ is countable relative to $e$, and a least upper bound of it would give, with Actuality and Tame Rigidity, an inextensible coextension of $\top_e$, which the recorded argument excludes.

arguments.text: The action of an arrow out of the evaluation object is undone by the action of its retraction, so it is injective at every type, and ND holds there (Proposition 3.24(i)).

conditions.text: Every arrow out of the evaluation object has a retraction: an arrow back after which it composes to the identity.
conditions.reason: The arrows out of $W_0$ are its identity and the sections $f_T$, each retracted by $\pi$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Let $V$ be the evaluation object or the target of an arrow out of it, and $w:=\{1_V\}$, in the domain at $V$. It is true at $1_V$. Under an arrow $f$ out of $V$ it becomes $\{k : k\circ f=1_V\}$, the set of retractions of $f$, which has at most one member and so lies below $q$ or below $\neg q$ for every proposition $q$ at $f$'s target. So Strong Actuality holds at $1_V$. A closed sentence holds at an arrow iff it holds at the identity of the arrow's target, so Strong Actuality holds at every world after the evaluation point, and □Strong Actuality holds there.

conditions.text: At the evaluation object, and at the target of every arrow out of it, the singleton of the identity arrow is in the domain.
conditions.reason: $\{1_{W_0}\}$ is pinned down by $\emptyset$, the identity being the only arrow from $W_0$ to $W_0$, and $\{1_{W_1}\}$ by $\{(0,0),(0,1)\}$, which no $e_T$ fixes pointwise (see the write-up, on Actuality).

conditions.text: At the evaluation object, and at the target of every arrow out of it, every arrow out of that object has at most one retraction.
conditions.reason: Out of $W_0$, the identity has only itself as retraction and each section $f_T$ only $\pi$, the one arrow back. Out of $W_1$, the identity has only itself; $\pi$ has none, since $f_T\circ\pi=e_T\ne1$; and no $e_T$ has one, since $e_T$ is not injective.

models.notes: Found on 27 September 2026 in answer to Cian Dorr's question whether Actuality implies Inextensible Comprehension, after the observation that Christopher Sun's witness $\lambda\bar z\, .\,\Diamond(w\land F\bar z)$ can fail only at worlds from which the actual world is reachable, and only through entities there that are not the images of actual ones. The write-up also records a sufficient condition for Inextensible Comprehension in models of this kind, which explains why every earlier model with Actuality satisfies it. Checked informally by Cian Dorr and Christopher Sun the same day.

meets.actual-world-pinned: $\{k_0\}$ is pinned down by $\{1\}$, since $k_n1=0$ for $n>0$.
meets.pinned-atoms: $\{k_0\}$ and each $\{k_n\}$ are pinned down by finite sets: $k_n$ is the only arrow sending $n+1$ to $1$.

meets.unbounded-haecceities: With $A$ the even numbers: the strongest persistent property pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ whose extension contains them has, at $k_m$, the evens, the odds with $0$, or all of $\mathbb N$ according as $m<n$ is even, $m<n$ is odd, or $m\ge n$.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 8 (pp. 78–79): the arrows are the maps $k_n$ with $k_nm=0$ for $m\le n$ and $k_nm=m-n$ otherwise, which compose as $k_n\circ k_m=k_{n+m}$; $k_0$ is the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. The individuals are the natural numbers, acted on by the arrows themselves. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals are the natural numbers.
met.arrows-finitely-determined: For $n\ge1$, $k_n(n+1)=1$ singles out $k_n$, and $k_0(1)=1$ singles out $k_0$; each singleton is pinned down by that one point.
met.actual-world-pinned: $\{k_0\}$ is pinned down by $\{1\}$, since $k_n1=0$ for $n>0$.
met.pinned-atoms: $\{k_0\}$ and each $\{k_n\}$ are pinned down by finite sets: $k_n$ is the only arrow sending $n+1$ to $1$.
met.d6-surjective: $k_n$ sends $0$ to $0$ and $m+n$ to $m$ for $m\ge1$, so it is a surjection of $\mathbb N$. So each arrow acts surjectively on the pinning sets, the finite subsets of $\mathbb N$, and on the individuals, whether these are the natural numbers or a single one that every arrow fixes.
met.unbounded-haecceities: With $A$ the even numbers: the strongest persistent property pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ whose extension contains them has, at $k_m$, the evens, the odds with $0$, or all of $\mathbb N$ according as $m<n$ is even, $m<n$ is odd, or $m\ge n$.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: An arrow $k_n$ is determined by its value at any $m\ge n$ and all $k_n$ with $n\ge N$ agree on $\{0,\ldots,N\}$, so the finitely pinned propositions are exactly the finite and cofinite sets of arrows. Let $F$ be the family of singletons $\{k_{2j}\}$: a finitely pinned superset of $\bigcup F$ is a cofinite set, and removing from it an odd-indexed member gives a strictly smaller one.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is in the domain, being pinned down by a finite set; at every arrow some composite is not the identity, since every other arrow is non-injective, so it is necessary at no arrow, and a non-identity arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: A non-identity arrow is non-injective, so no arrow composes it back to the identity.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 8 (pp. 78–79): the arrows are the maps $k_n$ with $k_nm=0$ for $m\le n$ and $k_nm=m-n$ otherwise, which compose as $k_n\circ k_m=k_{n+m}$; $k_0$ is the identity. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. There is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on $\mathbb N$, which supplies the pinning sets. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.one-individual: The only individual is fixed by every arrow, at the sole object.
met.arrows-finitely-determined: For $n\ge1$, $k_n(n+1)=1$ singles out $k_n$, and $k_0(1)=1$ singles out $k_0$; each singleton is pinned down by that one point.
met.actual-world-pinned: $\{k_0\}$ is pinned down by $\{1\}$, since $k_n1=0$ for $n>0$.
met.pinned-atoms: $\{k_0\}$ and each $\{k_n\}$ are pinned down by finite sets: $k_n$ is the only arrow sending $n+1$ to $1$.
met.d6-surjective: $k_n$ sends $0$ to $0$ and $m+n$ to $m$ for $m\ge1$, so it is a surjection of $\mathbb N$. So each arrow acts surjectively on the pinning sets, the finite subsets of $\mathbb N$, and on the individuals, whether these are the natural numbers or a single one that every arrow fixes.
met.unbounded-haecceities: With $A$ the even numbers: the strongest persistent property pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ whose extension contains them has, at $k_m$, the evens, the odds with $0$, or all of $\mathbb N$ according as $m<n$ is even, $m<n$ is odd, or $m\ge n$.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: An arrow $k_n$ is determined by its value at any $m\ge n$ and all $k_n$ with $n\ge N$ agree on $\{0,\ldots,N\}$, so the finitely pinned propositions are exactly the finite and cofinite sets of arrows. Let $F$ be the family of singletons $\{k_{2j}\}$: a finitely pinned superset of $\bigcup F$ is a cofinite set, and removing from it an odd-indexed member gives a strictly smaller one.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition, whose only member is the identity, is pinned down by a finite set, so it is in the domain and entails every truth; every other arrow is non-injective, so no composite with it is the identity.
met.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is in the domain, being pinned down by a finite set; at every arrow some composite is not the identity, since every other arrow is non-injective, so it is necessary at no arrow, and a non-identity arrow carries it to the empty set.
met.irreversible-arrow: A non-identity arrow is non-injective, so no arrow composes it back to the identity.

settings.monoid: Proposition D.5, part 6 (p. 78): the arrows are the identity and the truncations $g_n$, $g_nm=\min\{m,n\}$, which compose as $g_n\circ g_m=g_{\min\{n,m\}}$.

meets.uniformly-pinned-rigidity: An intension is pinned down by $[0,s]$ iff it is constant on $\{g_n:n\ge s\}\cup\{1\}$. Weak inextensibility at the identity, tested with $[0,s']$ for $s'>n$, where $g_n$ is the only arrow with its germ, forces $Y(g_n)=g_n\cdot Y(1)$ for every $n$; and $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is in the domain iff $g_n\cdot E=E$ for all large $n$, which, as $g_n\cdot E\subseteq\operatorname{Pin}([0,n])$, holds iff $E\subseteq\operatorname{Pin}([0,n_0])$ for some $n_0$.
meets.arrows-finitely-determined: Each $g_n$ is the only arrow with $g_n(n+1)=n$, so $\{g_n\}$ is pinned down by $\{n+1\}$.
meets.evens-avoidable: With $N_0\subseteq[0,M_0]$: $i:=g_n$ with $n\ge M_0$, an even $b>n$, and $N^{\prime}:=[0,n+1]$: the only arrow agreeing with $g_n$ on $[0,n+1]$ is $g_n$ itself, whose range $[0,n]$ omits $b$.
meets.pinned-atoms: Every nonempty proposition contains some $g_n$, and each $\{g_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set ($\{n-1,n,n+1\}$ for $n>0$, $\{0,1\}$ for $n=0$).
meets.unbounded-haecceities: With $A:=\mathbb N$: the strongest persistent property with extension $\mathbb N$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ becomes ever stronger.
meets.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of singletons $\{g_n\}$ for even $n$. A superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ contains, with any $g_m$ for $m\ge N$, every arrow agreeing with it on $\{0,\ldots,N\}$, so the least one is $\bigcup F\cup\{1_{\mathbb N}\}\cup\{g_m : m\ge N\}$, which strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.

arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type $e\to t$. In the source's terms an upper bound of the haecceities of the members of $A$ is a persistent property whose extension contains $A$. A least one, pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$, would be the strongest such property pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$, and would also lie below the strongest pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,m\}$ for each $m>n$, which by the condition is strictly stronger. So the haecceities have no least upper bound.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), answering Cian Dorr’s question whether the failure of Actuality can be sharpened to a failure of Inextensible Comprehension
arguments.text: At type $e\to t$, for the property of being even, which is in the domain as the constant intension $\{\langle b,h\rangle : b\text{ even}\}$, pinned down by $\emptyset$. Unpacking $\operatorname{Inextensible}$ as in the left-to-right half of Dorr’s rigidity criterion (draft, Lemma 14, p. 7, with Lemma 13): even the unboxed matrix, evaluated at the identity, says that $Y$ is contained in every persistent (transport-closed) $B$ in the domain whose extension includes $Y$’s. For a finite $N^{\prime}$, the smallest such $B$ pinned down by $N^{\prime}$ is $B_{N^{\prime}}:=\{\langle b^{\prime\prime},i^{\prime}\rangle : i^{\prime\prime}(b)=b^{\prime\prime}\text{ for some even }b\text{ and some arrow }i^{\prime\prime}\text{ agreeing with }i^{\prime}\text{ on }N^{\prime}\}$, which is transport-closed and pinned down by $N^{\prime}$. Now let $Y$ be coextensive with evenness and pinned down by a finite $N_0$; then $\langle b,i\rangle\in Y$ for every even $b$ and every arrow $i$ fixing $N_0$ pointwise. Take the arrow $i$, the even $b$ and the finite $N^{\prime}$ that the condition provides for $N_0$: no arrow agreeing with $i$ on $N^{\prime}$ sends an even number to $b$. So $\langle b,i\rangle\in Y\setminus B_{N^{\prime}}$, and $Y$ is not even weakly inextensible.

models.definition:
Proposition D.5, part 6 (p. 78): the arrows are the identity and the truncations $g_n$, $g_nm=\min\{m,n\}$, which compose as $g_n\circ g_m=g_{\min\{n,m\}}$. In every part, $W_0^\ddagger$ is the set of finite subsets of $\mathbb N$ and the model is ideally full: a proposition is a set of arrows whose membership depends only on the arrows’ values on some finite set of numbers (it is pinned down by that set), and an entity of a higher type is an applicative behaviour profile pinned down by a finite set in the same sense. The individuals are the natural numbers, acted on by the arrows themselves. Propositions and properties are thus about finitely many numbers and indifferent to how the arrows treat the rest. Evaluation point: the sole object, at the identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.finitely-pinned-domains: The model is ideally full: every entity is pinned down by a finite set of numbers, and every intension pinned down by one is in the domain (Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions that a given number is fixed by the arrow, one for each number, are pairwise distinct, each pinned down by that number (the shared argument axiom-of-infinity-t).
met.codomain-intensions: With one object such an intension is constant, so it is pinned down by $\emptyset$, and the domain holds every finitely pinned intension.
met.one-object-action-model: Each part of Proposition D.5 is a one-object category acting on $\mathbb N$ (Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3).
met.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$.
met.infinitely-many-individuals: The individuals are the natural numbers.
met.uniformly-pinned-rigidity: An intension is pinned down by $[0,s]$ iff it is constant on $\{g_n:n\ge s\}\cup\{1\}$. Weak inextensibility at the identity, tested with $[0,s']$ for $s'>n$, where $g_n$ is the only arrow with its germ, forces $Y(g_n)=g_n\cdot Y(1)$ for every $n$; and $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is in the domain iff $g_n\cdot E=E$ for all large $n$, which, as $g_n\cdot E\subseteq\operatorname{Pin}([0,n])$, holds iff $E\subseteq\operatorname{Pin}([0,n_0])$ for some $n_0$.
met.arrows-finitely-determined: Each $g_n$ is the only arrow with $g_n(n+1)=n$, so $\{g_n\}$ is pinned down by $\{n+1\}$.
met.evens-avoidable: With $N_0\subseteq[0,M_0]$: $i:=g_n$ with $n\ge M_0$, an even $b>n$, and $N^{\prime}:=[0,n+1]$: the only arrow agreeing with $g_n$ on $[0,n+1]$ is $g_n$ itself, whose range $[0,n]$ omits $b$.
met.pinned-atoms: Every nonempty proposition contains some $g_n$, and each $\{g_n\}$ is pinned down by a finite set ($\{n-1,n,n+1\}$ for $n>0$, $\{0,1\}$ for $n=0$).
met.unbounded-haecceities: With $A:=\mathbb N$: the strongest persistent property with extension $\mathbb N$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,n\}$ becomes ever stronger.
met.no-least-pinned-cover: Let $F$ be the family of singletons $\{g_n\}$ for even $n$. A superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$ contains, with any $g_m$ for $m\ge N$, every arrow agreeing with it on $\{0,\ldots,N\}$, so the least one is $\bigcup F\cup\{1_{\mathbb N}\}\cup\{g_m : m\ge N\}$, which strictly shrinks as $N$ grows.

models.definition:
Appendix D, p. 79, the paragraph beginning “One particularly interesting result”: two objects, $W_0=\mathbb N$ and $W_1=\{0\}$, with all functions between them as arrows, $W_i^\ddagger$ the finite subsets of $W_i$, and the model ideally full as in Proposition D.5. Evaluation point: $W_0$, at its identity arrow.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

meets.codomain-intensions: The model is ideally full at both objects, and an intension whose value at an arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain is pinned down by $\emptyset$ (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3).
meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.
meets.extensionally-full: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3).

arguments.text: BF holds at $W_0$, since every map agrees on any finite set with a surjection, and fails at $W_1$, where $\forall y\,\Box\,x=y$ holds of the one individual but $\Box\forall y\,x=y$ does not; so BF holds without $\Box$BF.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: The closed sentence that there is exactly one individual denotes the singleton of the unique map to $W_1$, a nonempty proposition with no nonempty proper subproposition.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The individuals are the natural numbers and identity at the evaluation arrow is literal, so no numeral counts them. The propositions that a given individual is fixed by the arrow, one for each individual, are pairwise distinct and each has that individual as finite support, so there are infinitely many propositions. The set of numerals at each type is invariant under every arrow, hence has empty support and lies in the domain, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property at either type.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: The transposition of $5$ and $6$ is an arrow with an inverse, so for any true $q$ the composite of a member of $q$ with the inverse carries the transposition into $q$, making $\Diamond q$ true there, while the true proposition that $5$ is fixed is false there.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr (observation); recorded by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: The model is ideally full, hence extensionally full at every object (Appendix D, the remark after Definition D.3): for any set $R$ of tuples from the domains at an object $V$, the intension that assigns to every arrow out of $V$ into an object $U$ a fixed set $R_U$ of tuples from $U$’s domains, with $R_V=R$, is pinned down by $\emptyset$, so it is the intension of an element of $V^{\bar\sigma\to t}$ with extension $R$ at $1_V$. Given a relation $U$ serial at $V$, choose for each $x$ a $y$ with $(Ux)y$, by choice in the metatheory; the graph is such an $R$, and its element $S$ is functional and a subrelation of $U$ at $1_V$, both conditions being unboxed. The closed Relational Choice instance is true at an arrow $h\colon W_0\to V$ iff it is true at $1_V$ in the truncation by $h$, whose domains at $V$ are those of the model, so it holds at every arrow and $\Box$Relational Choice follows.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: Any set $F$ of propositions is the extension of the profile $\langle h,p\rangle\mapsto\{i : i\cdot p\in F\}$, and for $F$ the family of propositions $A_m$ that a map $W_0\to W_0$ is constant on $\{0,\ldots,2m-1\}$ and first changes value at $2m$, the least superset of $\bigcup F$ pinned down by $\{0,\ldots,N\}$, the maps whose first change is at an even position or beyond $N$, strictly shrinks as $N$ grows, so $F$ has no least upper bound. The family is countable in the model's sense, the relation pairing $A_m$ with the numeral $m$ being in the domain by extensional fullness, so Countable Boolean Completeness fails too.

revisions.note: Refutes the instance of Countable Boolean Completeness counting at $e$, which the principle, now schematic in that type, includes.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: At $W_0$ the finite cardinalities are the standard numerals and $I^*$ is true; at $W_1$ the numerals remain pairwise distinct, because they differ at the arrows back into $W_0$ and identity is necessary, $I^*$ is again true, the numerals are the finite cardinalities by extensional fullness, and $\operatorname{Sum}$ and $\operatorname{Prod}$ are standard, their graphs being in the domain; so every arithmetical sentence has its standard truth value at every world.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The Necessity of Arithmetic is now a schema in the type $\sigma$ whose finite cardinalities are the numbers, and the argument covers every $\sigma$ unchanged. At $W_0$ every type has infinitely many entities, so $I^*_\sigma$ is true there, and the numerals at $\sigma$ are standard by the argument for the Axioms of Infinity, whose set of numerals at each type is invariant under every arrow. At $W_1$ the numerals at $\sigma$ still differ at the arrows back into $W_0$, the set of them is in the domain and closed under zero and successor, and the graphs of $\operatorname{Sum}_\sigma$ and $\operatorname{Prod}_\sigma$ are in the domain, as at $e$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: At $W_1$ the arrow $c_n\colon W_1\to W_0$ picking $n$ sends a proposition $q$ to $\{j : c_{j(n)}\in q\}$ (with the arrow to $W_1$ added when $q$ contains $1_{W_1}$), a proposition pinned down by $\{n\}$, so the proposition that $0$ and $1$ are collapsed is in no such image; the profile holding at $\langle h,d\rangle$ iff $h=1_{W_1}$ or $d$ is in the image of $h$, pinned down by $\{0\}$, is necessary of every proposition at $W_1$ but not universal at the world $c_0$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: At type $t\to t$, for the family $E$ of propositions $p_n$ that $n$ is fixed: for $Y$ inextensible with extension $E$ pinned down by the finite set $S$, pick $k\notin S$ and let $X$, pinned down by $S_X:=S\cup\{k\}$, hold at an arrow $h$ into $W_0$ exactly of the propositions $\{i : i(m)=n\}$ with $n\notin S_X$ and of the propositions $\{i : i(h(n))=n\}$ with $n\in S_X$; $X$ is necessary of every $p_n$, so $Y\le X$, yet at a map $h$ fixing $S$ pointwise and moving $k$, where $h\cdot Y=Y$, the extension of $X$ omits $p_k$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: A closed $\Sigma$-sentence denotes what $P(d,\ldots,d)$ denotes for a pure $P$ and the individual $d$, and from any world some arrow into $W_0$ carries the current image of $d$ back to $d$, as all maps are arrows.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), at Cian Dorr's request; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text:
Boxed Rigid Power, by lifting at each object; criterion (1) is part (1) of tame-rigidity-factorizable, which holds with several objects. Write $c$ for the map to the singleton and $i_n$ for the map from it with value $n$.
(a) Stable hulls. Let $F$ be rigid at $\mathbb N$ with extension $E$, $P$ a nonempty finite set containing a pin of $F$, and $A\subseteq E$ closed under the self-maps fixing $P$. Then $Y:=B_P(A)$ has extension $A$, lies below $F$, and is rigid. Weak rigidity at $\mathbb N$ is as in rigid-power-surjections, part (a), with self-maps (into the singleton, $r:=c$). For a self-map $h$, a member $k^{\prime}a$ of $Y_{kh}$ ($k^{\prime}$ agreeing with $kh$ on $P$) is $j(ra)$ with $ra\in Y_h$, $r$ agreeing with $h$ on $P$ and sending the rest of a pin of $a$ to fresh points, and $j$ agreeing with $k$ on any given finite $N\supseteq hP$; and $Y_c=cA=cY_h$ since $cr=c$; so $h\cdot Y$ is weakly rigid. At the singleton a weakly rigid relation is the exact image of its extension; $c\cdot F$ is rigid, so $F_{i_nc}=i_ncE$, and a member $x=ga$ of $Y_{i_nc}$ ($g$ agreeing with $i_nc$ on $P$) lies in $i_ncE$, so $x=i_ncx=i_ncga=i_nca$, $cg$ being $c$. So $c\cdot Y=T(cA)$, which is rigid.
(b) Lifting at $\mathbb N$. A weakly rigid $H$ with extension $E$ has $H_j=jE$ for every surjective self-map $j$, as in rigid-power-surjections, part (b). Given a rigid $F$, an arrow $k$, a finite $N$ containing a pin of $F$, and a rigid $X\le k\cdot F$ with extension $D$ pinned down by $T$: if $k$ is a self-map, extend $k|_N$ to a surjection $j$ with finitely many non-singleton fibres, all finite, take $P$ containing $N$, those fibres and preimages of $T$, and $A:=\{a\in E:ja\in D\}$; for $u$ fixing $P$, $ju=vj$ with $v$ fixing $T$, so $uA\subseteq A$, and $j\cdot B_P(A)=X$ by (a) and the exact-image fact. If $k=c$, take $A:=\{a\in E:ca\in D\}$, stable since $cu=c$, and $c\cdot B_P(A)=X$.
(c) At the singleton every rigid $F$ is $T(E)$ and every $T(A)$, $A\subseteq E$, is admitted; a rigid $X\le i_n\cdot F$ with extension $D$ is $i_n\cdot T(cD)$, since $ci_n=1$. So the power property of every rigid relation, at either object, is weakly rigid, and Rigid Power holds at every world. Weakly Rigid Power still fails, with Tame Rigidity.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Write $\mathrm{fix}_N$ for the arrows agreeing with the identity on the finite set $N$, the least true proposition pinned by $N$, and $\delta_N$ for the arrows injective on $N$. At $W_0$ the arrows are all maps $\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$ and the one map $c$ to $W_1=\{0\}$. $\Diamond\,\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N$ is the set of maps injective on $N$, together with $c$ when $|N|\le1$; the same set is $\hat\Diamond\,\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N$, since an injective-on-$N$ map is undone by a bijection and $c$ by the map picking the point of $N$, which returns to every truth at $W_1$ ($W_1$ is a point, so its domains are full and $c\circ v=1_{W_1}$). So $\Box_{\ne}$ and $\hat{\hat\Box}$ coincide at the evaluation point. BF at type $t$ holds for $\hat{\hat\Box}$ there: for $Y$ pinned by $X_Y$ and $N\supseteq X_Y$ with two elements, every $k\in\hat\Diamond\,\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N$ is a map injective on $N$, which agrees on $X_Y$ with a bijection $b$, and $Y_k=Y_b$ contains every transport along $b$, i.e. everything; so by Proposition D8 of The Bounds of Possibility $\Box_5$ implies two-hat necessity at $W_0$, and at $W_1$ too, which is full. The truth $\mathrm{fix}^{00}_{\{0\}}$ is not 5-necessary, since $\Box_5\le\hat{\hat\Box}$ fails on it (a bijection moving $0$ is in every $\hat\Diamond\,\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N$). At $W_1$, the maps $W_1\to W_0$ are retracted by $c$ but not invertible, so, $W_1$ being full, $\{1_{W_1}\}$ is two-hat necessary and not ND-necessary there: the identity $\Box_{\ne}=\hat{\hat\Box}$ fails. (The verdicts this argument also establishes but does not record are derived by the engine.)

models.definition:
A singleton-base specialization of Bacon’s full Boolean-valued construction in §B.2. Work in ZFC, let $A$ be a nontrivial complete atomless Boolean algebra, and set $B=\mathbf{2}\times A$, $D_e=\{*\}$, $D_t=B$, and $D_{\sigma\to\tau}=D_\tau^{D_\sigma}$ for every admitted function type. Use ordinary application and abstraction, Boolean connectives, quantifiers given by meets and joins, and crisp equality. Evaluation point: the atom $a=(1,0_A)$; a proposition is true iff its first coordinate is $1$.

For concreteness, $A$ is fixed as the regular open algebra of the real line. Other choices of $A$ can be put to interesting uses; for the principles on the map the choice matters, as far as is known, only to $\Box$Boolean Completeness (type $t$), whose failure below uses a real that forcing with $A$ adds.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

arguments.text: The full function domains and complete truth projection validate C, boxed BF, and boxed ND.
Extensional fullness and metatheoretic choice give Relational Choice; full function domains give Plenitude, hence Functional Choice.
The sole atom $a$ witnesses Actuality and refutes Atomlessness, while $(0,1_A)$ is nonzero with no atom below it, refuting Atomicity at type $t$ and the full schema.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's request
arguments.text: Write $\pi$ and $\rho$ for the two coordinate projections of $B=\mathbf 2\times A$, both complete homomorphisms; $\Box p$ is $p=\top$, so a closed sentence is necessary when it is true and its $\rho$-coordinate is $1_A$. Under $\rho$ a sentence without $\Box$ takes its value in the Boolean-valued universe $V^A$, each $D_\sigma$ read as a ground set with crisp identity and the $\rho$-parts of relations on it ranging over all names for subsets of it. So a theorem of ZFC about relations on well-orderable sets has $\rho$-value $1_A$. Transversal Choice is of this kind: the least element of each class, $F(y):=\bigwedge_{y^{\prime}<y}\neg R(y^{\prime},y)$, is a transversal. Its truth is already derived, so it is necessary.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's request
arguments.text: An effect of the single individual. The type-$e$ numerals are crisply three entities, $\mathbf 0_e$, $\mathbf 1_e$, and the empty cardinality, which is its own successor, so $\operatorname{Ctbl}(X)$ makes $X$ have at most three members internally; a finite subset of a ground set is a ground set, and finite families have joins in the complete pointwise order. So every closed instance has value $1_B$.

withdrawn.reason: Countable Boolean Completeness now measures countability at every type. The argument covers only the instances counting at $e$; at type $t$, where $B$ is infinite and the numerals are the standard ones, it says nothing.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's request
arguments.text: $B$ is infinite and identity is crisp. The crisp characteristic function of the standard numerals is inductive, so finite cardinality has value $0_B$ off the standard numerals, and the $n$th numeral holds of the universal property of propositions with the value of "$B$ has exactly $n$ elements", $0_B$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's request
arguments.text: For the algebra fixed in the definition. Take a countable maximal antichain $(a_n)$ in $A$, put $w_n:=(0,\neg a_n)$, choose $c_n\in A$, and let $X$ of type $t\to t$ have $\rho X(w_n)=c_n$ and $0$ elsewhere. With $s$ the fuzzy subset of $\omega$ given by the $c_n$, a direct computation gives $\rho[\![\exists y\, .\,\operatorname{GLB}_t(y,X)]\!]=\bigvee_{U\subseteq\omega}[\![s=\check U]\!]$, the value of "$s$ is a ground set". The regular open algebra of $\mathbb R$ adds a Cohen real; taking the $c_n$ to be its coordinates, $[\![s=\check U]\!]=0_A$ for every $U$, so the closed instance of Boolean Completeness (type $t$) has value exactly $a$: true, and not necessary. Whether it is necessary for an algebra adding no reals is open.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: At $\sigma=\tau=t$, for the property $X$ of type $t\to t$ in the argument for the failure of $\Box$Boolean Completeness (type $t$). The crisp relation pairing $w_n$ with the $n$-th numeral, and nothing else, is in the full domain; the numerals at $t$ are crisply the standard ones (the argument for the Axiom of Infinity (type $t$)), so $\operatorname{Ctbl}_{t,t}(X)$ has value $1_B$. The instance of Countable Boolean Completeness at $X$ in its greatest-lower-bound form then has the value of $\exists y\, .\,\operatorname{GLB}_t(y,X)$, whose $A$-coordinate is $0_A$, so the closed instance is not necessary.

models.notes:
Full verification is in the write-up.

The source uses an infinite individual domain and a particular regular-open algebra for its analysis of the continuum hypothesis. Neither feature is needed for this counterexample; the recorded specialization requires only ZFC. For an extensionally full model in ZFC, Relational Choice follows by representing a set-theoretic functional subrelation, and Plenitude then gives Functional Choice. The qualitative-contrast model of Classicism does not meet this fullness condition: its finite-support and symmetry restrictions exclude the needed selector. In the present model, $R(p,q):=(p\land q=\top)\lor(\neg p\land q=\bot)$ has Seriality and Functionality of value $1_B$, but $\exists f\,\forall p\,R(p,f(p))$ has value exactly $a$. The write-up includes the atomless-component calculation and the comparison with the older model. The finite check tests the Boolean calculation, not the infinite construction.

models.name: Full action model: double retraction with free sites, glued constants

certificate.produced_by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction, 14 October 2026, combining Cian Dorr's two-retraction category with Bacon's gluing construction (Logical Combinatorialism, Appendix A.3)

sources: Cian Dorr and Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), conversation of 14 October 2026 (transcript in the private notes); writeups/full-double-retraction-glued-constants.md.
Cian Dorr, the two-object retract with two retractions (model full-two-object-retract-double-retraction, 6 October 2026).
Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Appendix A.3 (the gluing of Σ-models at the sites of a self-similar frame); A Philosophical Introduction to Higher-Order Logics, §18.6, Definition 18.15.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.4–3.5, pp. 55–61 (full action models; Proposition 3.24).

references.note: The gluing construction, here carried out at the root of a two-object category.

models.definition: Let $\mathcal C$ be the category of the two-object retract with two retractions: objects $W_0,W_1$, generated by $h:W_0\to W_1$ and $j_1,j_2:W_1\to W_0$ with $j_i\circ h=1_{W_0}$, so that $e_i:=h\circ j_i$ are idempotents with $e_i\circ h=h$. Let $\mathcal D:=\mathcal C*_{W_0}F$ be obtained by freely adjoining at $W_0$ the free monoid $F$ on countably many generators $f_1,f_2,\ldots$ (the pushout over the object $W_0$; its arrows are the alternating reduced words of non-identity arrows of $\mathcal C$ and non-identity elements of $F$). Take the full action model over $\mathcal D$ with a single individual, evaluated at $1_{W_0}$, and glue the constants of Σ at the sites $f_k$: enumerate the pure formulas $P_k(\bar x)$, with $\bar x$ matching a tuple of distinct constants, whose existential closure is true at the root, choose a witness tuple for each, and let each constant denote the intension at $W_0$ whose value at an arrow $u\circ f_k$ is the extension at $u$ of the $k$-th witness and whose value at the remaining arrows is empty. Each part has one job (write-up, §4): the sites give Witnessed Possibility; the two retractions of $h$ make Strong Actuality fail at $W_0$ while it holds at $W_1$, so a pure sentence is contingent; and every arrow into $W_1$ factors through $h$, whose transports never yield the true atom of $W_1$, so Possibly Witnessed Possibility fails.

meets.full-model: Every intension of every relational type is present at both objects.
meets.full-action-model: A full action model with two objects.
meets.identity-singletons: The singletons $\{1_{W_0}\}$ and $\{1_{W_1}\}$ are in the domains, the model being full.
meets.rigid-haecceity-disjunctions: Every intension is present at both objects, so for any set $E$ the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is in the domain; a relation is weakly inextensible at a world iff it lies below that intension over its extension there, and with persistence a weakly rigid relation equals it, so the rigid relations are exactly these, as in the group of full action models.
meets.one-individual: The construction fixes a single individual at each object.
meets.infinitely-many-propositions: Infinitely many arrows leave $W_0$ (the sites $f_k$ alone), and the propositions are all sets of them.
meets.returning-arrow: $h$, which $j_1$ retracts.
meets.noninvertible-retracted-arrow: $h$ is retracted by $j_1$ and $j_2$ but has no inverse, since $h\circ j_i=e_i\ne1_{W_1}$.
meets.separated-retractions: $h$ has the retractions $j_1\ne j_2$, and these remain its only retractions in $\mathcal D$ (write-up, Corollary 3); the proposition $\{j_1\}$ at $W_1$ separates them.
meets.unretracted-arrow: $f_1$: by the cancellation lemma of the write-up, $x\circ f_1=1_{W_0}$ would need a left inverse of $f_1$ in the free monoid.
meets.trivial-isomorphisms-everywhere: By the cancellation lemma an isomorphism has only invertible syllables, and neither $\mathcal C$ nor $F$ has a non-identity invertible element ($h\circ j_i=e_i\ne1$).
meets.irreversible-arrow: The world $f_1$: no arrow $x$ has $x\circ f_1=1_{W_0}$, so no world after $f_1$ makes the actual-world proposition true.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The write-up, §§1–2, verifies the gluing at the root: the sites $f_k$ are right-cancellable with pairwise disjoint left ideals in $\mathcal D$, so the glued intensions are well defined and, the model being full, in the domain at $W_0$; at the site $f_k$ the constants denote the $k$-th witness tuple. If $\exists\bar x\,P$ is true at the root, $P$ is enumerated and $P[\bar c]$ holds at its site.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Strong Actuality fails at $W_0$, where $h$ has the two retractions $j_1,j_2$, and holds at $W_1$, where no non-identity arrow has a retraction (write-up, Corollary 3), so the true atom $\{1_{W_1}\}$ is a strong world there; a closed pure sentence being true at an arrow iff true at its target, the pure sentence SA is true exactly at the worlds with target $W_1$. Let $c$ be a constant of type $t$ and $P(x)$ say that SA holds and $x$ is a true atom. $\Diamond\exists x\,P$ holds at the root, at the world $h$. But every arrow $W_0\to W_1$ is $h\circ v$, so at any world with target $W_1$ the constant denotes a transport along $h$ of a proposition at $W_0$, which contains $1_{W_1}$ iff it contains $e_1$ (as $e_1\circ h=h$) and so is not $\{1_{W_1}\}$; at worlds with target $W_0$, SA fails. So $P[c]$ is possible nowhere (write-up, §3.3).

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Every object reaches every object ($h$ forward, $j_1$ back). A closed pure sentence true at the root is therefore possible at every world: at a world with target $W_0$ it holds there, and at one with target $W_1$ it holds after $j_1$ (write-up, §3.4).

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Let $p:=\{1\}$, in the domain since the model is full, and true. Any witness $q$ for $\Box_{\ne}p$ is true, so contains the identity; under an arrow $i\ne 1$ with a retraction $r$, the arrow $r\circ i=1$ makes $\Diamond q$ true, while $p$ is false. So no true $q$ has $\Box(\Diamond q\to p)$. (The surjection monoid's own argument of 23 September, stated once.)

arguments.text: In a full action model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain at every object. Taking it as the witness, $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains every arrow out of that object with a retraction (these are the arrows at which $\Diamond\{1\}$ holds), and $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of it (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible). Full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. With only identities invertible, $\Box_5$ is the identity operator at every reachable object, so every truth is 5-necessary everywhere.

arguments.text: Entailment is inclusion of intensions. Below a relation $Y\ne\bot_\tau$ lies the relation whose intension is the singleton of one of $Y$'s tuples, which is in the domain since the model is full, and is an atom: its only proper part is $\bot_\tau$. Every object being full, the same holds at every arrow, so Atomicity is necessary. The source notes that full models are atomic (p. 61); stated once for the topic, in place of the full models' own arguments.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Given $X$ of type $\tau$ at an object $W$, let $Y$ be the relation whose extension at an arrow $i$ out of $W$ is $X$'s extension at $W$ transported along $i$, which is in the domain since the model is full. It is coextensive with $X$. It is persistent, since its extension at $i\circ j$ is its extension at $i$ transported along $j$. And it is inextensible: if $\Box X'$ holds at $i$ of everything $Y$ holds of there, then at $i\circ j$ everything $Y$ holds of is the transport along $j$ of something $Y$ holds of at $i$, of which $X'$ then holds. Every object being full, the same holds at every arrow, so Rigid Comprehension is necessary. The source notes that full models satisfy it (p. 61); stated once for the topic, in place of the full models' own arguments.

arguments.text: Write $X_0(E)$ for the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$. The extension at an arrow $h$ of the power property $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is the set of rigid $X$ with $X\le h\cdot F$, the bound variable ranging over the domain untransported and the parameter transported. By the condition the rigid relations are the $X_0(E)$, and $X_0(T)\le X_0(S)$ iff $T\subseteq S$; so for rigid $F=X_0(S)$ the power property has extension $\{X_0(T'):T'\subseteq k\cdot S\}$ at $k$, while transporting its extension at the identity along $k$ gives $\{X_0(k\cdot T):T\subseteq S\}$. These coincide, since every $T'\subseteq k\cdot S$ is $k\cdot T$ for $T:=\{s\in S:k\cdot s\in T'\}$. So the power property is itself $X_0$ of its extension, hence rigid, and the same at every reachable object gives the boxed form.

arguments.text: Let $h$ out of the evaluation object have retractions $j\ne j^{\prime}$, and let $q$ at $h$'s target contain $j$ but not $j^{\prime}$. A true proposition $p$ contains the identity, so under $h$ it becomes a proposition containing $j$ and $j^{\prime}$, since $j\circ h=j^{\prime}\circ h=1$. arguments.text: In a full action model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain at every object. Taking it as the witness, $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains every arrow out of that object with a retraction (these are the arrows at which $\Diamond\{1\}$ holds), and $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of it (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible). settings.construction: Let M be the free monoid of finite sequences of natural numbers under concatenation; its induced Kripke frame is the infinitely branching tree with the initial-segment relation and the empty sequence as root. Take the standard model over this frame (propositions all sets of accessible worlds, function types all homomorphisms) whose individuals at a world are the functions from the infinite branches through that world to the natural numbers, with restriction as counterpart; equivalently, the full action model over M with this surjective M-set at type e. models.definition: Let $M:=F_\infty * E * B * \mathbb Z_2$ be the free product of monoids, where $F_\infty$ is the free monoid on countably many generators $f_1,f_2,\ldots$, $E=\{1,e\}$ with $e^2=e$, $B=\langle b,c\mid cb=1\rangle$ is the bicyclic monoid, and $\mathbb Z_2=\{1,s\}$ with $s^2=1$. Take the full one-object action model over $M$ (Classicism, §3.5) with a single individual, evaluated at the identity. The constants of Σ are glued at the sites $f_k$: enumerate the pure formulas $P_k(\bar x)$, with $\bar x$ matching a tuple of distinct constants, such that $\exists\bar x\,P_k$ is true at the identity, choose a witness tuple for each, and let each constant denote the intension whose value at an arrow $u\circ f_k$ is $u$ applied to the $k$-th witness and whose value at the remaining arrows is empty. Each factor has one job (write-up, §4): the free generators are the gluing sites that give Logical Necessity; the idempotent $e$ is a non-epic arrow, so BF fails; $b$ is retracted by $c$ but not invertible, so ND-necessity and two-hat necessity come apart; $s$ is a non-identity unit, so some truth is not 5-necessary.

It is coextensive with $X$. It is persistent, since its extension at $i\circ j$ is its extension at $i$ transported along $j$. And it is inextensible: if $\Box X'$ holds at $i$ of everything $Y$ holds of there, then at $i\circ j$ everything $Y$ holds of is the transport along $j$ of something $Y$ holds of at $i$, of which $X'$ then holds. Every object being full, the same holds at every arrow, so Rigid Comprehension is necessary. arguments.text: Write $X_0(E)$ for the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$. The extension at an arrow $h$ of the power property $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is the set of rigid $X$ with $X\le h\cdot F$, the bound variable ranging over the domain untransported and the parameter transported. By the condition the rigid relations are the $X_0(E)$, and $X_0(T)\le X_0(S)$ iff $T\subseteq S$; so for rigid $F=X_0(S)$ the power property has extension $\{X_0(T'):T'\subseteq k\cdot S\}$ at $k$, while transporting its extension at the identity along $k$ gives $\{X_0(k\cdot T):T\subseteq S\}$. These coincide, since every $T'\subseteq k\cdot S$ is $k\cdot T$ for $T:=\{s\in S:k\cdot s\in T'\}$. So the power property is itself $X_0$ of its extension, hence rigid, and the same at every reachable object gives the boxed form.

arguments.text: In a full action model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain at every object. Taking it as the witness, $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains every arrow out of that object with a retraction (these are the arrows at which $\Diamond\{1\}$ holds), and $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of it (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible). Full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. Let $u$ have a retraction but no inverse. The true proposition $\{1\}$ excludes $u$, so it is not ND-necessary, while every invertible arrow is the identity or excluded from no such test: $\{1\}$ is two-hat necessary iff no non-identity arrow is invertible, and in any case the proposition $\{1\}\cup\{\text{invertible arrows}\}$ is in the domain, true, two-hat necessary and not ND-necessary.

models.name: Full Henkin model: countably infinite individual domain
sources: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.2, Definition 3.6 and Proposition 3.7, pp. 47–48.
models.definition:
Use the ordinary full Henkin interpretation with $D_e$ countably infinite, $D_t=\{0,1\}$, and every admitted function type containing all functions between its domains; by Proposition 3.7 it is a model of C. Identity is genuine identity and $\Box$ is the identity on truth values, so $\Diamond$ is truth.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.

arguments.text: Because every domain is full, $\operatorname{FiniteCardinality}_\sigma$ holds exactly of the values of the numerals $\operatorname{Suc}_\sigma^k\mathbf{0}_\sigma$: the characteristic function of that set is in the domain and is inductive. At type $e$ the $k$-th numeral says that there are exactly $k$ individuals, which is false for every $k$, so the Axiom of Infinity at type $e$ holds, and with it the schema.

The remaining positive assertions hold as in every two-valued full model: each boxed principle reduces to its unboxed form; coextensive relations are identical, so Extensionality, the Fregean axiom and its modalized form hold; every relation is persistent, inextensible and Gallin-extensional, giving the comprehension principles; Actuality holds with top as the actual world; each relational type is the complete atomic Boolean algebra of subsets of a domain, giving Atomicity and Boolean Completeness; Tractarianism is a tautology; ND holds outright, giving C5; every closed sentence is non-contingent; and the choice principles hold because every function between domains is present, using choice in the metatheory to select from a serial relation on an infinite domain.

models.notes: Explicit specialization of the source's standard Henkin construction to an infinite individual domain, recorded to separate the type-$e$ infinity principles from the type-$t$ ones: it satisfies the Axiom of Infinity at type $e$, hence Possible Infinity at type $e$, while violating the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$. It also shows that the sentence used in pure-possibility-implies-axiom-of-infinity-t, that there could be any positive number of individuals, does not follow from the Axiom of Infinity at type $e$: here there is not possibly exactly one individual. It also witnesses the consistency of C with Goodsell's $I$, assumed in n. 14 of Arithmetic is Necessary: with infinitely many individuals the numerals are pairwise distinct, so $\operatorname{Suc}_e$ is injective on finite cardinalities and $I^*$, hence $I$, is true. With Boolean Completeness listed, the model also shows Countable Boolean Completeness consistent with C. Everything that implies these fails with them.

Corrected the reason given for the failures of Independence (signature Σ) and Distinctness (signature Σ): the true atom is denoted by no closed pure term, since such terms denote entities fixed by every arrow; the failures come from the other relational constants, which denote top. Added Transversal Choice, by the argument recorded for Relational Choice: a full model contains every intension, in particular one whose extension at the evaluation point is a transversal, chosen in the metatheory, of the extension there of an equivalence relation; the equivalence and transversal conditions are unboxed. Recorded on a question of Zachary Goodsell, after an observation of Christopher Sun.

Corrected the previously recorded necessary Strong Leibniz-t flag. Confirmed the trawl's Strong Leibniz-t failure: an admitted nonidentity-idempotent singleton shifts to a set containing both the identity and the idempotent, which a target-domain proposition separates. Quantifiers inside the box range over the entire target domain. The boxed failure follows by T.

Corrected the claim of 22 September 2026 that □Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t) hold: the argument that every singleton is a strong world needs the monoid to be right-cancellative, and here the transport of {k} along k is {1, k}. The type-t principle fails; see the notes.

models.definition:
The full model on {1,k} with k²=k, evaluated at its sole object.

Individuals, fixed for this record: at every object the individuals are the members of an infinite set $D$, the same at every object, and every arrow acts on them as the identity.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$; every other constant of Σ, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.

Metatheory, fixed for this record: the construction is carried out in ZF together with a countable family $(P_n)_{n\in\omega}$ of pairwise disjoint two-element sets that has no choice function (Russell's socks), which is consistent with ZF (Fraenkel's second permutation model, transferred to ZF by the Jech–Sochor theorem). Every infinite set the construction leaves unspecified (the individuals, the worlds, a carrier) is their union. The verdicts of this record are relative-consistency claims of the same standing as those of a record with choice.

met.rigid-haecceity-disjunctions: Every intension is present, so for any set $E$ the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is in the domain, and a relation is weakly inextensible at a world iff it lies below that intension over its extension there, since that is the smallest intension satisfying the hypothesis; with persistence, a rigid relation equals it (the argument deferred in extraction.md, 3 October 2026).
met.codomain-intensions: The domains are full at every object.
met.full-model: Every intension of every relational type is present at every object (Classicism, §3.5, p. 59).
met.full-action-model: An action model, full at every object (Classicism, §3.5, p. 59; Appendix D).
met.extensionally-full: A full model contains every intension, so in particular one with any given extension at the identity.
met.identity-singletons: The singleton of the identity arrow at any object is in the domain, the model being full.
met.actuality-contingent: The singleton $a$ of the identity arrow is in the domain, the model being full. It is necessary at no world: a world other than the identity sees itself, which lies outside $a$, and the identity sees an arrow other than itself. And a non-identity arrow $k$ does not fix it, since $1\in k\cdot a$ would need $1\circ k=1$.
met.fixed-infinite-individuals: This is the choice of individuals.
met.homogeneous-individuals: A permutation of $D$ commutes with every arrow's action, the identity, so it is an automorphism at type $e$ and extends, by conjugation, to the full domains of the other types, carrying each individual to its image.
met.unretracted-arrow: $m\cdot k=k$ for both arrows $m$, so $k$ has no retraction.
met.finitely-many-propositions-everywhere: There is one object, with four propositions, the sets of the two arrows.
met.sigma-apart: The construction does not mention Σ.
met.one-object-action-model: It has one object.
met.finitely-many-propositions: The propositions at the evaluation object are the subsets of the two arrows out of it, four in all.
met.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain, the model being full; under $k$, $x\circ k=k$ for both arrows, so no world outside it sees it.
met.irreversible-arrow: The arrow $k$: $x\circ k=k$ for both arrows $x$, so no composite with it is the identity.

models.name: Full action model: infinite S5
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 7 October 2026, as a basic reference model.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, pp. 58–61 (full action models).

references.note: Full action models; on this category the construction is the standard full S5 model.

settings.construction: The category whose objects are the members of an infinite set $W$, with exactly one arrow from each object to each object, evaluated at any object. The arrows out of an object correspond to the members of $W$, so this is the full S5 model with world set $W$ and a constant domain of individuals.

numbered-returning-arrows.text: $h_n$ is the arrow to world $n$, and $r_n$ the arrow back, once $W$ contains the natural numbers: by choice, or because $W$ is $\mathbb N$ in the variant without countable choice. With socks $W$ is their union, and no such arrows need be given.

meets.invertible-arrows: The unique arrow from $u$ to $v$ is inverted by the unique arrow from $v$ to $u$.
meets.epic-arrows: Every arrow is invertible; and on the individuals every arrow is the identity.
meets.retractions: Each arrow out of the evaluation object is retracted by the arrow back.
meets.unique-retractions-everywhere: Between two objects there is only one arrow, so an arrow has exactly one retraction.
meets.returning-arrow: The arrow to any other object, retracted by the arrow back.
meets.coherent-retractions: $r_g$ is the unique arrow back; any two arrows with the same ends are equal, so $r_{x\circ g}\circ x=r_g$.
meets.nonidentity-arrow: The arrow to any other object.
meets.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions are all the sets of arrows out of the evaluation object, one for each subset of $W$.
meets.sigma-apart: The construction does not mention Σ.

history.summary: Adopted the source’s relational type system at the user’s request. The cited construction now directly supplies the recorded model; the former type-extension obligation is removed.

Added Relational Choice at Cian Dorr's direction. With choice in the metatheory a serial relation has a functional subrelation, and a full model contains every intension, so that subrelation is in the domain; see Classicism, p. 61, on the principles common to full models. The propositions at the evaluation object are the subsets of the two arrows out of it, four in all, and every intension of a full model is present, so the numerals are the finite cardinalities and the fourth holds of the universal property of propositions: the Axiom of Infinity at type t fails, as does the fifth instance of the schema.
Fixed an interpretation of Σ (relational constants as top, individual constants as one fixed individual) and recorded the signature schemata it refutes, at Cian Dorr’s request.
Added □Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t): every singleton of an arrow is a strong world in a propositionally full one-object model; see the notes.
Boxed the Relational Choice claim; see the notes.
Re-fixed the interpretation of Σ so as to settle No Contingency (signature Σ) and B for sentences of Σ, at Cian Dorr’s request; see the notes.

Corrected the reason given for the failures of Independence (signature Σ) and Distinctness (signature Σ): the true atom is denoted by no closed pure term, since such terms denote entities fixed by every arrow; the failures come from the other relational constants, which denote top. No verdict changes.

Added Transversal Choice, by the argument recorded for Relational Choice: a full model contains every intension, in particular one whose extension at the evaluation point is a transversal, chosen in the metatheory, of the extension there of an equivalence relation; the equivalence and transversal conditions are unboxed. Recorded on a question of Zachary Goodsell, after an observation of Christopher Sun.
Corrected the justification of □Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t): the 22 September argument tacitly used that the monoid is right-cancellative, which holds here; no verdict changes.

models.name: Full action model: permutations of an infinite set
sources: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), construction and verification of 23 September 2026, at Cian Dorr’s suggestion (see the write-up).
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, pp. 58–59 (full M-set models, Proposition 3.24, No Pure Contingency); p. 61 and n. 84 (principles of full models).
Andrew Bacon, Logical Combinatorialism, Philosophical Review 129 (2020), Appendix A.2, Definitions A.1–A.4 and Proposition A.5, pp. 581–583 (M-set models).

references.note: The source describes full M-set models and proves the facts used: Proposition 3.24 on ND and BF, the one-object No Pure Contingency observation, and the principles common to full models. The specific group and the verification are in the write-up.

references.locator: Appendix A.2, Definitions A.1–A.4 and Proposition A.5, pp. 581–583
references.note: The M-set presentation of one-object action models: the division action on propositions and the function-space M-set.

settings.construction: The full one-object action model whose arrows are all the permutations of a countably infinite set $X$, composed as functions. Propositions are all sets of arrows with the division action $i\cdot p=\{j : j\circ i\in p\}$, and every function type carries the full function-space M-set, which here is the set of all functions since every arrow acts bijectively. Evaluate at the identity arrow.

meets.numbered-returning-arrows: With $X$ enumerated as $x_0,x_1,\ldots$, $h_0$ the identity and $h_n$ the transposition of $x_0$ and $x_n$, its own retraction.
meets.returning-arrow: Any permutation other than the identity, which its inverse retracts.
meets.nonidentity-arrow: Any permutation other than the identity.
meets.epic-arrows: Every arrow is invertible; and on the individuals every arrow is the identity.
meets.infinitely-many-propositions: The propositions are all the sets of arrows, and there are infinitely many permutations.
meets.sigma-apart: The construction does not mention Σ.

models.notes:
Full proofs are in the write-up. The model witnesses the joint consistency of $\Box$ND, the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ and $\Box$Relational Choice. Suggested by Cian Dorr on 23 September 2026 to fill a gap: no earlier record settled $\Box$ND, the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ and $\Box$Relational Choice together.
The write-up full-permutation-group-infinite-set treats the source's natural action, on the individuals $X$ by evaluation; the write-up full-permutation-group-one-individual records what changes with one individual, recorded separately until 3 October 2026, when it became this member at the group's default. The natural action, like the identity action on infinitely many individuals, is bijective and has the Axiom of Infinity at type $e$, which is all the map's principles see of the individuals here.

models.definition:
Use the monoid of surjections of an infinite set, at its sole object.

Individuals, fixed for this record: there is a single individual at every object, and every arrow sends it to the single individual at its target.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

Metatheory, fixed for this record: the axiom of choice is used freely, as in ordinary mathematics in ZFC, or in Lean's classical type theory for the verdicts certified there.

met.rigid-haecceity-disjunctions: Every intension is present, so for any set $E$ the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is in the domain, and a relation is weakly inextensible at a world iff it lies below that intension over its extension there, since that is the smallest intension satisfying the hypothesis; with persistence, a rigid relation equals it (the argument deferred in extraction.md, 3 October 2026).
met.codomain-intensions: The domains are full at every object.
met.full-model: Every intension of every relational type is present at every object (Classicism, §3.5, p. 59).
met.full-action-model: An action model, full at every object (Classicism, §3.5, p. 59; Appendix D).
met.extensionally-full: A full model contains every intension, so in particular one with any given extension at the identity.
met.identity-singletons: The singleton of the identity arrow at any object is in the domain, the model being full.
met.actuality-contingent: The singleton $a$ of the identity arrow is in the domain, the model being full. It is necessary at no world: a world other than the identity sees itself, which lies outside $a$, and the identity sees an arrow other than itself. And a non-identity arrow $k$ does not fix it, since $1\in k\cdot a$ would need $1\circ k=1$.

met.homogeneous-individuals: There is only one individual.

met.epic-arrows: A surjection $k$ is an epimorphism among the surjections, $m\circ k=m^{\prime}\circ k$ giving $m=m^{\prime}$; and on the individuals every arrow is the identity.
