models.definition:
A full action model over two objects $W_0$ and $W_1$, with one nonidentity arrow $f:W_0\to W_1$ besides the identities, evaluated at the identity of $W_0$. The individuals are $\{{a\}}$ at $W_0$ and $\{{b,c\}}$ at $W_1$, and $f$ sends $a$ to $b$. Every intension of every relational type is present at each object.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

meets.full-model: Every intension of every relational type is present at every object.
meets.full-action-model: An action model, full at every object.
meets.codomain-intensions: The domains are full at every object.
meets.extensionally-full: A full model contains every intension, so in particular one with any given extension at the identity.
meets.identity-singletons: The singleton of the identity arrow at any object is in the domain, the model being full.
meets.actuality-contingent: The singleton $a$ of the identity arrow at $W_0$ is in the domain. It is necessary at no world: the identity sees $f$, outside it, and $f$ does not fix it, since $1\in f\cdot a$ would need $1\circ f=1$.
meets.rigid-haecceity-disjunctions: Every intension is present, so for any set $E$ the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is in the domain, and with persistence a rigid relation equals it (as for the group full-action-models).
meets.relationally-epic-arrows: Out of $W_1$ there is only the identity, so $f$ is an epimorphism.
meets.unretracted-arrow: There is no arrow from $W_1$ back to $W_0$.
meets.fewer-propositions-after: $W_0$ has four propositions and $W_1$, after which there is only itself, two.
meets.finitely-many-propositions: The propositions at $W_0$ are the subsets of the two arrows out of it.
meets.finitely-many-propositions-everywhere: $W_0$ has four propositions and $W_1$ two.

arguments.text: At type $e$. The haecceity $H$ of $a$, with extension $\{{a\}}$ at the identity of $W_0$ and $\{{b\}}$ at $f$, is necessary of everything at $W_0$, whose only individual is $a$; but after $f$ it fails of $c$. arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: In a full action model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain at every object. Taking it as the witness, $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains every arrow out of that object with a retraction (these are the arrows at which $\Diamond\{1\}$ holds), and $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of it (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible). Full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. With only identities invertible, $\Box_5$ is the identity operator at every reachable object, so every truth is 5-necessary everywhere.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Entailment is inclusion of intensions. Below a relation $Y\ne\bot_\tau$ lies the relation whose intension is the singleton of one of $Y$'s tuples, which is in the domain since the model is full, and is an atom: its only proper part is $\bot_\tau$. Every object being full, the same holds at every arrow, so Atomicity is necessary. The source notes that full models are atomic (p. 61); stated once for the topic, in place of the full models' own arguments.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The relational half of full-epic-barcan. In an action model BF at a type $\sigma$ holds at a world iff transport along every arrow out of it is onto the entities of type $\sigma$ at its target: if some $z$ there is no transport, the property of being one is necessary of everything at the world and fails of $z$ after the arrow; and if transport is onto, a property necessary of everything holds of every transport. In a full model the transport of intensions along an epimorphism $k$ is onto at every relational type: an intension $Y$ at its target is the transport of $\{\langle\bar a,k\circ m\rangle:\langle\bar a,m\rangle\in Y\}$, since $k\circ m=k\circ m'$ only if $m=m'$. Nothing here concerns the individuals. So BF holds at every relational type at every object reachable from the evaluation point.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Given $X$ of type $\tau$ at an object $W$, let $Y$ be the relation whose extension at an arrow $i$ out of $W$ is $X$'s extension at $W$ transported along $i$, which is in the domain since the model is full. It is coextensive with $X$. It is persistent, since its extension at $i\circ j$ is its extension at $i$ transported along $j$. And it is inextensible: if $\Box X'$ holds at $i$ of everything $Y$ holds of there, then at $i\circ j$ everything $Y$ holds of is the transport along $j$ of something $Y$ holds of at $i$, of which $X'$ then holds. Every object being full, the same holds at every arrow, so Rigid Comprehension is necessary. The source notes that full models satisfy it (p. 61); stated once for the topic, in place of the full models' own arguments.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: At an object reachable from the evaluation point the propositions are all the sets of arrows out of it, so there are finitely many arrows out. A necessarily instantiated $F$ there assigns to each of them a nonempty set, and a finite family of nonempty sets has a choice function without the axiom of choice; the intension holding at each arrow of the chosen member alone is in the domain, the model being full, lies below $F$ and is necessarily uniquely instantiated. So Intensional Choice holds at every reachable object, at every type. (The finite-germ argument of the 3 October 2026 analysis, for full models; with choice the well-ordering argument gives the same.)

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), 3 October 2026 (full action models); extended by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), 4 October 2026, at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Write $X_0(E)$ for the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$. The extension at an arrow $h$ of the power property $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is the set of rigid $X$ with $X\le h\cdot F$, the bound variable ranging over the domain untransported and the parameter transported. By the condition the rigid relations are the $X_0(E)$, and $X_0(T)\le X_0(S)$ iff $T\subseteq S$; so for rigid $F=X_0(S)$ the power property has extension $\{X_0(T'):T'\subseteq k\cdot S\}$ at $k$, while transporting its extension at the identity along $k$ gives $\{X_0(k\cdot T):T\subseteq S\}$. These coincide, since every $T'\subseteq k\cdot S$ is $k\cdot T$ for $T:=\{s\in S:k\cdot s\in T'\}$. So the power property is itself $X_0$ of its extension, hence rigid, and the same at every reachable object gives the boxed form.

models.name: Full action model: two-object retract with two retractions
sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 6 October 2026, as a model of Actuality without Strong Actuality.
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, §3.5, pp. 58–61; Appendix D, pp. 73–74 (full action models).

references.note: Full action models; the category is the two-object retract's with its arrow back doubled.

settings.construction: The category with objects $W_0,W_1$ generated by $h:W_0\to W_1$ and $j_1,j_2:W_1\to W_0$ subject to $j_1\circ h=j_2\circ h=1_{W_0}$, evaluated at $W_0$. Its arrows are $1_{W_0}$; $h$; $j_1,j_2$; and $1_{W_1}$ with the idempotents $e_i:=h\circ j_i$, which compose by $e_i\circ e_k=e_k$, $j_i\circ e_k=j_k$ and $e_i\circ h=h$ (the rewriting $j_i\circ h\mapsto1$ has no overlaps, so these normal forms are distinct).

meets.returning-arrow: $h$, which $j_1$ retracts.
meets.retractions: The arrows out of $W_0$ are its identity and $h$, which $j_1$ retracts.
meets.finitely-many-propositions: $W_0$ has four propositions, the sets of its two arrows out.
meets.finitely-many-propositions-everywhere: $W_0$ has four propositions and $W_1$ thirty-two, the sets of its five arrows out.
meets.separated-retractions: $h$ has the retractions $j_1\ne j_2$, and $\{j_1\}$, in the domain at $W_1$ since the model is full, separates them.
meets.sigma-apart: The construction does not mention Σ.
meets.noninvertible-retracted-arrow: $h$ is retracted by $j_1$ and $j_2$ but has no inverse, since $h\circ j_i=e_i\ne 1_{W_1}$.

met.rigid-haecceity-disjunctions: Every intension is present, so for any set $E$ the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is in the domain, and a relation is weakly inextensible at a world iff it lies below that intension over its extension there, since that is the smallest intension satisfying the hypothesis; with persistence, a rigid relation equals it (the argument deferred in extraction.md, 3 October 2026).

Its arrows are $1_{W_0}$; $h$; $j_1,j_2$; and $1_{W_1}$ with the idempotents $e_i:=h\circ j_i$, which compose by $e_i\circ e_k=e_k$, $j_i\circ e_k=j_k$ and $e_i\circ h=h$ (the rewriting $j_i\circ h\mapsto1$ has no overlaps, so these normal forms are distinct).

Individuals, fixed for this record: at every object the individuals are the members of an infinite set $D$, the same at every object, and every arrow acts on them as the identity.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$; every other constant of Σ, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.

Metatheory, fixed for this record: the axiom of choice is used freely, as in ordinary mathematics in ZFC, or in Lean's classical type theory for the verdicts certified there.

met.rigid-haecceity-disjunctions: Every intension is present, so for any set $E$ the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is in the domain, and a relation is weakly inextensible at a world iff it lies below that intension over its extension there, since that is the smallest intension satisfying the hypothesis; with persistence, a rigid relation equals it (the argument deferred in extraction.md, 3 October 2026).
met.codomain-intensions: The domains are full at every object.
met.full-model: Every intension of every relational type is present at every object (Classicism, §3.5, p. 59).
met.full-action-model: An action model, full at every object (Classicism, §3.5, p. 59; Appendix D).
met.extensionally-full: A full model contains every intension, so in particular one with any given extension at the identity.
met.identity-singletons: The singleton of the identity arrow at any object is in the domain, the model being full.
met.actuality-contingent: The singleton $a$ of the identity arrow is in the domain, the model being full. It is necessary at no world: a world other than the identity sees itself, which lies outside $a$, and the identity sees an arrow other than itself. And a non-identity arrow $k$ does not fix it, since $1\in k\cdot a$ would need $1\circ k=1$.
met.fixed-infinite-individuals: This is the choice of individuals.
met.homogeneous-individuals: A permutation of $D$ commutes with every arrow's action, the identity, so it is an automorphism at type $e$ and extends, by conjugation, to the full domains of the other types, carrying each individual to its image.
met.returning-arrow: $h$, which $j_1$ retracts.
met.retractions: The arrows out of $W_0$ are its identity and $h$, which $j_1$ retracts.
met.finitely-many-propositions: $W_0$ has four propositions, the sets of its two arrows out.
met.finitely-many-propositions-everywhere: $W_0$ has four propositions and $W_1$ thirty-two, the sets of its five arrows out.
met.separated-retractions: $h$ has the retractions $j_1\ne j_2$, and $\{j_1\}$, in the domain at $W_1$ since the model is full, separates them.
met.sigma-apart: The construction does not mention Σ.
met.noninvertible-retracted-arrow: $h$ is retracted by $j_1$ and $j_2$ but has no inverse, since $h\circ j_i=e_i\ne 1_{W_1}$.
met.trivial-isomorphisms-everywhere: Out of $W_0$ only the identity is invertible; out of $W_1$, $j_i$ has no inverse ($h\circ j_i=e_i$) and the $e_i$ are non-identity idempotents.

sources: Cian Dorr, suggestion of 6 October 2026, as a model of Actuality without Strong Actuality.

models.notes: Proposed by Cian Dorr to separate Strong Actuality from Actuality: the model is full, so it has □Rigid Comprehension and hence □Actuality, while $h$'s two retractions keep every true proposition from being a strong world. Unlike the two-object retract it does not meet coherent-retractions: with $r_h=j_i$, the arrow $x=e_k$ after $h$ for $k\ne i$ gives $r_{x\circ h}\circ x=r_h\circ e_k=j_k\ne r_h$. Gallin Extensional Comprehension fails, since it implies Strong Actuality (gallin-comprehension-implies-strong-actuality), though ND and □Rigid Comprehension hold.

history.summary: Adopted the source’s relational type system at the user’s request. The cited construction now directly supplies the recorded model; the former type-extension obligation is removed.

Added Relational Choice at Cian Dorr's direction. With choice in the metatheory a serial relation has a functional subrelation, and a full model contains every intension, so that subrelation is in the domain; see Classicism, p. 61, on the principles common to full models.
Fixed an interpretation of Σ (relational constants as top, individual constants as one fixed individual) and recorded the signature schemata it refutes, at Cian Dorr’s request.
Added the failure of Strong Leibniz Biconditionals (type t) at W0; see the notes.
Boxed the Relational Choice claim; see the notes.
Recorded the Distinctness-preserving collapse; see the notes.

Recorded on a question of Zachary Goodsell, after an observation of Christopher Sun.
Added Gallin Extensional Comprehension at W0, and the failure of the Infinity Schema and of Possible Infinity at type t; see the notes.

sources: Cian Dorr and Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), conversation of 14 October 2026 (transcript in the private notes).
Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr, Classicism, draft of 16 May 2023, Appendix D, Definitions D.1–D.3 and Proposition D.4, pp. 73–74 (ideally full action models).
models.definition:
A two-object ideally full action model. Fix a fixed-point-free involution $\pi$ on $\mathbb N$ (say $2k\leftrightarrow 2k+1$), which partitions $\mathbb N$ into two-element blocks. The objects are $W_0$, with individuals $\mathbb N$, and $V$, with individuals $\mathbb N\sqcup\{\star\}$ where $\star$ forms a block by itself. The arrows are all surjective block-respecting maps between these sets: $g(\pi c)\in\{g(c),\pi g(c)\}$ for every $c$, so a block maps into a block, either injectively or collapsed to a point, there are surjective arrows $W_0\to V$, obtained by collapsing one block onto $\star$ and mapping the remaining blocks onto all blocks; and the new individual $\star$ can be hit only by collapsing a block onto it. The pinning action is the identity on individuals, the ideal is the finite sets, and the individuals are the type-$e$ domains, so the model is ideally full in the sense of Classicism, Appendix D, and a model of C by its Proposition D.4. The evaluation point is the identity on $V$, the object with the new individual $\star$; every object is reachable from it, since there are surjective arrows $V\to W_0$ (send $\star$ anywhere).


Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.
meets.codomain-intensions: The model is ideally full with the ideal of finite sets and no symmetry group, so every intension pinned down by the empty set, i.e. whose value at an arrow depends only on the codomain, is in the domain at every object (Classicism, Definition D.3).
meets.extensionally-full: Ideally full action models are extensionally full (Classicism, p. 74).

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Every arrow is surjective on individuals, hence on finite sets of individuals, so Proposition D.6 of Classicism gives BF at every type with any object as the evaluation point.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: At $V$ let $p:=\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_{\{\star\}}$, the true proposition that $\star$ is fixed. For any true $q$ at $V$, pinned by $N_q$, the surjection $u\colon V\to W_0$ that is the identity on $\mathbb N$ and sends $\star$ into a block $B$ disjoint from $N_q$ lies in $\Diamond q$ (a surjection fixing $N_q$ and collapsing $B$ onto $\star$ brings it back into $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_{N_q}$) but not in $\hat\Diamond p$, since every $v$ with $vu\in p$ collapses $B$ onto $\star$ and so cannot return to $\mathrm{fix}^{00}_B$. So B fails for $\Box_{\ne}$ at $p$. By Proposition D11 of The Bounds of Possibility, $p\to\hat{\hat\Box}\hat\Diamond p$, so $\hat\Diamond p$ is two-hat necessary; it is not ND-necessary, which is what the failure of B says. Actuality fails: the true propositions $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_N$ descend strictly.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: As in the record evaluated at $W_0$, the three-hat operator $\hat{(3)}\Box$ is necessarily B in this model, so it is an S5 operator and $\Box_5\le\hat{(3)}\Box$; at $V$ its cluster on $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_N$ is the set of surjective block-bijections of $V$ fixing $\star$ and block-injective on $N$, which contains arrows moving any given point of $\mathbb N$, so the truth $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_N$ is not 5-necessary.

models.notes: The surjective paired-individuals model with its other object as the evaluation point. Necessary BF holds at every type, yet Two-hat necessity implies ND-necessity fails here, so BF at no type, boxed or not, yields that collapse. Built in the conversation of 14 October 2026.

Let $p_0$ be the proposition that the world is $W_0$, the set of arrows $W_0\to W_0$, true and pinned by $\emptyset$. It is not two-hat necessary: every $C_1(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)$ contains a surjective arrow $\iota\colon W_0\to V$ injective on $N$, collapsing a block outside $N$ onto $\star$ (given $r$ true at $V$ pinned by $N_1$, let $v\colon V\to W_0$ be the identity on $\mathbb N$ with $\star$ sent to a block $\{e,\pi e\}$ disjoint from $N_1$; then $v\iota=1_{W_0}$, and the map collapsing that block onto $\star$ and fixing everything else brings $v$ back into $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_{N_1}$). It is 5-necessary: let $Y_k$, for an arrow $k$ out of $W_0$, be the set of propositions at $\mathrm{trg}(k)$ pinned by a finite set of individuals in the range of some arrow from $W_0$ (at $W_0$ all propositions, at $V$ those pinned by old individuals); $Y$ is pinned by $\emptyset$. For $z$ pinned by $S$ put $N_z:=S\cup\pi S$; an arrow injective on $N_z$ cannot collapse a block of $S$ onto $\star$, so $k^tz\in Y_k$ for every $k\in C_1(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_{N_z})$ and $\hat{\hat\Box}(Yz)$ holds for every $z$. Since $\hat{\hat\Box}\le\Box_5$ and $\Box_5$ satisfies BF at type $t$ (Theorem D16 and Corollary D6 of The Bounds of Possibility), $\Box_5\forall z\,Yz$ holds, and $\forall z\,Yz=p_0$ because at $V$ the proposition that $\star$ is fixed is pinned by no set of old individuals (the identity and a surjection sending $\star$ into $\mathbb N$ and collapsing a block away from that set onto $\star$ agree on it).

The three-hat operator $\hat{(3)}\Box$ is necessarily B here: at $W_0$, $C_2(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)=C_3(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N)$ is the set of arrows $W_0\to W_0$ injective and block-injective on $N$ (arrows into $V$ drop out at $C_2$ by the argument for $p_0$, and block-bijections, which are surjective, are in every $C_n$), and at $V$ likewise $C_1=C_2$ on $\mathrm{fix}^{VV}_{N}$. So it is an S5 operator, and $\Box_5\le\hat{(3)}\Box$. But $\mathrm{fix}^{00}_N$ is true and not $\hat{(3)}\Box$-necessary, since a block-bijection moving a point of $N$ lies in every $C_2(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_{N^\prime})$. The argument for the non-surjective model carries over, every arrow used in it being surjective or replaceable by a surjective one that agrees with it on the finite set in question.

models.definition:
A two-object ideally full action model. Fix a fixed-point-free involution $\pi$ on $\mathbb N$ (say $2k\leftrightarrow 2k+1$), which partitions $\mathbb N$ into two-element blocks. The objects are $W_0$, with individuals $\mathbb N$, and $V$, with individuals $\mathbb N\sqcup\{\star\}$ where $\star$ forms a block by itself. The arrows are all block-respecting maps between these sets: $g(\pi c)\in\{g(c),\pi g(c)\}$ for every $c$, so a block maps into a block, either injectively or collapsed to a point, and the new individual $\star$ can be hit only by collapsing a block onto it. The pinning action is the identity on individuals, the ideal is the finite sets, and the individuals are the type-$e$ domains, so the model is ideally full in the sense of Classicism, Appendix D, and a model of C by its Proposition D.4. The evaluation point is the identity on $W_0$.


Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

For $z$ pinned by $S$ put $N_z:=S\cup\pi S$; an arrow injective on $N_z$ cannot collapse a block of $S$ onto $\star$, so $k^tz\in Y_k$ for every $k\in C_1(\mathrm{fix}^{00}_{N_z})$ and $\hat{\hat\Box}(Yz)$ holds for every $z$. settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers. Its arrows are all the surjections of that set, and its symmetry group is all the permutations. A relational domain holds exactly the intensions that are symmetric, meaning indifferent to relabelling the individuals of a world, and pinned down by some finite set. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

meets.all-surjection-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$.
meets.section-arrows: Given $k$, $N$ and $T$, let $k^{\prime}$ agree with $k$ on $N$, send distinct fresh points $x_t\notin N$ to $t$ for $t\in T$, and extend it to a surjection; let $\sigma$ be any surjection with $\sigma t=x_t$.
meets.factorizable-arrows: Take $N^{\prime\prime}:=S$ and, enlarging $N$, assume $h(N^{\prime\prime})\subseteq N$. Let $k^{\prime\prime}$ agree with $h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$; for $m\in M\setminus N^{\prime\prime}$ let $k^{\prime\prime}m$ be some $n\in N$ with $kn=k^{\prime}m$ if there is one, and otherwise a fresh point outside $N$, one for each value of $k^{\prime}$. Let $j$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send each fresh point to its value. Both extend to surjections, infinitely many points being left free, and $jk^{\prime\prime}$ agrees with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$.
meets.finitely-pinned-domains: A relational domain holds exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set, and every individual $n$ is pinned down by $\{n\}$.
meets.collapse-onto-point: Take $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, so $p\notin F_h$. $h$ is any surjection constant on $N\cup\{a\}$, and a transposition of $y$ with a point outside $N\cup\{a,p\}$ fixes $p$ and moves $y$.
meets.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
meets.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual outside $N$ is a permutation, so lies in the symmetry group.
meets.surjective-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$.
meets.homogeneous-individuals: Every permutation of $\mathbb N$ is in the symmetry group, and relabelling by it is an automorphism of the model, carrying each individual to its image.
meets.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\emptyset$ (the draft's argument for this model): every finite set is amalgamable, since an arrow is prescribed only on a finite set and extends freely to a surjection, and points can always be moved off a given finite set by a permutation fixing another.
meets.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.
meets.retractable-means-actual-pattern: With $N^\prime=N$: if $x\circ u$ is the identity on $N$ then $u$ is injective on $N$, so it agrees on $N$ with a permutation.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), after Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice over the individuals cannot be finitely pinned down
arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

conditions.text: For each finite set $N$ of individuals at the evaluation object, some property $A$ in the domain has a nonempty extension there, and each individual $y$ in that extension is moved by a member of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise and fixes $A$.
conditions.reason: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual outside $N$ is a permutation, so lies in the symmetry group.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: At type $e$. Let $F$ and $a$ be as the condition gives them, and suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, which we may take to contain $a$; call it $N$. Let $h$ be the arrow the condition gives for $N$. Then $G_h=\{y\}$ for some $y$ in $F_h$. If $\sigma$ in the symmetry group fixes $p$, then $\sigma\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, so $G_{\sigma\circ h}=G_h$ by pinning, while symmetry gives $G_{\sigma\circ h}=\{\sigma y\}$. So no symmetry fixing $p$ moves $y$, and by the condition $y=p$. Each model's witness takes $F$ with $p$ outside its extension at $h$, a contradiction. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T.

conditions.text: A group $G$ acts on the individuals at the evaluation object, and every element of a relational domain there is symmetric, meaning that $\langle\bar x,h\rangle\in D$ implies $\langle g\cdot\bar x,g\circ h\rangle\in D$ whenever $g\in G$ and $g\circ h$ is an arrow, and is pinned down by a finite set of individuals, its extension at an arrow depending only on the arrow's values there.
conditions.reason: The relational domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set (Dorr, draft, Definitions 15–18).

conditions.text: The individuals at the evaluation object are those the construction acts on, and the arrows act on them as the construction says.
conditions.reason: The individuals are the base, acted on as the construction says.

conditions.text: There are an individual $a$ and a necessarily instantiated property $F$ in the domain such that, for every finite set $N$ of individuals at the evaluation object, some arrow $h$ sends $N\cup\{a\}$ to a single individual $p$, and every individual $y\ne p$ in $F$'s extension at $h$ is moved by a member $\sigma$ of the symmetry group that fixes $p$, with $\sigma\circ h$ again an arrow.
conditions.reason: Take $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, so $p\notin F_h$. $h$ is any surjection constant on $N\cup\{a\}$, and a transposition of $y$ with a point outside $N\cup\{a,p\}$ fixes $p$ and moves $y$.

models.notes:
This is the draft's headline separation. Boolean Completeness holds while Rigid Comprehension fails, and since Actuality fails too, Weak Rigid Comprehension fails here as well, which is recorded as a derived verdict. The source is a work in progress.

Open question: is there a closed term of the language, at each type, that denotes this classifier $F$? Pairwise distinctness over a variable number of individuals is expressible with a plural variable $Y^{e\to t}$, as $\forall y\,y'\,((Yy\land Yy'\land y\ne y')\to\Box(\exists z\, .\,Xz\to y\ne y'))$. What is not obvious is how to say in the object language that $X$ is minimally pinned down by the $Y$s.

history.summary: Added both Axioms of Infinity at Cian Dorr's direction. The individuals are the natural numbers and identity at the identity arrow is literal, so no numeral counts them. The propositions that a given individual is fixed by the arrow, one for each individual, are pairwise distinct, symmetric and pinned by that individual, so there are infinitely many propositions. The set of numerals at each type is invariant under every arrow, hence symmetric and pinned by the empty set, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property at either type.
Fixed an interpretation of Σ (relational constants as top, individual constants as one fixed individual) and recorded the signature schemata it refutes, at Cian Dorr’s request.
Re-fixed the interpretation of Σ so as to settle No Contingency (signature Σ) and B for sentences of Σ, at Cian Dorr’s request; see the notes.

Recorded the failure of Relational Choice, at types (e→t) and e: a functional subrelation of the serial relation pairing each property with its members would be symmetric and finitely pinned, and a symmetry fixing its pinning set would carry its choice for the property of lying outside that set to a second choice. Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice cannot be finitely pinned; argument in the notes.
Noted why Inextensible Comprehension is left unknown: its type-t and type-(e→t) instances hold here, so the failure of Actuality does not sharpen to it at those types.

models.definition:
A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers. Its arrows are all the surjections of that set, and its symmetry group is all the permutations. A relational domain holds exactly the intensions that are symmetric, meaning indifferent to relabelling the individuals of a world, and pinned down by some finite set. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

Individuals, fixed for this record: there is a single individual at every object. The arrows still act on the base as the construction says, and the base still supplies the pinning sets and the symmetry groups.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

met.symmetric-domains: The relational domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set (Dorr, draft, Definitions 15–18).
met.one-individual: There is a single individual at every object.
met.homogeneous-individuals: Every permutation of $\mathbb N$ is in the symmetry group, and relabelling by it is an automorphism of the model, carrying each individual to its image.
met.all-surjection-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$.
met.section-arrows: Given $k$, $N$ and $T$, let $k^{\prime}$ agree with $k$ on $N$, send distinct fresh points $x_t\notin N$ to $t$ for $t\in T$, and extend it to a surjection; let $\sigma$ be any surjection with $\sigma t=x_t$.
met.factorizable-arrows: Take $N^{\prime\prime}:=S$ and, enlarging $N$, assume $h(N^{\prime\prime})\subseteq N$. Let $k^{\prime\prime}$ agree with $h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$; for $m\in M\setminus N^{\prime\prime}$ let $k^{\prime\prime}m$ be some $n\in N$ with $kn=k^{\prime}m$ if there is one, and otherwise a fresh point outside $N$, one for each value of $k^{\prime}$. Let $j$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send each fresh point to its value. Both extend to surjections, infinitely many points being left free, and $jk^{\prime\prime}$ agrees with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$.
met.finitely-pinned-domains: A relational domain holds exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set, and every individual $n$ is pinned down by $\{n\}$.
met.collapse-onto-point: Take $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, so $p\notin F_h$. $h$ is any surjection constant on $N\cup\{a\}$, and a transposition of $y$ with a point outside $N\cup\{a,p\}$ fixes $p$ and moves $y$.
met.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
met.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual outside $N$ is a permutation, so lies in the symmetry group.
met.surjective-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$.
met.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\emptyset$ (the draft's argument for this model): every finite set is amalgamable, since an arrow is prescribed only on a finite set and extends freely to a surjection, and points can always be moved off a given finite set by a permutation fixing another.
met.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.
met.retractable-means-actual-pattern: With $N^\prime=N$: if $x\circ u$ is the identity on $N$ then $u$ is injective on $N$, so it agrees on $N$ with a permutation.

meets.surjective-arrows: The arrows are permutations and surjections.
meets.symmetry-group-pinned: Membership in the symmetry group is detected by the fixed pair: an arrow is in it iff it does not collapse the pair.
meets.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition is the symmetry group, the set of arrows that are permutations, pinned down by the fixed pair; no composite with a non-bijective arrow is a permutation.
meets.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition, the symmetry group, is in the domain; at every world a collapsing arrow leads outside it, and a collapsing arrow carries it to the empty set.

models.notes: This model is not a second witness to the draft's main result but a counterweight to it. Rigid Comprehension holds, so the failure of Actuality in the all-surjections model is no accident. Because Atomicity fails here, the model settles a question left open in Classicism: Rigid Comprehension does not imply Atomicity. The boxed forms of Actuality and Rigid Comprehension use the draft's one-object observation, which it states for Boolean Completeness and applies in the same way in its final section. The source is a work in progress. Everything that implies these fails with them.

history.summary: Added both Axioms of Infinity at Cian Dorr's direction. The individuals are the natural numbers and identity at the identity arrow is literal, so no numeral counts them. The propositions that a given individual is fixed by the arrow, one for each individual, are pairwise distinct, symmetric and pinned by that individual, so there are infinitely many propositions. The set of numerals at each type is invariant under every arrow, hence symmetric and pinned by the empty set, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property at either type.
Fixed an interpretation of Σ (relational constants as top, individual constants as one fixed individual) and recorded the signature schemata it refutes, at Cian Dorr’s request.
Recorded the Distinctness-preserving collapse; see the notes.
Re-fixed the interpretation of Σ so as to settle No Contingency (signature Σ) and B for sentences of Σ, at Cian Dorr’s request; see the notes.

Corrected the reason given for the failures of Independence (signature Σ) and Distinctness (signature Σ): the true atom is denoted by no closed pure term, since such terms denote entities fixed by every arrow; the failures come from the other relational constants, which denote top. No verdict changes.

Recorded the failure of Relational Choice, at types (e→t) and e: a functional subrelation of the serial relation pairing each property with its members would be symmetric and finitely pinned, and a symmetry fixing its pinning set would carry its choice for the property of lying outside that set to a second choice. Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice cannot be finitely pinned; argument in the notes.

models.definition:
A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers. Its symmetry group is the permutations that preserve a fixed pair of individuals setwise, and its arrows are those permutations together with all the surjections that collapse the two members of that pair. Every arrow is therefore invertible or a collapser, and which it is can be read off from its behaviour on that pair. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

Individuals, fixed for this record: there is a single individual at every object. The arrows still act on the base as the construction says, and the base still supplies the pinning sets and the symmetry groups.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition, the symmetry group; every other constant of Σ, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers, equipped with an equivalence relation that has infinitely many classes, each infinite. Its arrows are all the surjections of that set, as in Base 1 of the draft, and its symmetry group is the automorphism group of the equivalence relation: the permutations that map classes onto classes. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

meets.all-surjection-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$, as in Base 1.
meets.section-arrows: As in symmetric-all-surjections, the arrows being all the surjections: let $k^{\prime}$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send distinct fresh points $x_t\notin N$ to $t\in T$, and let $\sigma$ be a surjection with $\sigma t=x_t$.
meets.factorizable-arrows: Take $N^{\prime\prime}:=S$ and, enlarging $N$, assume $h(N^{\prime\prime})\subseteq N$. Let $k^{\prime\prime}$ agree with $h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$; for $m\in M\setminus N^{\prime\prime}$ let $k^{\prime\prime}m$ be some $n\in N$ with $kn=k^{\prime}m$ if there is one, and otherwise a fresh point outside $N$, one for each value of $k^{\prime}$. Let $j$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send each fresh point to its value. Both extend to surjections, infinitely many points being left free, and $jk^{\prime\prime}$ agrees with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$.
meets.finitely-pinned-domains: A relational domain holds exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set, and every individual $n$ is pinned down by $\{n\}$.
meets.collapse-onto-point: Take $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, so $p\notin F_h$. $h$ is any surjection constant on $N\cup\{a\}$; a transposition inside $y$'s class that fixes $p$ is an automorphism of the equivalence relation, and moves $y$.
meets.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
meets.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual of its class outside $N$, which exists since the classes are infinite, maps classes onto classes, so lies in the symmetry group.
meets.surjective-arrows: The arrows are all the surjections of $\mathbb N$, as in Base 1.
meets.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\emptyset$, as in Base 1: an arrow is prescribed only on a finite set and extends freely to a surjection; and a point outside $N$ can be transposed with a member of its own class outside $N\cup Q$, the classes being infinite, by a class-preserving permutation fixing $N$ pointwise.
meets.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.

arguments.text: At type e. The class of a fixed individual is the extension of a property pinned down by that individual. A classifier F pinned down by a finite set cannot choose a representative for the class of an individual in a class disjoint from that set: by symmetry and uniqueness the representative is fixed by every automorphism that fixes the pinning set of F and preserves the class, so its least pinning set lies inside the pinning set of F, and then its extension would be preserved by an automorphism that swaps the class with another.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), after Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice over the individuals cannot be finitely pinned down
arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The members' seven copies, which differed in the property $A$ and the transposition, stated once; each member's $A$ and transposition moved to the condition transposable. The qualitative-contrast model's second argument (OpenAI Codex, 24 September) was dropped.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The condition transposable no longer mentions the finite set $M$ or the pinning of $A$ by $N\cup M$: the argument uses only that $g$ fixes $N$, the set pinning down $S$, and that $A$ is in the domain. So $g$ is now said to fix $N$ pointwise. Proved in Lean.

conditions.text: For each finite set $N$ of individuals at the evaluation object, some property $A$ in the domain has a nonempty extension there, and each individual $y$ in that extension is moved by a member of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise and fixes $A$.
conditions.reason: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual of its class outside $N$, which exists since the classes are infinite, maps classes onto classes, so lies in the symmetry group.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: At type $e$. Let $F$ and $a$ be as the condition gives them, and suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, which we may take to contain $a$; call it $N$. Let $h$ be the arrow the condition gives for $N$. Then $G_h=\{y\}$ for some $y$ in $F_h$. If $\sigma$ in the symmetry group fixes $p$, then $\sigma\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, so $G_{\sigma\circ h}=G_h$ by pinning, while symmetry gives $G_{\sigma\circ h}=\{\sigma y\}$. So no symmetry fixing $p$ moves $y$, and by the condition $y=p$. Each model's witness takes $F$ with $p$ outside its extension at $h$, a contradiction. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Recorded from the collapse lemma deferred in extraction.md on 3 October until the model records' new format landed (not yet checked by a human). It needs the individuals the construction gives. Not covered: the qualitative-links model, whose arrows preserve a ternary relation and so cannot send everything to one point, and the qualitative-contrast model, whose arrows are bijections and where Intensional Choice holds.

revisions.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Moved from the group symmetric-ideally-full to the topic, so that the symmetry-constrained full models use it too: in those models every intension is pinned down by the finite set of all individuals, and the collapses are the constant maps. The group's `when: individuals: base` is now the condition construction-individuals, met by that parameter value.

conditions.text: A group $G$ acts on the individuals at the evaluation object, and every element of a relational domain there is symmetric, meaning that $\langle\bar x,h\rangle\in D$ implies $\langle g\cdot\bar x,g\circ h\rangle\in D$ whenever $g\in G$ and $g\circ h$ is an arrow, and is pinned down by a finite set of individuals, its extension at an arrow depending only on the arrow's values there.
conditions.reason: The relational domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set (Dorr, draft, Definitions 15–18).

conditions.text: The individuals at the evaluation object are those the construction acts on, and the arrows act on them as the construction says.
conditions.reason: The individuals are the base, acted on as the construction says.

conditions.text: There are an individual $a$ and a necessarily instantiated property $F$ in the domain such that, for every finite set $N$ of individuals at the evaluation object, some arrow $h$ sends $N\cup\{a\}$ to a single individual $p$, and every individual $y\ne p$ in $F$'s extension at $h$ is moved by a member $\sigma$ of the symmetry group that fixes $p$, with $\sigma\circ h$ again an arrow.
conditions.reason: Take $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, so $p\notin F_h$. $h$ is any surjection constant on $N\cup\{a\}$; a transposition inside $y$'s class that fixes $p$ is an automorphism of the equivalence relation, and moves $y$.

models.notes:
The first recorded model refuting Transversal, so Transversal is not a theorem of C. Since the coalesced roots make every pure sentence consistent with C possible, □Transversal fails there too. The classes must be infinite: with finite classes, being identical to one of the members of a class is a canonical representative. The mechanism is a failure of weak elimination of imaginaries: the class, as a definable set, has no canonical finite set of parameters. Structures with weak elimination of imaginaries, such as a dense linear order or the random graph, give no such failure, and in the binary tree with a parent function the levels are fixed as soon as one node is. Since Inextensible Comprehension holds, it does not imply Transversal. Left unknown: the Axiom of Infinity at type e, and every signature schema, since no interpretation of Σ has been fixed. Vicinity fails by derivation: Weakly Inextensible Comprehension holds, and with Vicinity it would give Actuality.
Since 2 October the Axiom of Infinity at type e holds by the group's argument, and the record's interpretation of Σ is its own text saying that none is fixed; its variants with each of the group's interpretations are generated.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction, correcting the argument given by Claude Fable 5.1
arguments.text: For the universal property of individuals at $E$. A coextensive $Y$ holds of everything at every arrow to $E$, by symmetry and pinning; inextensibility at $E$, with the property of being old, keeps the new individuals out of $Y$ at the inclusion $\iota:E\to O$. At $\iota$ every $Y$-thing is necessarily distinct from $0'$, yet after any arrow $m:O\to E$, $Y$ holds of $m(0')$; so $Y$ is not weakly inextensible at $\iota$.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The haecceities of the even numbers have no least upper bound: one pinned down by $N$ would, by a symmetry fixing $N$, hold at the identity of an odd $m\notin N$, while the property of differing from the image of $m$ is an upper bound that does not.

arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), at Cian Dorr's request; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: Let $U$ hold of every individual at arrows into $E$ and of exactly the old individuals at arrows into $O$. It is symmetric, pinned down by $\emptyset$, and equal to $B_N$ of its extension for every finite $N$, so weakly rigid. At the inclusion $i:E\to O$ its extension is the old individuals, each necessarily distinct from a new individual $b$, all arrows being injective; but after any arrow $m:O\to E$ the transported relation holds of $mb$. So $i\cdot U$ is not weakly inextensible, $U$ is not rigid, and Tame Rigidity fails at type $e$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), after Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice over the individuals cannot be finitely pinned down
arguments.text: At the types $(e\to t)$ and $e$. Let $U:=\lambda Xy\, .\,Xy\lor\neg\exists z\, .\,Xz$, a closed term, hence in the domain, and serial. A functional subrelation $S$ of $U$ would lie in the domain at the evaluation object, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set $N$. Two facts about such an $S$ (Dorr, draft, Lemma 19(iv)): every $g\in G$ fixing $N$ pointwise satisfies $g^{[\sigma]}S=S$, and symmetry gives $\langle gA,gy,g\rangle\in S$ whenever $\langle A,y,1\rangle\in S$; together, $\langle gA,gy,1\rangle\in S$. Now let $A$ be the property the condition gives for $N$. Its extension is nonempty, so $S$ relates $A$ at the identity to some $y$ in its extension. The condition gives a member $g$ of the symmetry group that fixes $N$ pointwise, fixes $A$ and moves $y$ to some $gy\ne y$, so $S$ relates $A$ to $gy$ as well, and $S$ is not functional at the identity arrow. The well-ordering of the individuals that Cian Dorr had in mind is refuted by the same two facts, but the direct route needs no derivation of a well-ordering from Relational Choice in C.

arguments.text: With one individual every entity is fixed by every symmetry, and is a union of finitely many classes, one for each kind of arrow (to $E$, from $E$ to $O$, in $G_O$, in $K$) and tuple of arguments; by induction on types, so every domain is finite and complete. Transport along an arrow then depends only on its kind, and the kind of a composite on the kinds of its factors, so the intension whose extension at $h$ is $X$'s extension at the identity transported along $h$ is a union of classes, in the domain; it is persistent and inextensible, at both objects.

settings.construction: Appendix D, p. 79, the final construction, the paper’s precursor of the symmetric ideally-full models of Dorr’s draft (Definitions 15–18, p. 8): the base has two objects $W_0$ and $W_1$, both copies of $\mathbb N$, all permutations of $\mathbb N$ as the arrows between any pair of objects, the ideal of finite sets at each, and the symmetry groups $G_{W_0}$ = all permutations and $G_{W_1}$ trivial. The paper states the symmetry condition on propositions only, as the constraint that a set of arrows in $W_i^t$ containing an arrow $h$ into $W_0$ contains $g\circ h$ for every permutation $g$ of $W_0$, and takes the finitely pinned entities at higher types; since every arrow is invertible, that is the draft’s symmetry condition at every type, applied to the entities’ values. meets.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition is the set of all arrows $W_0\to W_0$, in the domain by the source argument; at every world an arrow into $W_1$ leads outside it, and such an arrow carries it to the empty set.

models.notes: The cited construction is a model of the map’s relational-type framework. The description identifies its evaluation point; construction and verification are given at the PDF locations in References. Everything that implies these fails with them. Plenitude still holds by C5 plus Actuality and Propositions 2.5 and 2.14, so this model separates it from Functional Choice even under C5, Rigid Comprehension and Boolean Completeness. history.summary: Adopted the source’s relational type system at the user’s request. The cited construction now directly supplies the recorded model; the former type-extension obligation is removed.

Added both Axioms of Infinity at Cian Dorr's direction. The individuals are the natural numbers and identity at the evaluation arrow is literal, so no numeral counts them. The propositions that a given individual is fixed by the arrow, one for each individual, are pairwise distinct and each has that individual as finite support, so there are infinitely many propositions. The set of numerals at each type is invariant under every arrow, hence has empty support and lies in the domain, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property at either type.
Fixed an interpretation of Σ (relational constants as top, individual constants as one fixed individual) and recorded the signature schemata it refutes, at Cian Dorr’s request.
Expanded the description from Appendix D; settled the Distinctness-preserving collapse.
Noted why Relational Choice is left unknown: the construction goes beyond ideal fullness, so the extensional-fullness argument used for the other Appendix D models does not apply as stated.
Relabelled as a symmetric ideally-full model, the precursor of the draft’s construction, at Cian Dorr’s direction; the id changed from finite-support-qualitative-contrast, which nothing referenced.

Recorded the failure of Relational Choice, at types (e→t) and e: a functional subrelation of the serial relation pairing each property with its members would be symmetric and finitely pinned, and a symmetry fixing its pinning set would carry its choice for the property of lying outside that set to a second choice. Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice cannot be finitely pinned; argument in the notes.

Resolved the choice questions by the finite-support transposition argument in the accompanying write-up. Relational Choice fails already for selection from two-element properties of individuals; haecceity coding gives an admitted relational-output counterinstance to Functional Choice. The original construction and its source attribution are unchanged; these choice verifications are new.

models.definition:

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object whose individuals carry qualitative structure. A ternary relation holds of two points and a third individual when that individual is a link over the two if they differ, and a companion of them if they coincide, so the relation's fibres are infinite over distinct points and of size two over a repeated point. meets.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
meets.transposable: $M=\emptyset$, and for $N$ the property of being a link not in $N$ (links are carried to links by every member of the symmetry group, whose inverse is again $R$-preserving): a chosen $y$ is a link $\langle m,n,k\rangle$, and its transposition with a link $\langle m,n,k'\rangle\notin N$, which exists since the fibre is infinite, preserves $R$ and fixes every point, so lies in the symmetry group.
meets.separable-collapses: The pairs $\{0,m\}$ for points $m$ other than the distinguished pair $0,1$: by the draft's extension step (proof of its Proposition 50), an $R$-coherent prescription on a closed finite set containing $0$, $1$, $m$ and $m'$ that merges $0$, $1$ and $m$ but not $m'$ extends to a collapsing arrow, as in the record's argument for the failure of Atomicity (type t).
meets.surjective-arrows: The arrows are relation-preserving permutations and surjective relation-preserving maps.
meets.symmetry-group-pinned: Membership in the symmetry group is the condition that the distinguished pair is not collapsed, so the group is pinned down by that pair.
meets.actual-world-isolated: The actual-world proposition is the symmetry group, pinned down by the distinguished pair; under a collapsing arrow $i$, a composite $k\circ i$ would have to be a permutation, and no composite with a map that collapses the distinguished pair is injective.
meets.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition, the symmetry group, is in the domain; at every world a collapsing arrow leads outside it, and a collapsing arrow carries it to the empty set.
meets.irreversible-arrow: A collapsing arrow: no composite with it is injective.
meets.finite-pinning: Every object carries the ideal of finite sets.

models.notes:

The type-e instance of BF holds, and necessarily, since every arrow is surjective, so a property necessarily had by everything is the top property.

models.definition:
A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object whose individuals carry qualitative structure. The domain is the disjoint union of points, of two companions for each point, and of infinitely many links for each ordered pair of distinct points. A ternary relation holds of two points and a third individual when that individual is a link over the two if they differ, and a companion of them if they coincide, so the relation's fibres are infinite over distinct points and of size two over a repeated point. The arrows are required to preserve that relation. The symmetry group is the relation-preserving permutations that fix a distinguished pair of points setwise, and the remaining arrows are the surjective relation-preserving maps that collapse that pair. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

Individuals, fixed for this record: there is a single individual at every object. The arrows still act on the base as the construction says, and the base still supplies the pinning sets and the symmetry groups.

Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

settings.construction: A symmetric ideally-full intensional action model over one object, the set of natural numbers. Its arrows are of two disjoint kinds: the surjections for which the distinguished individual is its own only preimage, and the functions that omit the distinguished individual from their range. Its symmetry group is the permutations fixing that individual, which is now a proper subset of the first kind. An arrow's value at the distinguished individual still tells the two kinds apart, but no finite set separates any arrow. The evaluation point is the identity arrow.

meets.factorizable-arrows: As in symmetric-range-gap, with $d$ in $S$ and $N$ and the kinds told apart by the value at $d$, the first kind now being the surjections for which $d$ is its own only preimage. For $m\in M\setminus N^{\prime\prime}$ let $k^{\prime\prime}m$ be some $n\in N$ with $kn=k^{\prime}m$ when $k$ is of the first kind and there is one (then $n\ne d$, as $k^{\prime}m\ne d$), and otherwise a fresh point outside $N\cup\{d\}$, one for each value of $k^{\prime}$; let $j$ agree with $k$ on $N$ and send each fresh point to its value, never $d$. Arrows of the first kind need only be surjective with $d$ the only preimage of $d$, so $k^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ extend to arrows of the kinds of $h$ and $k$, and $jk^{\prime\prime}$ agrees with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$.
meets.finitely-pinned-domains: A relational domain holds exactly the symmetric intensions pinned down by a finite set, and every individual $n$ is pinned down by $\{n\}$.
meets.collapse-onto-point:
As for the range-gap model: $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x
e a\land
eg Ex$ with $E$ the constant intension $\{d\}$ of the distinguished individual, and $h$ a range-deficient function constant with value $p
e d$ on $N\cup\{a\}$; $F_h$ omits $p$ and $d$, and permutations fixing $p$ and $d$ move every other point.
meets.one-object-action-model: It has one object (Dorr, draft, §3.1: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow).
meets.transposable: $M=\{0\}$, the distinguished individual, and for $N$ the property of not belonging to $N\cup\{0\}$: the transposition of $y$ with another individual outside $N\cup\{0\}$ fixes $0$, so lies in the symmetry group.
meets.fixes-or-omits: The arrows are the surjections for which $0$ is its own only preimage, which fix it, and the functions omitting $0$ from their range.
meets.transport-gap: Take $N=\{0\}$, $i$ any arrow with $i0\ne0$, so that every arrow agreeing with it on $N$ omits $0$ from its range, and $q:=\{k : k0=0\}$, the first class of arrows, pinned down by $\{0\}$ and symmetric: an arrow $k$ of the first class and the arrow $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with it off $0$ but sending $0$ elsewhere, which omits $0$ from its range since $0$ is $k$’s only preimage of $0$, are separated by $q$. The intension the argument uses is pinned down by $N$, and symmetric, since $g\cdot q=q$ for $g$ fixing $0$ and $(g\circ j)0=0$ iff $j0=0$, so it lies in the domain.
meets.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\{0\}$, the distinguished individual (the draft's argument for this model). Two arrows agreeing there lie in the same one of the two classes, and a prescription taken from the two of them extends within that class, by nonzero values in the second case and by surjective nonzero values in the first; points are moved off a finite set by a permutation fixing $0$.
meets.retractable-means-actual-pattern: With $N^\prime=N\cup\{0\}$: if $x\circ u$ is the identity on $N^\prime$ then $u$ fixes $0$, so is of the first kind, and is injective on $N^\prime$; it therefore agrees on $N$ with a permutation fixing $0$, a member of the symmetry group.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At type e. Take the property of being positive unless things are as they actually are, which is pinned down by the distinguished individual and is symmetric. Every individual necessarily has it, since an arrow either fixes the distinguished individual or omits it from its range and so sends everything to something positive; but it is not necessary that everything has it, since any arrow moving the distinguished individual leaves it out.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: At type $e$. Let $F$ and $a$ be as the condition gives them, and suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, which we may take to contain $a$; call it $N$. Let $h$ be the arrow the condition gives for $N$. Then $G_h=\{y\}$ for some $y$ in $F_h$. If $\sigma$ in the symmetry group fixes $p$, then $\sigma\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, so $G_{\sigma\circ h}=G_h$ by pinning, while symmetry gives $G_{\sigma\circ h}=\{\sigma y\}$. So no symmetry fixing $p$ moves $y$, and by the condition $y=p$. Each model's witness takes $F$ with $p$ outside its extension at $h$, a contradiction. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T.

models.notes: The second of the draft's two variants in which BF fails, arranged so that the range deficiency no longer brings Actuality with it. Since Actuality fails, Weak Rigid Comprehension and Rigid Comprehension fail too, which are recorded as derived verdicts. Atomlessness is the Proposition 45 argument for Atomicity read for an arbitrary nonzero proposition, and the failure of ND at type e follows from the non-injective arrows; neither is displayed separately in the draft. The source is a work in progress. Everything that implies these fails with them.

history.summary: Added both Axioms of Infinity at Cian Dorr's direction. The individuals are the natural numbers and identity at the identity arrow is literal, so no numeral counts them. The propositions that a given individual is fixed by the arrow, one for each individual, are pairwise distinct, symmetric and pinned by that individual, so there are infinitely many propositions. The set of numerals at each type is invariant under every arrow, hence symmetric and pinned by the empty set, so finite cardinality is standard and no finite cardinality holds of the universal property at either type.
Fixed an interpretation of Σ (relational constants as top, individual constants as one fixed individual) and recorded the signature schemata it refutes, at Cian Dorr’s request.

Recorded the failure of Relational Choice, at types (e→t) and e: a functional subrelation of the serial relation pairing each property with its members would be symmetric and finitely pinned, and a symmetry fixing its pinning set would carry its choice for the property of lying outside that set to a second choice. Cian Dorr’s observation that a choice cannot be finitely pinned; argument in the notes.
Noted why Inextensible Comprehension is left unknown: its type-t and type-(e→t) instances hold here, so the failure of Actuality does not sharpen to it at those types.
Recorded the failure of BF at type t, sharpening the failure of BF; argument in the notes.

met.hull-conditions: With $M_0=\{0\}$, the distinguished individual (the draft's argument for this model). models.notes: With three individuals, Intensional Choice fails at type $e$ by the shared argument and at type $t$ by the argument above; with one individual only the type-$t$ failure remains, which is why this member and not the collapse member carries the one-individual variant's refutation. BF and ND fail at type $e$ with three individuals (the image intension $h\mapsto h(X)$ is symmetric; a collapse identifies distinct individuals), derived from the group's type-$t$ arguments. references.note: The symmetry condition, here imposed on a full model over three individuals.

settings.construction: The arrows are the six permutations of $X$ and the three collapses $c_i$, the constant maps with value $i\in X$; they compose as maps, so $c_i\circ h=c_i$ and $g\circ c_i=c_{g(i)}$.

models.notes: The propositions are $\bot$, the set $P$ of the six permutations, the set of the three collapses, and $\top$: the symmetry condition makes a proposition contain all the permutations or none, and all the collapses or none. $P$ is the strongest true proposition, the true atom. The variant with one individual therefore refutes nothing that the two-arrow full model does not. BF also fails at type $e$ when there are three individuals: the image intension $h\mapsto h(X)$, $X$ at a permutation and $\{i\}$ at $c_i$, is symmetric, holds necessarily of every individual, yet is not necessarily universal. That failure, and the failure of ND at type $e$ from two individuals that a collapse identifies, are derived from the group's arguments at type $t$ and are not recorded separately.

sources: Branden Fitelson, with Claude (Anthropic) and GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), A proposed counterexample to Proposition 2.11, note communicated to Cian Dorr, 1 October 2026; Isabelle/HOL verification at github.com/fitelson/hom-isabelle, commit 4042cc0, Applications/2.11.

Cian Dorr, with Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), A counterexample to Proposition 2.11 of 'Classicism': Fitelson's model, as an intensional action model, draft of 1 October 2026, sources/prop-2-11-counterexample.pdf.

references.note: Verifies the failure of Rigid Comprehension under the hypotheses; the boxed forms of Boolean Completeness and BF are not formalized there.
Definitions of intensional action models and the rigidity criterion used in the verification.
The proposition this model refutes.

models.definition: An intensional action model with one individual. The objects are the root $o$, $s$, $u$, and $n$ for each $n\ge1$; besides identities the arrows are $h_s\colon o\to s$, $j\colon s\to u$, $h_u:=j\circ h_s$ and $h_n\colon o\to n$, so the root reaches each object by exactly one arrow and worlds may be identified with objects. The domains at $s$, $u$ and each $n$ are full. Identify the domains at the terminal objects $u$ and $n$ with one finite full type structure $M$ over one individual. Fix a non-principal ultrafilter $\mathcal U$ on the positive integers. At the root, an element of a relational type is any element of the full intension space whose extension at $u$ is the $\mathcal U$-limit of its extensions at the worlds $n$; its extensions at $o$, at $s$ and at each $n$ are unconstrained. So a root proposition is any choice of truth values at $o$, $s$ and the $n$s, with its value at $u$ fixed as the limit. Evaluation point: the root. Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.

meets.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.
meets.one-individual: The definition fixes one individual, at every world.
meets.extensionally-full: At the root an element's extension at $o$ is unconstrained, so every set of tuples is the extension there of an element of the domain; the domains at $s$, $u$ and each $n$ are full.
meets.infinitely-many-propositions: A root proposition is any choice of truth values at $o$, $s$ and the $n$s, so there are infinitely many.
meets.fewer-propositions-after: The root has at least three distinct propositions, while each world $n$, which sees only itself, has two.
meets.actual-world-isolated: The proposition true at $o$ alone (false at $s$, at every $n$, and so in the limit at $u$) is in the root domain and entails every truth, every true proposition being true at $o$; no world other than $o$ sees $o$.

arguments.text: At the root, the map sending an element to its extensions at $o$, $s$ and the $n$s is an order isomorphism onto a product of powerset algebras, the extension at $u$ being recomputed as the limit. So every family has a meet and a join, computed coordinatewise except at $u$, and every nonzero element lies above an atom with one tuple in one free coordinate. The other worlds carry finite full powerset algebras. Hence Boolean Completeness and Atomicity hold at every world and every relational type.
Every arrow acts surjectively at every type, so BF holds at every world (write-up, Proposition 4).

At type $t\to t$ (write-up, Theorem 6). Let $A_0$ be the root propositions false at $s$ and at $u$, and $X$ the property with extension $A_0$ at the root and empty extensions elsewhere. A persistent property coextensive with $X$ contains both truth values at every world $n$, since members of $A_0$ take both values there; the limit condition then puts the true proposition in its extension at $u$. Rigidity at the root forces its extension at $s$ to be the proposition false at $s$ and $u$, and rigidity at $s$, tested against that proposition's haecceity, forbids the true proposition at $u$. The least upper bound of the haecceities of the $X$s, the candidate rigid coextension in the proof of Proposition 2.11, is weakly rigid but fails the rigidity condition at $s$. The model therefore refutes Proposition 2.11 (necessary-atomicity-completeness-bf-imply-rigid-comprehension); the gap is the normalization step of n. 42, part (iv), which the write-up runs inside the model (§5).

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's suggestion
arguments.text: At the root: given $F$ with $\Box\exists x\, .\,Fx$, let $G$ pick the least element of $F$ at $o$, $s$ and each $n$, under fixed well-orderings, the same ordering of $M^\sigma$ at every $n$. The sets $\{n : G(n)=\{a\}\}$ for $a\in M^\sigma$ partition the positive integers into finitely many pieces, so exactly one is in $\mathcal U$, say for $a_0$; then $\lim_{\mathcal U}G(n)=\{a_0\}$, and $a_0\in F(u)=\lim_{\mathcal U}F(n)$. Setting $G(u):=\{a_0\}$ puts $G$ in the root domain, with $G\le F$ and every extension a singleton. At $s$, $u$ and the $n$ the domains are full, and the well-ordering argument (arguments/intensional-choice-well-ordering) applies there, so the boxed form holds too.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text:
At every relational type and every world. Write $k\cdot E$ for the transport of a set $E$ of tuples along an arrow $k$, and $X_0(E)$ for the relation $k\mapsto k\cdot E$, the disjunction of the haecceities of the members of $E$. At $s$, $u$ and each $n$ the model is full, and Rigid Power holds there as in every full model (arguments/rigid-power-tight). At the root, call a set $E$ of root tuples admissible when $X_0(E)$ is in the domain, that is, when $h_u\cdot E$ is the $\mathcal U$-limit of the sets $h_n\cdot E$ (subsets of a finite set, so the limit is the set taken at $\mathcal U$-many $n$). Since each member of $E$ has its value at $u$ as the limit of its values at the $n$, $h_u\cdot E$ is always included in that limit; and every finite $E$ is admissible, the finitely many limits being attained together at $\mathcal U$-many $n$.

(1) The rigid relations at the root are exactly the $X_0(E)$ with $E$ admissible. Such an $X_0(E)$, being in the domain, is rigid: it is persistent, and at every world $w$ it is $X_0(w\cdot E)$ there, included in every $X$ that necessarily holds of the members of $w\cdot E$. Conversely let $Y$ be rigid with extension $E$. Persistence gives $Y_k\supseteq k\cdot E$ at every arrow $k$. The root element $X$ with extensions $E$ at $o$, $h_s\cdot E$ at $s$, $h_n\cdot E$ at each $n$, and the limit at $u$, necessarily holds of every member of $E$ (its extension at $u$ includes $h_u\cdot E$, by the above), so inextensibility at the root gives $Y\le X$: $Y$ has extension $h_s\cdot E$ at $s$ and $h_n\cdot E$ at each $n$. Rigidity at $s$, in the full model on $s$ and $u$, makes the extension of $Y$ at $u$ the transport $j\cdot(h_s\cdot E)=h_u\cdot E$, and since $Y$ is in the domain that is also the limit of the $h_n\cdot E$. So $E$ is admissible and $Y=X_0(E)$.

(2) Let $F=X_0(S)$ be rigid at the root, and $P:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$, in the domain since it is definable from $F$. By (1) its extension at the root is $E_P:=\{X_0(T) : T\subseteq S\text{ admissible}\}$, and at a world $k$ among $s$, $u$ and the $n$ it is the set of rigid relations there below $k\cdot F$, which in those full models are the $X_0(T')$ with $T'\subseteq k\cdot S$. Each such $T'$ is finite, the domains there being finite, so it is $k\cdot T$ for a finite, hence admissible, $T\subseteq S$ (one preimage for each member), and $X_0(T')=k\cdot X_0(T)$. So the extension of $P$ at every $k$ is $k\cdot E_P$: $P=X_0(E_P)$, a rigid relation. Hence Rigid Power holds at the root, and so at every world.

arguments.text: At the root by the general argument transversal-choice-extensionally-full, the model being extensionally full there; at $s$, $u$ and each $n$ by the same argument, those worlds' domains being full and so extensionally full.

arguments.text: The category is a poset: no non-identity arrow has a retraction. The actual-world proposition is in the domain at every object (at the root the proposition true at $o$ alone; the other objects are full), so $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains $\Diamond\{1\}=\{1\}$, i.e. iff $p$ is true: $\Box_{\ne}$ is the identity operator at every object, hence so are $\hat{\hat\Box}$ and $\Box_5$, and every truth is 5-necessary everywhere.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
arguments.text: For a true $p$, $a\le p$, since $a$ entails every truth. Take $q:=a$ in the definition of $\Box_{\ne}p$: at a world in $a$, $p$ holds; at a world outside $a$, $\Diamond a$ fails. So every truth is $\Box_{\ne}$-necessary.

arguments.text: The natural numbers are the finite cardinalities at type $e$ (Background, after Goodsell), and with a single individual there are three: $\mathbf{0}_e$, true of the empty property; $\operatorname{Suc}_e\mathbf{0}_e$, true of the universal one; and the empty cardinality, which is $\operatorname{Suc}_e$ of the second and of itself. By extensional fullness the property of being one of these three is in the domain, so it bounds natural numberhood. A countable property therefore has at most three members in its extension, and their join is its least upper bound.

revisions.note: The Relational Choice and Transversal Choice arguments merged into one, stated for every extensionally full model.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Moved from the group finite-support-one-object to the topic. Its first sentence, deriving extensional fullness from ideal fullness, is now the group's reason for meeting extensionally-full.

conditions.text: The model is extensionally full at every object: every set of tuples from the domains at an object is the extension, at the identity arrow, of an element of the domain of the matching relational type there.
conditions.reason: At the root an element's extension at $o$ is unconstrained, so every set of tuples is the extension there of an element of the domain; the domains at $s$, $u$ and each $n$ are full.

models.notes: It is a model: the limit condition commutes with every finite operation, so every term denotes in the domains (write-up, Lemma 2).

met.sigma-top: This is the interpretation the definition fixes.
met.one-individual: The definition fixes one individual, at every world.
met.extensionally-full: At the root an element's extension at $o$ is unconstrained, so every set of tuples is the extension there of an element of the domain; the domains at $s$, $u$ and each $n$ are full.
met.infinitely-many-propositions: A root proposition is any choice of truth values at $o$, $s$ and the $n$s, so there are infinitely many.
met.fewer-propositions-after: The root has at least three distinct propositions, while each world $n$, which sees only itself, has two.
met.actual-world-isolated: The proposition true at $o$ alone (false at $s$, at every $n$, and so in the limit at $u$) is in the root domain and entails every truth, every true proposition being true at $o$; no world other than $o$ sees $o$.
