arguments.text: At type e. Take the property of being positive unless things are as they actually are, which is pinned down by the distinguished individual and is symmetric. Every individual necessarily has it, since an arrow either fixes the distinguished individual or omits it from its range and so sends everything to something positive; but it is not necessary that everything has it, since any arrow moving the distinguished individual leaves it out.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The range-gap model's argument, which its variant without Actuality invoked ("by the argument of the previous variant, which goes through verbatim"), stated once.

arguments.by: Cian Dorr
arguments.text: At every relational type: a property $F$ of type-$\tau$ entities has a least upper bound, the union of the hulls of its instances. Let $F$ be pinned down by $N\supseteq M_0$. For each instance $u$ of $F$ at the identity, its hull is the closure of $u$ under the arrows that $N$ does not separate from the identity, transported along the arrows agreeing with the identity on $N$; it is symmetric, pinned down by $N$ (by (B1), which splices an arrow agreeing with $h'$ on the instance's pinning set with $h$ on $N$), and an upper bound of $u$. Every upper bound $z$ of all the instances, pinned down by $N'$, contains every hull: given a member of a hull, (B2) supplies a symmetry fixing $N$ and moving the instance's pinning set off $N'$, whose image is again an instance (by the orbit lemma, Lemma 35), lying under $z$; and $z$, pinned down by $N'$, cannot tell the moved instance's tuple from the original. The union of the hulls is pinned down by $N$ and symmetric, so it is in the domain, and it is the least upper bound.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The draft's main theorem, which the all-surjections and collapse-pair models each applied in an argument of their own, stated once; what each member does to meet its hypotheses is its reason for meeting hull-conditions. Proved in Lean (SymBase.lub_of_hull).

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: No longer requires one-object-action-model: as the draft notes (proof of Proposition 40), nothing in the theorem uses a single object, pinning, separation, amalgamability and hulls all quantifying over arrows with a fixed target; the condition hull-conditions now says so.

groups.name: Symmetry-constrained full models

references.note: The symmetry condition on intensions, here imposed on a full action model over finitely many individuals instead of on a finitely pinned one over the natural numbers.
Full action models.

construction.text: The monoid of arrows on the three individuals, as the member gives it.

individuals.text: What the individuals are. Each member is recorded with the three individuals the arrows act on; its variant with a single individual, the arrows still acting on the three-element set that supplies the symmetry, is generated.

three.text: Individuals, fixed for this record: the individuals are the three elements of $X$, acted on by the arrows themselves.
three.label: three individuals

meets.construction-individuals: The individuals are the three elements the arrows act on.
meets.homogeneous-individuals: Relabelling by a permutation of $X$ is an automorphism of the model, carrying each individual to its image.
meets.collapse-onto-point: Take an individual $a$ and $F:=\lambda x\, .\,x\ne a$, whose extension at every arrow $h$ is $X\setminus\{h(a)\}$, nonempty. For any $N$, the collapse $c_p$ onto any $p$ sends $N\cup\{a\}$ to $p$, and the transposition $\sigma$ of the two individuals other than $p$ fixes $p$, moves every $y\ne p$, and has $\sigma\circ c_p=c_p$ an arrow.

singleton.text: Individuals, fixed for this record: there is a single individual, which every arrow fixes; the arrows still act on the three-element set $X$, which supplies the symmetry.
singleton.label: one individual

meets.one-individual: The only individual is fixed by every arrow, at the sole object.

sigma.text: The interpretation of Σ. Each member is recorded with Σ top; its variant with the other is generated.

top.text: Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.
top.label: Σ top

true-atom.text: Interpretation of Σ, fixed for this record: one designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the unique true atom of the model, the actual-world proposition, which is the orbit of the identity arrow under the symmetry group; every other constant of Σ, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.
true-atom.label: Σ true atom

meets.one-object-action-model: An action model with a single object.
meets.rigid-haecceity-disjunctions: For any set $E$ the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$ is symmetric (as in the argument for Rigid Comprehension), so in the domain, and it is the smallest symmetric intension containing the transports of the members of $E$; so a weakly inextensible relation lies below it over its extension, and a rigid one equals it (as in the argument for Tame Rigidity).
meets.symmetric-domains: The domains hold exactly the symmetric intensions; every intension is pinned down by the finite set $X$ of all individuals.
meets.extensionally-full: Any set $S$ of tuples at the identity is the extension there of a symmetric intension: put $S$ at the identity, $g\cdot S$ at each permutation $g$, and the empty set at every other arrow.
meets.finitely-many-propositions: The propositions are the symmetric sets of arrows, finitely many since there are finitely many arrows.
meets.actuality-contingent: The actual-world proposition $a$ is the orbit of the identity under the symmetry group, the set of permutations; it is in the domain, true, and entails every truth, since a symmetric true proposition contains the identity and so its orbit. It is necessary at no world, since every world sees a collapse, which lies outside $a$; and a collapse $c$ does not fix it, since $l\circ c$ is a collapse for every $l$, so $c\cdot a$ is empty.
meets.irreversible-arrow: A collapse $c$: $l\circ c$ is a collapse for every arrow $l$, so from $c$ no world in $a$ is seen.
meets.actual-world-isolated: $a$, the orbit of the identity, is in the domain and entails every truth; from a world outside $a$, a non-permutation $h$, every $l\circ h$ is again a non-permutation, outside $a$.

conditions.text: The construction does not itself interpret Σ, so either of the group's interpretations can be added to it.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: At every type the domain is finite and closed under the pointwise lattice operations, since the union and intersection of symmetric intensions are symmetric; in a finite lattice every nonzero element has an atom below it.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The entailment order is the pointwise order on intensions, and the pointwise intersection of any set of symmetric intensions is symmetric and in the domain, so every set has a greatest lower bound at every type.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: For a set $S$ of tuples at the identity, the intension $Y$ with $Y(h):=h\cdot S$, the transports of the members of $S$ along $h$, is symmetric: relabelling by $g$ the transport of a tuple along $h$ gives its transport along $g\circ h$ (when the permutations are arrows because transport composes; otherwise because $g\cdot(c\cdot z)=c_{g(i)}\cdot z$ for a collapse $c=c_i$ and every admissible $z$, the collapses being absorbed, $l\circ c=l$ for $l\ne1$, and $z$ symmetric). $Y$ is coextensive with $S$, persistent, and inextensible at every world $h$, since any persistent $B$ with $B(h)\supseteq Y(h)$ has $B(k\circ h)\supseteq k\cdot Y(h)= Y(k\circ h)$. So every extension has a rigid coextension, at every type.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Let $Y$ be weakly rigid with extension $E$ at the identity. The intension $h\mapsto h\cdot E$ is symmetric, as in the argument for Rigid Comprehension, and satisfies the hypothesis of weak inextensibility, so $Y(h)\subseteq h\cdot E$ for every $h$; persistence gives the converse. So $Y$ is that intension, which is rigid.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: Transport along a collapse $c$ sends every proposition to $\bot$ or $\top$: $l\circ c$ is the constant map with value $l(i)$ for $c=c_i$, and the constant maps form one orbit of the symmetry group, so a symmetric proposition contains all of them or none. The intension $X$ of type $t\to t$ with $X(c):=\{\bot,\top\}$ at every collapse and $X(h):=$ every proposition elsewhere is symmetric, since both values are fixed by every relabelling. So $\forall p\, .\,\Box Xp$ holds at the identity while $\Box\forall p\, .\,Xp$ fails.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: The actual-world proposition $a$ and $\bot$ are distinct, and a collapse $c$ transports both to $\bot$, since $l\circ c$ is a collapse for every $l$ and so never in $a$.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: There are finitely many propositions, $n$ say, with literal identity. The numerals are closed terms, so in the domain, and the numeral $n$ holds of the universal property of propositions, so the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ fails, as does the instance of the schema asking for $n+1$ pairwise distinct propositions.

arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
arguments.text: There are exactly three individuals at every world, with literal identity, so the numeral $3$ holds of the universal property at type $e$ necessarily, and no four individuals are pairwise distinct.

arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), from Cian Dorr's observation
arguments.text: The constant maps form one orbit of the symmetry group, so the proposition $C$ that the arrow is constant (for individuals $a,b,c$, the proposition that $a=b=c$) is an atom: it is possible, and a symmetric proposition contains all the constant maps or none. It is not a strong world. At a constant map $c_i$, every composite $l\circ c_i$ is constant, so $C$ transported there is $\top$; and $\top$ there lies neither below the proposition $P$ that the arrow is a permutation nor below its negation, both being possible. As an atom, $C$ has no possible proposition below it but itself, so no strong world lies below it, and the type-$t$ Strong Leibniz Biconditionals fail.

conditions.text: The model is an action model (Classicism, Appendix D), or an intensional action model in the sense of Dorr's draft (Boolean Completeness does not imply Rigid Comprehension), with a single object.

The model is extensionally full at every object: every set of tuples from the domains at an object is the extension, at the identity arrow, of an element of the domain of the matching relational type there.
The model is an ideally full action model in which every arrow out of the evaluation object acts surjectively both on the individuals and on the pinning sets (Proposition D.6's hypothesis).
Every constant of Σ is relational, and each denotes the top element of its type.
There is exactly one individual, at every world.
The model is full: at each object, the domain of each relational type contains every intension of that type.
The model is a full action model: an action model (Classicism, Appendix D) that is full at every object.
At every object reachable from the evaluation point, the domain contains every intension whose value at an arrow depends only on the arrow's codomain.
At every object the individuals are the same infinite set, and every arrow acts on them as the identity.
The model's automorphisms carry every individual to every other.
There are finitely many propositions at the evaluation world.

Σ has a designated relational constant $c$ of type $\tau=\bar\sigma t$ denoting $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$, where $a$ is the actual-world proposition, the unique true atom; every other constant, of which there is at least one, is relational and denotes the top element of its type.
The actual-world proposition $a$, the strongest truth, is in the domain; it is necessary at no world, and some arrow does not fix it.
Some world sees no world at which the actual-world proposition is true.
The actual-world proposition $a$ is in the domain and entails every truth, and no world outside $a$ sees a world in $a$.

The model is a one-object action model whose entities are finitely pinned, and there are a finite set $N$, an arrow $i$ and a proposition $q$ in the domain such that $q$ separates two arrows that agree on the range of every arrow agreeing with $i$ on $N$, and the intension $\{\langle r,j\rangle : r\ne q\text{ or }j\text{ disagrees with }i\text{ on }N\}$ is in the domain.

A group $G$ acts on the individuals at the evaluation object, and every element of a relational domain there is symmetric, meaning that $\langle\bar x,h\rangle\in D$ implies $\langle g\cdot\bar x,g\circ h\rangle\in D$ whenever $g\in G$ and $g\circ h$ is an arrow, and is pinned down by a finite set of individuals, its extension at an arrow depending only on the arrow's values there.
The individuals at the evaluation object are those the construction acts on, and the arrows act on them as the construction says.

There are an individual $a$ and a necessarily instantiated property $F$ in the domain such that, for every finite set $N$ of individuals at the evaluation object, some arrow $h$ sends $N\cup\{a\}$ to a single individual $p$, and every individual $y\ne p$ in $F$'s extension at $h$ is moved by a member $\sigma$ of the symmetry group that fixes $p$, with $\sigma\circ h$ again an arrow.

At every object reachable from the evaluation point, the rigid relations of each relational type are exactly the intensions $k\mapsto k\cdot E$, the disjunctions of the haecceities of the members of $E$, for $E$ any set of tuples from the domains there; in particular every such intension is in the domain.
Every arrow out of every object reachable from the evaluation point is an epimorphism (arrows after it that agree after it are equal) and acts surjectively on the individuals.
There are infinitely many individuals at the evaluation world.
There are infinitely many propositions at the evaluation world.
There are finitely many propositions at every object reachable from the evaluation point.
Every arrow out of every object reachable from the evaluation point is invertible.
Every arrow out of the evaluation object has a retraction: an arrow back after which it composes to the identity.
Some arrow out of the evaluation object has no retraction.
Some arrow out of the evaluation object is not its identity.
Some arrow out of the evaluation object is not an epimorphism: two distinct arrows after it agree after it.
Some arrow out of the evaluation object other than its identity has a retraction: an arrow back after which it composes to the identity.
Every arrow $g$ out of the evaluation object has a retraction $r_g$, chosen so that $r_{x\circ g}\circ x=r_g$ for every arrow $x$ after $g$.
For some $n$, the evaluation object has $n$ distinct propositions, while some world after it, and every world after that one, has fewer.
At the evaluation object, and at the target of every arrow out of it, the singleton of the identity arrow is in the domain.
At the evaluation object, and at the target of every arrow out of it, every arrow out of that object has at most one retraction.
Some arrow out of the evaluation object has two retractions that some proposition in the domain at its target separates.
There are pairwise distinct arrows $h_n$ out of the evaluation object, one for each natural number $n$, each with a retraction $r_n$, all given by the construction without choice.

The construction is carried out in ZF together with a countable family $(A_n)_{n\in\omega}$ of nonempty sets of sets of natural numbers that has no choice function ($\neg\mathrm{AC}_\omega(\mathbb R)$).

The construction is carried out in ZF with a countable family $(P_n)_{n\in\omega}$ of pairwise disjoint two-element sets that has no choice function, and every infinite set the construction leaves unspecified is their union.
The construction uses an infinite set that it leaves unspecified: any infinite set will do.

Write an entity of relational type at the evaluation object as its intension $k\mapsto Y_k$ over the arrows $k$ out of it, so that $Y\bar a$ holds at $k$ iff $k\cdot\bar a\in Y_k$; $Y$ is pinned down by a finite set $N$ of the points the arrows act on when $Y_k=Y_{k^{\prime}}$ for any arrows $k,k^{\prime}$ agreeing on $N$. Every entity in a domain is pinned down by a finite set, in the sense that $k\cdot x=k^{\prime}\cdot x$ for arrows agreeing on it, and the domain of each relational type at the evaluation object holds every intension pinned down by a finite set (in a symmetric model, every symmetric one).

For every arrow $h$ out of the evaluation object and finite sets $N,S$ there is a finite $N^{\prime\prime}\supseteq S$ such that, whenever $k^{\prime}$ agrees with $k\circ h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$, for every finite $M$ some arrows $k^{\prime\prime}$ agreeing with $h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$ have $j\circ k^{\prime\prime}$ agreeing with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$.

For every arrow $k$ out of the evaluation object and finite sets $N,T$ of the points the arrows act on, there are arrows $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$ and $\sigma$ such that $k^{\prime}\circ\sigma$ is the identity on $T$.
The arrows out of the evaluation object are exactly the surjections of the set of points it acts on.

Every arrow out of every object reachable from the evaluation point is an epimorphism: arrows after it that agree after it are equal. (Unlike epic-arrows, nothing is required of its action on the individuals.)
Out of every object reachable from the evaluation point, the identity is the only invertible arrow.
Some arrow out of the evaluation object has a retraction but is not invertible.
Out of every object reachable from the evaluation point, every arrow that has a retraction is invertible.

For every finite set $N$ of individuals at the evaluation object there is a finite $N^\prime\supseteq N$ such that every arrow $u$ out of that object for which some arrow $x$ makes $x\circ u$ agree with the identity on $N^\prime$ agrees on $N$ with a member of the symmetry group (with the identity, when the model has no symmetry group).
Some invertible arrow out of the evaluation object is not its identity.

general_arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
general_arguments.text: By Proposition D.6.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The finite-support members' citations of Proposition D.6 stated once, then moved to the topic; each model's reason for meeting D.6's hypothesis is under its `meets`.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), answering Cian Dorr’s question whether the failure of BF sharpens to type $t$
general_arguments.text: In a one-object finitely pinned model, BF (type t) fails as soon as there are a finite $N$, an arrow $i$ and a proposition $q$ in the domain that is the transport $i^{\prime}\cdot p=\{k : k\circ i^{\prime}\in p\}$ of no proposition $p$ along any arrow $i^{\prime}$ agreeing with $i$ on $N$: the intension $X:=\{\langle r,j\rangle : r\ne q\text{ or }j\text{ disagrees with }i\text{ on }N\}$, which the condition puts in the domain, contains $\langle i^{\prime}\cdot p,i^{\prime}\rangle$ for every $p$ and $i^{\prime}$, so $\forall p\, .\,\Box Xp$ holds at the identity, and omits $\langle q,i\rangle$, so $\Box\forall p\, .\,Xp$ fails there. Since membership of $k$ in $i^{\prime}\cdot p$ depends only on $k$ restricted to the range of $i^{\prime}$, it suffices that $q$ separate two arrows agreeing on every such range, as the condition provides.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The finite-support group's argument and the symmetric range-gap models' copies stated once for the topic; that $X$ is in the domain (pinned down by $N$, and in a symmetric model symmetric) is now part of each record's reason for meeting transport-gap.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Given $X$ with extension $E$ at the evaluation object, let $Y$ hold at an arrow $g$ of a tuple $\bar b$ at $g$'s target iff $r_g\cdot\bar b\in E$; it is in the domain since the model is full. It is coextensive with $X$, since $r_1=1$. And whether it holds is unchanged along every arrow: at $x\circ g$, of $x\cdot\bar b$, it holds iff $r_{x\circ g}\cdot x\cdot\bar b=r_g\cdot\bar b\in E$. So $Y$ and its negation are persistent. (The retract's own argument of 25 September, generalized.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $(A_n)$ be the family with no choice function. For a set $C$ of natural numbers let $p_C:=\{h_m : m\in C\}$, a proposition at the evaluation object since the model is full; along $h_n$ it becomes $h_n\cdot p_C$, from which $C$ is recovered as $\{m : h_m\circ r_n\in h_n\cdot p_C\}$, since $h_m\circ r_n\circ h_n=h_m$. Intensional Choice at type $t$: let $F$ hold at $h_n$ of the propositions $h_n\cdot p_C$ with $C\in A_n$, and at every other arrow of every proposition. It is in the domain, the model being full, and necessarily instantiated. A $G\le F$ necessarily uniquely instantiated holds at $h_n$ of a single $h_n\cdot p_{C_n}$ with $C_n\in A_n$, and $n\mapsto C_n$ would be a choice function. Relational Choice at types $t$ and $t$: let $U$ relate $p_{\{n\}}$ to each $p_C$ with $C\in A_n$, and every other proposition to every proposition. It is serial, and a functional subrelation would relate each $p_{\{n\}}$ to a single $p_{C_n}$ with $C_n\in A_n$, again a choice function. Both principles therefore fail. (The analysis of 3 October 2026: Intensional Choice is choice over worlds, Relational Choice over the elements of a domain.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
general_arguments.text: For a true $p$, $a\le p$, since $a$ entails every truth. Take $q:=a$ in the definition of $\Box_{\ne}p$: at a world in $a$, $p$ holds; at a world outside $a$, $\Diamond a$ fails. So every truth is $\Box_{\ne}$-necessary.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The finite-support, symmetric and full action models' copies (eight records) stated once for the topic; what varied, why no world outside the actual world sees back into it, is each record's reason for meeting actual-world-isolated.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $p$ be true, pinned by $N$ (and symmetric, when there is a symmetry group), and let $N^\prime$ be as in the condition. Let $q$ be the set of arrows that some arrow composes to agree with the identity on $N^\prime$; it is true, pinned by $N^\prime$, symmetric, and $\Diamond q=q$. By the condition every member of $q$ agrees on $N$ with a symmetry (or the identity), so lies in $p$ together with the identity. Hence $\Box(\Diamond q\to p)$ with $q$ true, i.e. $\Box_{\ne}p$.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $p:=\{1\}$, in the domain since the model is full, and true. Any witness $q$ for $\Box_{\ne}p$ is true, so contains the identity; under an arrow $i\ne 1$ with a retraction $r$, the arrow $r\circ i=1$ makes $\Diamond q$ true, while $p$ is false. So no true $q$ has $\Box(\Diamond q\to p)$. (The surjection monoid's own argument of 23 September, stated once.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: The pure sentence $\exists p_1\ldots p_n\bigwedge_{i<j}p_i\ne p_j$ is true at the evaluation object and false at the world $V$ after it and at every world after $V$; so $\Diamond$ of it is false at $V$, and $\Box\Diamond$ of it false at the evaluation object. (The chain's own argument of 25 September, stated once.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: At a world with $n$ propositions, the numeral $\operatorname{Suc}^n_t\mathbf{0}_t$, a finite cardinality, holds of the universal property of propositions, so the Axiom of Infinity at type $t$ fails there. It fails at every world, so Possible Infinity at type $t$ fails.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: The propositions at the evaluation world are finitely many, and every intension of a full model is present, so the numerals are the finite cardinalities and one of them holds of the universal property of propositions: the Axiom of Infinity at type t fails, as does an instance of the schema.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The copies in three full action models (each with four propositions) stated once for the topic; each record's count is its reason for meeting finitely-many-propositions.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The Axiom of Infinity's failure, which the text states, recorded as a verdict of its own, so that it is certified without the result that the Axiom implies the schema.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: In a full model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain, and with it as witness $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ holds at the identity iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of the evaluation object (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible); full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. A non-identity invertible arrow lies outside the true proposition $\{1\}$, which is therefore not 5-necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: In a full action model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain at every object. Taking it as the witness, $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains every arrow out of that object with a retraction (these are the arrows at which $\Diamond\{1\}$ holds), and $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of it (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible). Full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. With only identities invertible, $\Box_5$ is the identity operator at every reachable object, so every truth is 5-necessary everywhere.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Entailment is inclusion of intensions. Below a relation $Y\ne\bot_\tau$ lies the relation whose intension is the singleton of one of $Y$'s tuples, which is in the domain since the model is full, and is an atom: its only proper part is $\bot_\tau$. Every object being full, the same holds at every arrow, so Atomicity is necessary. The source notes that full models are atomic (p. 61); stated once for the topic, in place of the full models' own arguments.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: The relational half of full-epic-barcan. In an action model BF at a type $\sigma$ holds at a world iff transport along every arrow out of it is onto the entities of type $\sigma$ at its target: if some $z$ there is no transport, the property of being one is necessary of everything at the world and fails of $z$ after the arrow; and if transport is onto, a property necessary of everything holds of every transport. In a full model the transport of intensions along an epimorphism $k$ is onto at every relational type: an intension $Y$ at its target is the transport of $\{\langle\bar a,k\circ m\rangle:\langle\bar a,m\rangle\in Y\}$, since $k\circ m=k\circ m'$ only if $m=m'$. Nothing here concerns the individuals. So BF holds at every relational type at every object reachable from the evaluation point.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: BF holds at an object whose arrows out all act surjectively at every type (Proposition 3.24(ii)). In a full model the transport of intensions along an epimorphism $k$ is onto: an intension $Y$ at its target is the transport of $\{\langle\bar a,k\circ m\rangle : \langle\bar a,m\rangle\in Y\}$, since $k\circ m=k\circ m'$ only if $m=m'$; and on the individuals the arrows are onto by the condition. So BF holds at every object reachable from the evaluation point, and BF is necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Given $X$ of type $\tau$ at an object $W$, let $Y$ be the relation whose extension at an arrow $i$ out of $W$ is $X$'s extension at $W$ transported along $i$, which is in the domain since the model is full. It is coextensive with $X$. It is persistent, since its extension at $i\circ j$ is its extension at $i$ transported along $j$. And it is inextensible: if $\Box X'$ holds at $i$ of everything $Y$ holds of there, then at $i\circ j$ everything $Y$ holds of is the transport along $j$ of something $Y$ holds of at $i$, of which $X'$ then holds. Every object being full, the same holds at every arrow, so Rigid Comprehension is necessary. The source notes that full models satisfy it (p. 61); stated once for the topic, in place of the full models' own arguments.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: The Infinity schema holds, there being $n$ distinct individuals for every $n$. For the Axiom: by extensional fullness the domain has a property of cardinalities true of $Z$ exactly when every property $Z$ holds of has a finite extension. It holds of $\mathbf{0}_e$, which holds only of empty properties, and passes from $Y$ to $\operatorname{Suc}_e Y$, which holds of $F$ only if $Y$ holds of $F$ less one of its instances. So every finite cardinality has it, and none holds of the universal property, whose extension is infinite.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: As for individuals (the argument infinitely-many-individuals), at type $t$: the Infinity schema holds, and by extensional fullness the property of cardinalities that hold only of properties with finite extensions is in the domain, has every finite cardinality, and excludes those holding of the universal property of propositions, whose extension is infinite.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
general_arguments.text: At type $e$. Let $F$ and $a$ be as the condition gives them, and suppose $G\le F$ is necessarily uniquely instantiated. $G$ is in the domain, so it is symmetric and pinned down by a finite set, which we may take to contain $a$; call it $N$. Let $h$ be the arrow the condition gives for $N$. Then $G_h=\{y\}$ for some $y$ in $F_h$. If $\sigma$ in the symmetry group fixes $p$, then $\sigma\circ h$ agrees with $h$ on $N$, so $G_{\sigma\circ h}=G_h$ by pinning, while symmetry gives $G_{\sigma\circ h}=\{\sigma y\}$. So no symmetry fixing $p$ moves $y$, and by the condition $y=p$. Each model's witness takes $F$ with $p$ outside its extension at $h$, a contradiction. $\Box$Intensional Choice fails with it, by T.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Recorded from the collapse lemma deferred in extraction.md on 3 October until the model records' new format landed (not yet checked by a human). It needs the individuals the construction gives. Not covered: the qualitative-links model, whose arrows preserve a ternary relation and so cannot send everything to one point, and the qualitative-contrast model, whose arrows are bijections and where Intensional Choice holds.

revisions.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Moved from the group symmetric-ideally-full to the topic, so that the symmetry-constrained full models use it too: in those models every intension is pinned down by the finite set of all individuals, and the collapses are the constant maps. The group's `when: individuals: base` is now the condition construction-individuals, met by that parameter value.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: At an object reachable from the evaluation point the propositions are all the sets of arrows out of it, so there are finitely many arrows out. A necessarily instantiated $F$ there assigns to each of them a nonempty set, and a finite family of nonempty sets has a choice function without the axiom of choice; the intension holding at each arrow of the chosen member alone is in the domain, the model being full, lies below $F$ and is necessarily uniquely instantiated. So Intensional Choice holds at every reachable object, at every type. (The finite-germ argument of the 3 October 2026 analysis, for full models; with choice the well-ordering argument gives the same.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's suggestion
general_arguments.text: For each object $U$ and type $\sigma$ fix a well-ordering $<_U$ of the domain $D^\sigma_U$, and let $W$ be the intension of type $\sigma\to\sigma\to t$ with $W(h):={<_{\operatorname{cod}h}}$. Its value depends only on the arrow's codomain, so by the condition it is in the domain, and at every world its extension well-orders that world's type-$\sigma$ domain. Given $F$ with $\Box\exists x\, .\,Fx$, put $G:=\lambda x\, .\,Fx\land\forall y\, .\,(Fy\to\neg Wyx)$, the $W$-least $F$. It is definable from $F$ and $W$, so in the domain; $G\le F$, and its extension at every arrow is the singleton of the least element of $F$'s. So Intensional Choice holds, and the same at every reachable object gives $\Box$Intensional Choice. Cian Dorr's observation that such models are qualitatively full, made precise.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Every arrow's action is a bijection at every type, so ND and BF hold at every object reachable from the evaluation point (Proposition 3.24(i) and (ii)), and are necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: At any reachable object $W$, let $U$ be a serial relation in the domain there. Using the axiom of choice, pick for each $x$ a $y$ with $(x,y)$ in the extension of $U$ at the identity, and let $S$ be the intension whose value at every arrow $W\to W$ is the graph of this choice and whose value at arrows with any other codomain is empty; it depends only on the codomain, so the condition puts it in the domain, and at the identity it is a functional subrelation of $U$. Likewise a set of representatives of an equivalence relation at $W$, made into such an intension, is a transversal. Since $W$ was any reachable object, both principles hold at every world.

general_arguments.by: Andrew Bacon and Cian Dorr
general_arguments.text: Closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow (§3.5, p. 58). With a single object, a proposition fixed by every arrow contains every arrow if it contains the identity and no arrow otherwise, so a true closed pure sentence is necessary: the source's one-object No Pure Contingency observation (p. 79), applied to each closed instance.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Moved from the group finite-support-one-object to the topic, for every one-object action model; the reason the source's observation holds is spelled out in place of "Boxed positive flags use the source’s explicit one-object No Pure Contingency observation, applied separately to each closed instance."

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $k$ out of the evaluation object have distinct $j\ne j^{\prime}$ after it with $j\circ k= j^{\prime}\circ k$. The proposition $\{j\circ k\}$, in the domain since the model is full, is possible, and the only possible proposition below it is itself. It is not a strong world: under $k$ it becomes $\{m : m\circ k=j\circ k\}$, which contains $j$ and $j^{\prime}$, and the proposition $\{j\}$ at $k$'s target, in the domain there, neither contains nor excludes it. So the type-$t$ Strong Leibniz Biconditionals fail. (The idempotent monoid's and the retract's own arguments of 22–23 September, stated once.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: The propositions $\top$ and $\{1\}$ are in the domain, the model being full; they are both true at the evaluation point and differ at the other arrow, so the Fregean Axiom fails.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: No two individuals are distinct, and the numeral $\operatorname{Suc}_e\mathbf{0}_e$ holds of the universal property at type $e$ at every world.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Moved from the group finite-support-one-object to the topic.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic)
general_arguments.text: The truncation of a full action model at any arrow is again a full action model, its domains at the reachable objects being unchanged, and Relational Choice holds in every full model given choice in the metatheory (Classicism, p. 61).

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The two-object full action models' copies stated once for the topic, for every full action model.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: With choice in the metatheory a serial relation has a functional subrelation, and a full model contains every intension, so that subrelation is in the domain; see Classicism, p. 61, on the principles common to full models.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The full action models' copies stated once for the topic.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: The action of an arrow out of the evaluation object is undone by the action of its retraction, so it is injective at every type, and ND holds there (Proposition 3.24(i)).

general_arguments.by: GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), at Cian Dorr's request; checked and recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
general_arguments.text:
Write $F_h$ for the extension of $F$ at the arrow $h$, so $(h\cdot F)_k=F_{kh}$, and $B_N(E)$ as in tame-rigidity-factorizable, whose part (1) is the criterion used throughout: a relation pinned down by $S$ with extension $E$ is weakly rigid iff it equals $B_N(E)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$; Tame Rigidity holds at every type by that argument. Fix a type tuple.
(a) Stable sets. If a set $A$ of argument tuples is closed under the surjections fixing a finite $P$ pointwise, then $B_P(A)$ has extension $A$ and is weakly rigid, hence rigid. Given $Q\supseteq P$ and $l^{\prime}a$ with $l^{\prime}$ agreeing with $l$ on $P$ and $a\in A$ pinned down by $M$, take a surjection $u$ fixing $P$ that sends $M\setminus P$ to distinct fresh points outside $Q$, and a surjection $r$ agreeing with $l$ on $Q$ with $ru=l^{\prime}$ on $M$ (compatible finite prescriptions); then $ua\in A$ and $l^{\prime}a=r(ua)\in B_Q(A)_l$, so $B_P(A)=B_Q(A)$.
(b) Exact images. Let $F$ be weakly rigid, pinned down by $S$, with extension $E$. By weak persistence $uE\subseteq E$ for every surjection $u$ fixing $S$. For any surjection $j$, $F_j=jE$: a member $la$ of $B_S(E)_j$, with $l$ agreeing with $j$ on $S$ and $a\in E$ pinned down by $M$, is $j(ua)$ for a surjection $u$ fixing $S$ with $ju=l$ on $M$, preimages being supplied by the surjectivity of $j$.
(c) Lifting. Let $F$ be rigid, pinned down by $S$, $k$ an arrow, $N\supseteq S$ finite, and $X\le k\cdot F$ rigid, pinned down by $T$, with extension $D$. Extend $k|_N$ to a surjection $j$ whose non-singleton fibres are finitely many and finite (send the points outside $N$ bijectively onto the values not yet taken); then $j\cdot F=k\cdot F$ and $D\subseteq F_j=jE$. Let $P$ be finite, containing $N$, every non-singleton fibre of $j$, and a preimage of each point of $T$, and put $A:=\{a\in E:ja\in D\}$. For a surjection $u$ fixing $P$, $ju$ is constant on the fibres of $j$, so $ju=vj$ for a surjection $v$, which fixes $T$; so $vD\subseteq D$ by the weak persistence and pinning of $X$, and $uE\subseteq E$ by (b); hence $uA\subseteq A$. By (a), $Y:=B_P(A)$ is rigid, $Y\le F$ since $A\subseteq E$ and $P\supseteq S$, and by (b) $(j\cdot Y)_1=jA=D$. Weakly rigid relations with the same extension are identical, so $X=j\cdot Y$ with $j$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$.
(d) The power property of $F$ is persistent, and by (c) its extension at $k$ is contained in $B_N$ of its extension at the identity for every $N\supseteq S$; so it is weakly rigid by the criterion, and rigid by Tame Rigidity. So Rigid Power holds at every type. Nothing about the symmetry group is used beyond its being a group of permutations, and the individuals play no role, so the argument covers every member and variant meeting the conditions.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), 3 October 2026 (full action models); extended by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), 4 October 2026, at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Write $X_0(E)$ for the intension $k\mapsto k\cdot E$. The extension at an arrow $h$ of the power property $\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is the set of rigid $X$ with $X\le h\cdot F$, the bound variable ranging over the domain untransported and the parameter transported. By the condition the rigid relations are the $X_0(E)$, and $X_0(T)\le X_0(S)$ iff $T\subseteq S$; so for rigid $F=X_0(S)$ the power property has extension $\{X_0(T'):T'\subseteq k\cdot S\}$ at $k$, while transporting its extension at the identity along $k$ gives $\{X_0(k\cdot T):T\subseteq S\}$. These coincide, since every $T'\subseteq k\cdot S$ is $k\cdot T$ for $T:=\{s\in S:k\cdot s\in T'\}$. So the power property is itself $X_0$ of its extension, hence rigid, and the same at every reachable object gives the boxed form.

revisions.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The argument deferred in extraction.md on 3 October for the full action models, where every intension is present, stated under the condition it actually uses, which the symmetry-constrained full models also meet.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), on Cian Dorr's request to settle Rigid Rigidity where it was open
general_arguments.text: Fix the type tuple $\bar\sigma$, let $\mathcal R$ be the set of rigid relations of type $\bar\sigma t$, and let $R:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)$, the value of a closed pure term, so fixed by every arrow; in a one-object model its extension at every arrow is $\mathcal R$, and it is pinned down by $\emptyset$. Write $B_N(E)$ as in tame-rigidity-factorizable. By part (1) of that argument at type $(\bar\sigma t)t$, $R$ is weakly rigid iff $\mathcal R=B_N(\mathcal R)_k$ for every arrow $k$ and finite $N$; and since $h\cdot R=R$ for every arrow $h$, part (2) then makes $R$ rigid. The inclusion $B_N(\mathcal R)_k\subseteq\mathcal R$ holds because a transport of a rigid relation is rigid, rigidity being a necessitated condition. For the converse let $Z\in\mathcal R$ be pinned down by $T$, and let $k$ and $N$ be given. The condition gives $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$ and $\sigma$ with $k^{\prime}\circ\sigma$ the identity on $T$. Then $Z^{\prime}:=\sigma\cdot Z$ is rigid, and $k^{\prime}\cdot Z^{\prime}=(k^{\prime}\circ\sigma) \cdot Z=Z$, since $k^{\prime}\circ\sigma$ agrees with the identity on $T$. So $Z\in B_N(\mathcal R)_k$. Hence Rigid Rigidity holds at every type. This is the lifting of Rigid Power at $F:=\top$ by a section of $k$, noted for the symmetric all-surjections model on 9 October; without the condition the lift can still hold through rigid relations that are not transports of $Z$ (for instance the haecceity of any $x$ with $k^{\prime}x=1$ lifts that of $1$), so the condition is sufficient, not necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $h$ out of the evaluation object have retractions $j\ne j^{\prime}$, and let $q$ at $h$'s target contain $j$ but not $j^{\prime}$. A true proposition $p$ contains the identity, so under $h$ it becomes a proposition containing $j$ and $j^{\prime}$, since $j\circ h=j^{\prime}\circ h=1$. That proposition lies neither below $q$ nor below $\neg q$, so $p$ is not a strong world. No true proposition is.

general_arguments.by: Cian Dorr (observation); recorded by Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)
general_arguments.text: Each constant of Σ denotes what the closed pure term $\top_\tau$ of its type denotes, so a closed sentence of the language of Σ denotes what the pure sentence with $\top_\tau$ in place of each constant denotes; if true it is necessary by No Pure Contingency, which holds here. So No Contingency (signature Σ) holds, and B for sentences of Σ with it: a true Σ-sentence is necessary, hence necessarily possible.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The argument sigma-single-top, for Σ a single constant of type $t$ denoting $\top$, stated for every interpretation of Σ by top elements, now that such interpretations have no individual constants. It replaces that argument and nc-sigma-homogeneous, which reached the same verdicts through an individual constant when the model's automorphisms carry every individual to every other. With an individual constant and no such automorphisms the verdicts were unknown in 19 models, and nowhere did the individual constants settle a verdict differently.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr’s request
general_arguments.text: Let $c\in\Sigma$ have relational type $\tau$, so $c=\top_\tau$ necessarily. Witnessed Possibility fails for the pure formula $x\ne\top_\tau$, witnessed by $\bot_\tau$ but impossible of $c$; Separated Structure fails since $\lambda x\, .\,x$ and $\lambda x\, .\,\top_\tau$ agree on $c$ and differ; Independence (signature Σ) fails since $c$ denotes what the closed pure term $\top_\tau$ denotes; Distinctness Maximalism (signature Σ) fails since $c=\top_\tau$ is a true identity that C(Σ) does not prove.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Moved from the group finite-support-one-object to the topic; it uses nothing about the model.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr’s request
general_arguments.text: B for sentences of Σ fails: the Σ-sentence $\forall\bar x\, .\,c\bar x$ denotes $a$, which is true, and under an arrow from which no world in $a$ is accessible $\Diamond a$ is false, so $\Box\Diamond a$ fails.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The B clause of the records' Σ-as-true-atom argument, stated once for the topic.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr’s request
general_arguments.text: No Contingency (signature Σ) fails, since the Σ-sentence $\forall\bar x\, .\,c\bar x$ denotes $a$, true and contingent; Witnessed Possibility fails for the pure formula $x=\top_\tau$, witnessed by $\top_\tau$, since $\Diamond(c=\top_\tau)$ is $\Diamond\Box a$ and $a$ is necessary at no world; Separated Structure fails with it, being equivalent to Possibly Witnessed Possibility; Independence (signature Σ) and Distinctness Maximalism (signature Σ) fail through the other relational constants: such a constant $c'$ of type $\tau'$ denotes what the closed pure term $\top_{\tau'}$ denotes, and $c'=\top_{\tau'}$ is a true identity that C(Σ) does not prove. The designated constant refutes neither: closed pure terms denote entities fixed by every arrow (Classicism, §3.5, p. 58), whereas some arrow does not fix $a$, so no closed pure term denotes $\lambda\bar x\, .\,a$.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The verbatim copies in ten records (finite-support, symmetric and full action models) stated once for the topic. Its B clause is now sigma-true-atom-b, which needs an arrow from which the actual world is out of reach. "$a$ is fixed by no arrow but the identity" became "some arrow does not fix $a$": in a symmetric model the actual-world proposition is the symmetry group, which its members fix, and the conclusion needs only the weaker claim.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: At type $e$. The individuals, which every arrow fixes, are an unspecified infinite set, so here the union $D=\bigcup_n P_n$. Let $F$ hold at $h_n$ of the members of $P_n$, and at every other arrow of every individual. It is in the domain, the model being full, and necessarily instantiated. A $G\le F$ necessarily uniquely instantiated holds at $h_n$ of a single member of $P_n$, and $n\mapsto$ that member would be a choice function for the socks. (The witness of the 3 October 2026 analysis, with the numbered arrows in place of the transpositions of the pairs.)

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: At type $e$. The individuals, which every arrow fixes, are an unspecified infinite set, so here the union $D=\bigcup_n P_n$. Let $U$ relate each member of $P_n$ to the members of $P_{n+1}$; it is in the domain, the model being full, and serial. A functional subrelation would send each sock to a sock of the next pair, and iterated from one member of $P_0$ it would choose a sock from every pair.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $V$ be the evaluation object or the target of an arrow out of it, and $w:=\{1_V\}$, in the domain at $V$. It is true at $1_V$. Under an arrow $f$ out of $V$ it becomes $\{k : k\circ f=1_V\}$, the set of retractions of $f$, which has at most one member and so lies below $q$ or below $\neg q$ for every proposition $q$ at $f$'s target. So Strong Actuality holds at $1_V$. A closed sentence holds at an arrow iff it holds at the identity of the arrow's target, so Strong Actuality holds at every world after the evaluation point, and □Strong Actuality holds there.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), on Cian Dorr's request to settle Tame Rigidity where it was open
general_arguments.text: Write $B_N(E)$ for the intension $k\mapsto\bigcup\{k^{\prime}\cdot E:k^{\prime}\text{ agrees with }k \text{ on }N\}$; it is pinned down by $N$, and symmetric when the model is, since the symmetry group consists of arrows and $(gk)\cdot E=g\cdot(k\cdot E)$, so it is in the domain. (1) A relation $Y$ pinned down by $S$, with extension $E$ at the identity, is weakly rigid iff $Y=B_S(E)=B_N(E)$ for every finite $N\supseteq S$: weak persistence gives $k\cdot E\subseteq Y_k$, and with pinning $B_S(E)\subseteq Y$; a domain element $X$ with $\Box X$ true of each member of $E$, pinned down by $N$, contains $B_N(E)$, so weak inextensibility says exactly that $Y\subseteq B_N(E)$ for every finite $N$, and $B_N(E)\subseteq B_S(E)$ for $N\supseteq S$. (2) Rigidity is (1) at every world: for each arrow $h$, $h\cdot Y$, with $(h\cdot Y)_k=Y_{kh}$, must satisfy $k\cdot Y_h\subseteq Y_{kh}\subseteq B_N(Y_h)_k$ for all $k$ and finite $N$. (3) Let $Y$ be weakly rigid. Persistence at $h$: $k\cdot Y_h=\bigcup\{(kk^{\prime\prime})\cdot E:k^{\prime\prime}\text{ agrees with }h\text{ on }S\}\subseteq B_S(E)_{kh}=Y_{kh}$. Inextensibility at $h$: given $N$, take $N^{\prime\prime}$ from the condition. By (1), $Y_{kh}=B_{N^{\prime\prime}}(E)_{kh}$, so a member of it is $k^{\prime}\cdot e$ with $e\in E$, pinned down by some finite $M$, and $k^{\prime}$ agreeing with $kh$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$. The condition gives $k^{\prime\prime}$ agreeing with $h$ on $N^{\prime\prime}$ and $j$ agreeing with $k$ on $N$ with $jk^{\prime\prime}$ agreeing with $k^{\prime}$ on $M$, so $k^{\prime}\cdot e=j\cdot(k^{\prime\prime}\cdot e)$, where $k^{\prime\prime}\cdot e\in B_{N^{\prime\prime}}(E)_h=Y_h$; hence $k^{\prime}\cdot e\in B_N(Y_h)_k$. So every weakly rigid relation, at every type, is rigid. With No Pure Contingency, which holds in one-object models, the map's results give $\Box$Tame Rigidity.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), on Cian Dorr's question whether the failure of Boolean Completeness at type $t$ refutes its countable form here
general_arguments.text: The natural numbers are the finite cardinalities at type $e$ (Background, after Goodsell), and with a single individual there are three: $\mathbf{0}_e$, true of the empty property; $\operatorname{Suc}_e\mathbf{0}_e$, true of the universal one; and the empty cardinality, which is $\operatorname{Suc}_e$ of the second and of itself. By extensional fullness the property of being one of these three is in the domain, so it bounds natural numberhood. A countable property therefore has at most three members in its extension, and their join is its least upper bound.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Moved from the group finite-support-one-object to the topic.

withdrawn.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
withdrawn.reason: Countable Boolean Completeness now measures countability at every type, not only by the finite cardinalities of individuals. The argument shows only the instance counting at $e$; at a type with infinitely many entities a countable property may have infinitely many instances, so the verdict no longer follows.

general_arguments.by: Cian Dorr (observation); recorded by Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), on a question of Zachary Goodsell, after an observation of Christopher Sun
general_arguments.text: For an equivalence relation at the evaluation point, a transversal of its extension there, chosen in the metatheory, is by extensional fullness the extension of an element of the domain; the equivalence and transversal conditions are unboxed.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: The Relational Choice and Transversal Choice arguments merged into one, stated for every extensionally full model.

revisions.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
revisions.note: Moved from the group finite-support-one-object to the topic. Its first sentence, deriving extensional fullness from ideal fullness, is now the group's reason for meeting extensionally-full.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: In a full action model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain at every object. Taking it as the witness, $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains every arrow out of that object with a retraction (these are the arrows at which $\Diamond\{1\}$ holds), and $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of it (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible). Full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. Let $u$ have a retraction but no inverse. The true proposition $\{1\}$ excludes $u$, so it is not ND-necessary, while every invertible arrow is the identity or excluded from no such test: $\{1\}$ is two-hat necessary iff no non-identity arrow is invertible, and in any case the proposition $\{1\}\cup\{\text{invertible arrows}\}$ is in the domain, true, two-hat necessary and not ND-necessary.

general_arguments.by: Claude Fable 5.1 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: In a full action model the actual-world proposition $\{1\}$ is in the domain at every object. Taking it as the witness, $\Box_{\ne}p$ holds at an identity iff $p$ contains every arrow out of that object with a retraction (these are the arrows at which $\Diamond\{1\}$ holds), and $\hat{\hat\Box}p$ iff $p$ contains every invertible arrow out of it (an arrow lies in $\hat\Diamond\{1\}$ iff some retraction of it has a retraction, i.e. iff it is invertible). Full models satisfy necessary Actuality, so $\Box_5=\hat{\hat\Box}$ by Proposition D21 of The Bounds of Possibility. When every retracted arrow is invertible, the two boxes coincide at every reachable object, so $\Box_{\ne}=\hat{\hat\Box}$.

general_arguments.by: Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), at Cian Dorr's direction
general_arguments.text: Let $k$ out of the evaluation object have no retraction. The propositions $\bot$ and $\{1\}$ are in the domain, the model being full, and $k$ transports both to $\bot$: no arrow $m$ after $k$ has $m\circ k=1$. So $k$'s action at type $t$ is not injective, and ND fails there (Proposition 3.24(i)).

data.notes: Does adding Boolean Completeness to Relational Choice suffice for Transversal Choice in C? The question without Boolean Completeness is recorded separately. No proof was supplied. A proof of this implication, or a model of C satisfying both premises and failing Transversal Choice, would settle this conjecture.

The restriction of the signature schema to pure P gives ◇≠P for every pure P consistent with Max(C(Σ)); the pure schema asks for every pure P consistent with Max(C). So the arrow holds iff Max(C(Σ)), equivalently Max(C) plus Separated Structure, is conservative over Max(C) for pure sentences: every pure sentence consistent with Pure Maximalist Classicism must remain consistent when Separated Structure is added. Adjoining constants is conservative for C, which is why Possibility Maximalism (signature Σ) implies Possibility Maximalism (pure), but for the maximalization a model of Max(C) + P would need its constants interpreted so that each realizes every consistent role at some truncation, which is not automatic. A proof of that conservativity, or a pure sentence consistent with Max(C) but not with Max(C) + Separated Structure, would settle it.

Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 11 October 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. The proof of Theorem 8.2 in the book has a gap, found while formalizing it in Lean and confirmed by Cian Dorr; the write-up sets out the book's argument with the gap marked. The argument proves $\forall p\,.\,Wp\to p=r$ at the evaluation point and then boxes it as following "from necessary assumptions". But step (i), that a $W$-proposition $p$ falls under some member of $H$ at every world, uses the claim that the world property $U=\lambda q\,.\,v\land q=p$ is $H$ because it is a world property accessible to $W$; that holds at the evaluation point, where $H$ is coextensive with the accessible world properties, but at another world $H$ is known only to be rigid, and need not contain the world properties built there from that world's $v$ and $p$. The step is needed exactly at such worlds, since $W$ may have no actual instance. Boxing Rigid Comprehension does not obviously help, since $r$ must be defined from a single actual $H$. What would settle the conjecture: a repair of step (i), or a model of C with □Strong Leibniz and Rigid Comprehension in which BF fails at some relational type. No recorded model refutes it, and without this record the map does not derive it. With □Rigid Comprehension and Rigid Power in place of Rigid Comprehension the conclusion holds (strong-leibniz-necessary-rigid-comprehension-and-rigid-power-imply-bf-relational, Cian Dorr), so a countermodel must fail one of those. The converse half of Theorem 8.2, atomicity-and-bf-relational-imply-strong-leibniz and its boxed form, is unaffected.

The converse of weakly-rigid-power-implies-tame-rigidity and weakly-rigid-power-implies-rigid-power. With □Tame Rigidity in place of Tame Rigidity it is proved (necessary-tame-rigidity-and-rigid-power-imply-weakly-rigid-power). The unboxed argument fails at weak inextensibility: for weakly rigid $F$, $P_F:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is weakly persistent, but $Z:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ satisfies $\forall X\, .\,P_FX\to\Box ZX$, so the weak inextensibility of $P_F$ requires $P_F\le Z$, which is Tame Rigidity below $F$ at every accessible world. Weakly Rigid Power implies □Tame Rigidity at type $t$ (and, with BF, at every type: barcan-and-weakly-rigid-power-imply-necessary-tame-rigidity), so the conjecture would follow from Tame Rigidity + Rigid Power ⇒ □Tame Rigidity, and a countermodel must satisfy Tame Rigidity and Rigid Power while failing □Tame Rigidity at type $t$. No recorded model yet separates Tame Rigidity from □Tame Rigidity.

Does Relational Choice alone give a transversal for every equivalence relation? Christopher Sun observed that the literature claims this without proof. The converse is recorded. The quotient argument chooses from each cell $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$ and needs the cells of two members of one class to be the same property; in C that is necessary coextension, and the hypothesis gives actual coextension only. No definable substitute for the cell helps, since an operation definable from $R$ identifies $x$ with $x'$ only when they are necessarily indiscernible with respect to $R$. A Zermelo-style well-ordering argument breaks at the same point: coextensive but distinct stages receive different chosen elements. The expectation is that the implication fails. What would settle it: a proof that uses the chosen relation to break the symmetry between coextensive cells, or a model of C with Relational Choice that is not extensionally full at its evaluation point. Every recorded model of Relational Choice is extensionally full there, in that every set of tuples from the domains is the extension of a rigid element, and that fullness verifies Transversal Choice by the same metatheoretic choice, so none separates the two. Symmetric Henkin models in the Fraenkel–Mostowski style cannot separate them either; see the write-up.
Update of 28 September 2026: Christopher Sun showed on 26 September that Transversal Choice is equivalent to Relational Choice together with Transversal (transversal-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice), so this question is equivalent to whether Relational Choice implies Transversal. Anything that implies Transversal, such as Actuality, closes the gap.

Cian Dorr proposed it on 10 October 2026, with an argument that assumed rigidity is closed under conjunction. It is not, in C: if $x\ne y$ but possibly $x=y$, the conjunction of their haecceities is persistent but not weakly inextensible, since weak inextensibility would require $\Box\,x\ne y$. Under □ND conjunctions of rigid relations are rigid and the argument goes through, but C5 already gives □Rigid Power. A countermodel must therefore have contingent identity at some accessible world: a rigid $Y$ not below a rigid $X$ that comes below it at an accessible world by identifications, without becoming identical there to any rigid subrelation of $X$ at the evaluation point. With the recorded results, the conjecture would make Rigid Rigidity equivalent to □BF + Rigid Power, and Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity equivalent to BF + Weakly Rigid Power. Since Rigid Rigidity implies its necessitation, the conjecture is equivalent to Rigid Rigidity ⇒ □Rigid Power.

Conjectured by Cian Dorr, 14 October 2026. Actuality suffices (see the proved result), and so does Vicinity with BF at type $t$. Without BF, the two places where the Actuality proof uses the atom resist the Vicinity substitution: the characterization $\hat{\hat\Box}p\leftrightarrow\Box(\hat\Diamond w\to p)$ needs $\Box(\hat\Diamond w\to\hat\Diamond q)$ for an arbitrary true $q$, which is B for $\Box_{\ne}$ at $q$; and step 1 of Proposition D19 applies the atom to the truth $\forall z\,\Box(\hat\Diamond w\to Yz)$, which is ND-necessary only if $\Box_{\ne}$ already commutes with $\forall z$. A countermodel would need Vicinity without Actuality at a world where the two-hat cluster is non-principal; the paired-individuals and star-graph models fail Vicinity.

Equivalent to the claim that a finite count of propositions is necessary whenever it is true. It holds with No Pure Contingency and with BF (type $t$), by the recorded results. If some finite $Z$ holds of $\lambda p\, .\,\top$ then every proposition is one of finitely many, and NI carries each identity across, but collecting them under a box is an instance of BF at type $t$, which C does not prove. A proof would need to bypass that; a countermodel would need a world with finitely many propositions that can see one with more, and must violate both BF (type $t$) and No Pure Contingency.

Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 28 September 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. The source's proof (Proposition 2.11, note 42) has two gaps, found that day by an agent working in the Lean-Classicism formalization project; the write-up sets out the paper's argument with the gaps marked. (a) Part (iv) of note 42 boxes a claim that holds pointwise in the object variables by BF, where □BF would be needed. Cian Dorr agreed. (b) The same part's "without loss of generality" step replaces the atom $w'$ by $w''$, the greatest lower bound of the propositions $p$ with $w\le(p=w')$. The proof then needs $w\le(w''=w')$, so that $w''$ is still possible and below $X^*z\land\neg Yz$ where $w$ holds; nothing in the premises gives this, and □BF does not help. A propositional structure in which that step fails is sketched in the project's VERIFICATION.md; it has not been extended to a model of C with all the premises, so it shows that the step needs an argument, not that the proposition is false. What is proved there: Actuality, Boolean Completeness and BF (at the relevant types), together with a restriction principle, give Rigid Comprehension with the paper's witness $X^*$. The restriction principle says that for all $p,q$ there is an $r$ with $p\le(r=q)$ such that $r\le s$ whenever $p\le(q\le s)$. It holds in C5, with $r:=q\land\Diamond p$. Restructured this way, gap (a) disappears, and gap (b) becomes the question whether the premises here give the restriction principle. What would settle the conjecture: a derivation of the restriction principle, or another argument, from boxed Atomicity, Boolean Completeness and BF; or a model of C with those three principles that fails Rigid Comprehension. The source's first cross-reference to Proposition 2.6 was replaced in the earlier transcription by Proposition 2.7; the statement and premises are unchanged.

Refuted, 1 October 2026: the model ultralimit-fork, from Branden Fitelson (with Claude and GPT-6 Astra), satisfies Classicism, □Atomicity, □Boolean Completeness, □BF and □Actuality, and fails Rigid Comprehension at type $t\to t$. It extends the propositional structure mentioned above to a model of C with all the premises, so gap (b) is a genuine gap. The record stays conjectured, as the map's convention requires; the model is the refuting evidence. Gap-free in the end is part (ii), which gets Actuality: Atomicity (type $t$) and Weak Inextensible Comprehension imply Actuality (atomicity-t-and-weakly-inextensible-comprehension-imply-actuality), and Boolean Completeness implies Weak Inextensible Comprehension.

Equivalent to the claim that a finite count of individuals is necessary whenever it is true. It holds with No Pure Contingency and with BF, by the recorded results. A countermodel would need a world with finitely many individuals that can see one with more, and must violate both BF at type $e$ and No Pure Contingency; the coalesced sums on the map do not supply one, since their roots have infinitely many individuals.

Weakly Rigid Power implies □Tame Rigidity at type $t$ (and, with BF, at every type: barcan-and-weakly-rigid-power-imply-necessary-tame-rigidity), so the conjecture would follow from Tame Rigidity + Rigid Power ⇒ □Tame Rigidity, and a countermodel must satisfy Tame Rigidity and Rigid Power while failing □Tame Rigidity at type $t$. No recorded model yet separates Tame Rigidity from □Tame Rigidity.

conjectures.notes: Conjectured by Cian Dorr, 14 October 2026. Actuality suffices (see the proved result), and so does Vicinity with BF at type $t$. Without BF, the two places where the Actuality proof uses the atom resist the Vicinity substitution: the characterization $\hat{\hat\Box}p\leftrightarrow\Box(\hat\Diamond w\to p)$ needs $\Box(\hat\Diamond w\to\hat\Diamond q)$ for an arbitrary true $q$, which is B for $\Box_{\ne}$ at $q$; and step 1 of Proposition D19 applies the atom to the truth $\forall z\,\Box(\hat\Diamond w\to Yz)$, which is ND-necessary only if $\Box_{\ne}$ already commutes with $\forall z$. A countermodel would need Vicinity without Actuality at a world where the two-hat cluster is non-principal; the paired-individuals and star-graph models fail Vicinity.

Does Relational Choice alone give a transversal for every equivalence relation? Christopher Sun observed that the literature claims this without proof. The converse is recorded. The quotient argument chooses from each cell $\lambda z\, .\,(Rx)z$ and needs the cells of two members of one class to be the same property; in C that is necessary coextension, and the hypothesis gives actual coextension only. No definable substitute for the cell helps, since an operation definable from $R$ identifies $x$ with $x'$ only when they are necessarily indiscernible with respect to $R$. A Zermelo-style well-ordering argument breaks at the same point: coextensive but distinct stages receive different chosen elements. The expectation is that the implication fails. What would settle it: a proof that uses the chosen relation to break the symmetry between coextensive cells, or a model of C with Relational Choice that is not extensionally full at its evaluation point. Every recorded model of Relational Choice is extensionally full there, in that every set of tuples from the domains is the extension of a rigid element, and that fullness verifies Transversal Choice by the same metatheoretic choice, so none separates the two. Symmetric Henkin models in the Fraenkel–Mostowski style cannot separate them either; see the write-up.
Update of 28 September 2026: Christopher Sun showed on 26 September that Transversal Choice is equivalent to Relational Choice together with Transversal (transversal-and-relational-choice-imply-transversal-choice), so this question is equivalent to whether Relational Choice implies Transversal. Anything that implies Transversal, such as Actuality, closes the gap.

The restriction of the signature schema to pure P gives ◇≠P for every pure P consistent with Max(C(Σ)); the pure schema asks for every pure P consistent with Max(C). So the arrow holds iff Max(C(Σ)), equivalently Max(C) plus Separated Structure, is conservative over Max(C) for pure sentences: every pure sentence consistent with Pure Maximalist Classicism must remain consistent when Separated Structure is added. Adjoining constants is conservative for C, which is why Possibility Maximalism (signature Σ) implies Possibility Maximalism (pure), but for the maximalization a model of Max(C) + P would need its constants interpreted so that each realizes every consistent role at some truncation, which is not automatic. A proof of that conservativity, or a pure sentence consistent with Max(C) but not with Max(C) + Separated Structure, would settle it.

The converse of weakly-rigid-power-implies-tame-rigidity and weakly-rigid-power-implies-rigid-power. With □Tame Rigidity in place of Tame Rigidity it is proved (necessary-tame-rigidity-and-rigid-power-imply-weakly-rigid-power). The unboxed argument fails at weak inextensibility: for weakly rigid $F$, $P_F:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{WeaklyRigid}(X)\land X\le F$ is weakly persistent, but $Z:=\lambda X\, .\,\operatorname{Rigid}(X)\land X\le F$ satisfies $\forall X\, .\,P_FX\to\Box ZX$, so the weak inextensibility of $P_F$ requires $P_F\le Z$, which is Tame Rigidity below $F$ at every accessible world. Weakly Rigid Power implies □Tame Rigidity at type $t$ (and, with BF, at every type: barcan-and-weakly-rigid-power-imply-necessary-tame-rigidity), so the conjecture would follow from Tame Rigidity + Rigid Power ⇒ □Tame Rigidity, and a countermodel must satisfy Tame Rigidity and Rigid Power while failing □Tame Rigidity at type $t$. No recorded model yet separates Tame Rigidity from □Tame Rigidity.

Cian Dorr proposed it on 10 October 2026, with an argument that assumed rigidity is closed under conjunction. It is not, in C: if $x\ne y$ but possibly $x=y$, the conjunction of their haecceities is persistent but not weakly inextensible, since weak inextensibility would require $\Box\,x\ne y$. Under □ND conjunctions of rigid relations are rigid and the argument goes through, but C5 already gives □Rigid Power. A countermodel must therefore have contingent identity at some accessible world: a rigid $Y$ not below a rigid $X$ that comes below it at an accessible world by identifications, without becoming identical there to any rigid subrelation of $X$ at the evaluation point. With the recorded results, the conjecture would make Rigid Rigidity equivalent to □BF + Rigid Power, and Weakly Rigid Weak Rigidity equivalent to BF + Weakly Rigid Power. Since Rigid Rigidity implies its necessitation, the conjecture is equivalent to Rigid Rigidity ⇒ □Rigid Power.

Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 28 September 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. The source's proof (Proposition 2.11, note 42) has two gaps, found that day by an agent working in the Lean-Classicism formalization project; the write-up sets out the paper's argument with the gaps marked. (a) Part (iv) of note 42 boxes a claim that holds pointwise in the object variables by BF, where □BF would be needed. Cian Dorr agreed. (b) The same part's "without loss of generality" step replaces the atom $w'$ by $w''$, the greatest lower bound of the propositions $p$ with $w\le(p=w')$. The proof then needs $w\le(w''=w')$, so that $w''$ is still possible and below $X^*z\land\neg Yz$ where $w$ holds; nothing in the premises gives this, and □BF does not help. A propositional structure in which that step fails is sketched in the project's VERIFICATION.md; it has not been extended to a model of C with all the premises, so it shows that the step needs an argument, not that the proposition is false. What is proved there: Actuality, Boolean Completeness and BF (at the relevant types), together with a restriction principle, give Rigid Comprehension with the paper's witness $X^*$. The restriction principle says that for all $p,q$ there is an $r$ with $p\le(r=q)$ such that $r\le s$ whenever $p\le(q\le s)$. It holds in C5, with $r:=q\land\Diamond p$. Restructured this way, gap (a) disappears, and gap (b) becomes the question whether the premises here give the restriction principle. What would settle the conjecture: a derivation of the restriction principle, or another argument, from boxed Atomicity, Boolean Completeness and BF; or a model of C with those three principles that fails Rigid Comprehension. The source's first cross-reference to Proposition 2.6 was replaced in the earlier transcription by Proposition 2.7; the statement and premises are unchanged.

Refuted, 1 October 2026: the model ultralimit-fork, from Branden Fitelson (with Claude and GPT-6 Astra), satisfies Classicism, □Atomicity, □Boolean Completeness, □BF and □Actuality, and fails Rigid Comprehension at type $t\to t$. It extends the propositional structure mentioned above to a model of C with all the premises, so gap (b) is a genuine gap. The record stays conjectured, as the map's convention requires; the model is the refuting evidence. Gap-free in the end is part (ii), which gets Actuality: Atomicity (type $t$) and Weak Inextensible Comprehension imply Actuality (atomicity-t-and-weakly-inextensible-comprehension-imply-actuality), and Boolean Completeness implies Weak Inextensible Comprehension.

Does adding Boolean Completeness to Relational Choice suffice for Transversal Choice in C? The question without Boolean Completeness is recorded separately. No proof was supplied. A proof of this implication, or a model of C satisfying both premises and failing Transversal Choice, would settle this conjecture.

Downgraded from proved to conjectured on 11 October 2026, at Cian Dorr's request. The proof of Theorem 8.2 in the book has a gap, found while formalizing it in Lean and confirmed by Cian Dorr; the write-up sets out the book's argument with the gap marked. The argument proves $\forall p\,.\,Wp\to p=r$ at the evaluation point and then boxes it as following "from necessary assumptions". But step (i), that a $W$-proposition $p$ falls under some member of $H$ at every world, uses the claim that the world property $U=\lambda q\,.\,v\land q=p$ is $H$ because it is a world property accessible to $W$; that holds at the evaluation point, where $H$ is coextensive with the accessible world properties, but at another world $H$ is known only to be rigid, and need not contain the world properties built there from that world's $v$ and $p$. The step is needed exactly at such worlds, since $W$ may have no actual instance. Boxing Rigid Comprehension does not obviously help, since $r$ must be defined from a single actual $H$. What would settle the conjecture: a repair of step (i), or a model of C with □Strong Leibniz and Rigid Comprehension in which BF fails at some relational type. No recorded model refutes it, and without this record the map does not derive it. With □Rigid Comprehension and Rigid Power in place of Rigid Comprehension the conclusion holds (strong-leibniz-necessary-rigid-comprehension-and-rigid-power-imply-bf-relational, Cian Dorr), so a countermodel must fail one of those. The converse half of Theorem 8.2, atomicity-and-bf-relational-imply-strong-leibniz and its boxed form, is unaffected.

Equivalent to the claim that a finite count of individuals is necessary whenever it is true. It holds with No Pure Contingency and with BF, by the recorded results. A countermodel would need a world with finitely many individuals that can see one with more, and must violate both BF at type $e$ and No Pure Contingency; the coalesced sums on the map do not supply one, since their roots have infinitely many individuals.
